column2: I think/believe/feel (that) + clause · I do not think/believe + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

State a personal judgment.

1. I think/believe/feel (that) + clause

Usage: State your judgment; think/believe overlap, while feel can emphasize a personal impression. Believe can sound more considered, but none of these words establishes an objective certainty level.
I think the simpler design is easier to maintain.
I believe the simpler design is easier to maintain.
I feel that the team needs more uninterrupted time.

2. I do not think/believe + clause

Usage: Give a negative judgment politely, or say you withhold belief.
I do not think the deadline is realistic.
I do not believe the estimate includes testing.

column2: In my opinion/view, + clause · From my perspective/point of view, + clause · Personally, + clause · As far as I am concerned, + clause · If you ask me, + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Mark a view as your own.

1. In my opinion/view, + clause

Usage: Mark a judgment as your opinion; opinion and view are close alternatives. These expressions mark perspective, not different levels of certainty. Use in my opinion, but from my point of view.
In my opinion, the shorter commute is worth the higher rent.
In my view, the shorter commute is worth the higher rent.

2. From my perspective/point of view, + clause

Usage: Frame the same kind of judgment from your particular standpoint.
From my perspective, the main problem is the lack of clear ownership.
From my point of view, the main problem is the lack of clear ownership.

3. Personally, + clause

Usage: Mark your own preference or judgment.
Personally, I would rather have flexible hours than a private office.

4. As far as I am concerned, + clause

Usage: State your position; this can sound firm when setting a boundary.
As far as I am concerned, the matter is settled.

5. If you ask me, + clause

Usage: Offer a conversational, often frank opinion.
If you ask me, that meeting could have been an email.

column2: I would say + clause · I guess/suppose/imagine + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Offer a tentative judgment.

1. I would say + clause

Usage: Soften an assessment rather than presenting it as certain.
I would say the trial was successful, although we still have some bugs to fix.

2. I guess/suppose/imagine + clause

Usage: Guess/suppose can sound hesitant; imagine can infer someone else's experience. Imagine often infers a situation you have not experienced yourself; tone allows substantial overlap.
I guess we could postpone it.
I suppose we could postpone it. — Either can signal hesitant acceptance.
I imagine working across three time zones gets exhausting.

column2: I bet/I'll bet + clause
column3:
1. I bet/I'll bet + clause

Usage: Express an informal confident expectation or inference, often as a friendly reaction. A real wager is unnecessary. This is conversational; use a more neutral judgment when presenting evidence in formal writing.
I bet the earlier flight will be cheaper.
I'll bet the earlier flight will be cheaper.
You had three interviews today? I bet you're exhausted.

column2: In my experience, + clause · As far as I know, + clause · From what I have heard, + clause · Apparently, + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Identify the basis or limits of a claim.

1. In my experience, + clause

Usage: Ground the claim in your firsthand experience.
In my experience, written decisions reduce misunderstandings across time zones.

2. As far as I know, + clause

Usage: Limit the claim to your knowledge or observations; you may be missing information.
As far as I know, the office is still open on Fridays.
As far as I can tell, the rollout succeeded; the error rate is back to normal.

3. From what I have heard, + clause

Usage: Attribute the information to something you heard.
From what I have heard, the new manager is very approachable.

4. Apparently, + clause

Usage: Present something as apparently true from reports or evidence, without guaranteeing it.
Apparently, the venue has changed; I just received a new invitation.

column2: It seems/appears that + clause · It seems/looks/sounds/feels like + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Present an impression rather than a confirmed fact.

1. It seems/appears that + clause

Usage: Present an impression with a that-clause; appears often sounds more formal.
It seems that the update helped.
It appears that the update helped.

2. It seems/looks/sounds/feels like + clause

Usage: Present an impression with a like-clause; looks/sounds can express an inference too.
It seems like we have enough time.
It looks like we have enough time.
It sounds like the client wants a smaller first release.
It feels like we are solving the same problem twice.

column2: look/sound/feel/taste/smell + adjective · look/sound/feel/taste/smell like + noun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe a perceived quality with an adjective; use like before a thing you compare it with.

1. look/sound/feel/taste/smell + adjective

Usage: Put an adjective after the perception verb to describe the subject's quality. Use tastes/smells good for a pleasant quality; well normally describes how an action is performed.
The interface looks clean, the proposal sounds reasonable, and the controls feel responsive.
The sauce tastes smoky, and the kitchen smells wonderful.

2. look/sound/feel/taste/smell like + noun

Usage: Put a noun after like to say what the subject resembles.
It looks like a charger, sounds like a fan, and feels like rubber.
The soup tastes like coconut, and the room smells like fresh paint.

column2: What does X look like? · How does X look?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Ask about appearance; descriptions and evaluations can overlap.

1. What does X look like?

Usage: Ask for a description or resemblance.
What does the new office look like? — It has large windows and an open kitchen.

2. How does X look?

Usage: Ask about appearance or invite an evaluation; the answers can overlap with the first question.
How does the new office look? — Bright and welcoming.

column2: I assume/presume + clause · Assuming (that) + clause, main clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Accept something as true without confirmation, or state a working premise.

1. I assume/presume + clause

Usage: Accept a premise without confirmation; presume often sounds more formal.
I assume the meeting is still at three.
I presume the meeting is still at three.
For this estimate, let's assume everyone is available for two hours.

2. Assuming (that) + clause, main clause

Usage: State the premise your conclusion depends on.
Assuming the requirements stay the same, we can finish by Friday.

column2: I suspect + clause · I have a feeling (that) + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Present an unconfirmed belief or intuition.

1. I suspect + clause

Usage: Offer an unconfirmed belief or possible explanation; wrongdoing is not required.
I suspect the cache is involved, but we need more evidence.

2. I have a feeling (that) + clause

Usage: Present an intuition more explicitly.
I have a feeling that she would prefer a quieter restaurant.

column2: I am sure/certain/convinced/confident (that) + clause
column3:
1. I am sure/certain/convinced/confident (that) + clause

Usage: State a strong belief or assurance. Sure and certain are close alternatives; convinced stresses that you hold a belief firmly. Confident often stresses assurance about an outcome or ability. Context allows substantial overlap; the wording does not prove the claim. Pretty sure softens sure: you feel fairly confident while leaving room for doubt.
I am sure this is the right address.
I am certain this is the right address.
I am pretty sure this is the right address.
I am convinced that the old process needs to change.
I am confident that we can finish the migration this month.

column2: I realize/understand (that) + clause · I can see that + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Acknowledge or recognize a situation.

1. I realize/understand (that) + clause

Usage: Acknowledge a situation; realize often highlights becoming aware of it.
I realize that the deadline is tight, but we still need to check the results.
I understand that you need an answer today.

2. I can see that + clause

Usage: Signal recognition of a situation or reasoning, without necessarily agreeing.
I can see that the current process is causing frustration.

column2: I am not sure whether/if + clause · I have no idea + wh-/whether-clause · I am not entirely convinced that + clause · I could be wrong, but + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Express uncertainty or qualified doubt.

1. I am not sure whether/if + clause

Usage: Leave a yes-or-no question unresolved; whether and if both work here.
I am not sure whether this plan includes dental coverage.
I am not sure if it includes dental coverage.

2. I have no idea + wh-/whether-clause

Usage: Say you have no information; follow with a question-word clause in statement order.
I have no idea why the build failed.

3. I am not entirely convinced that + clause

Usage: Express qualified doubt; unconvinced by names the explanation that failed to persuade you. Also use be/remain unconvinced by an explanation or unconvinced that + clause. This does not prove the claim false.
I am not entirely convinced that adding more meetings would help.
I remain unconvinced by that explanation.

4. I could be wrong, but + clause

Usage: Allow that your own judgment could be mistaken before giving it.
I could be wrong, but I think we tested a different version.

column2: may/might/could + base verb · There is a chance/possibility that + clause · be likely/unlikely to + verb · be bound to + verb
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Express possibility or likelihood without claiming certainty.

1. may/might/could + base verb

Usage: Present something as possible; these modals do not encode fixed percentages.
The release may slip.
The release might slip.
The release could slip.

2. There is a chance/possibility that + clause

Usage: Introduce a possible outcome explicitly with a that-clause.
There is a chance that the venue will be available.
There is a possibility that the venue will be available.

3. be likely/unlikely to + verb

Usage: Present a probable or improbable outcome; likely also allows it is likely that. Likely suggests probable, and unlikely suggests improbable, rather than fixed numerical probabilities.
Traffic is likely to get worse after five; the roads are unlikely to clear before seven.
It is likely that we will need another reviewer.

4. be bound to + verb

Usage: Make a confident prediction, often based on experience.
Something is bound to go wrong on the first day, so plan some extra time.

column2: There is evidence that + clause · The results suggest/indicate/show/confirm that + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Report evidence and the conclusion drawn from it.

1. There is evidence that + clause

Usage: Say that supporting information exists, without automatically claiming proof.
There is evidence that the new schedule has reduced staff turnover.

2. The results suggest/indicate/show/confirm that + clause

Usage: Choose the reporting verb to fit the evidence: suggest allows uncertainty; confirm verifies an earlier claim. Indicate points to a conclusion and can overlap with suggest/show; show presents a finding as demonstrated. There is no fixed verb-by-verb certainty scale. Singular evidence takes suggests/indicates/shows/confirms; plural results take suggest/indicate/show/confirm.
The results suggest/indicate that network latency is affecting response times.
We suspected the cache was serving old data. The logs showed/confirmed that it was returning last week’s results.

column2: According to + source, + clause
column3:
1. According to + source, + clause

Usage: Attribute information to a person, report, or other source. This does not necessarily mean you endorse the claim. To state your own view directly, use in my opinion rather than according to me.
According to the latest report, bus ridership rose last year.
According to Maya, the revised estimate includes testing.

column2: always/usually/often/sometimes/occasionally/rarely/hardly ever/never + main verb · be + frequency adverb · every now and then / from time to time · How often ...?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe how frequently something happens; these expressions do not represent fixed percentages.

1. always/usually/often/sometimes/occasionally/rarely/hardly ever/never + main verb

Usage: Put a frequency adverb before an ordinary main verb, or after the first auxiliary. Always means every time; usually most of the time; often frequently; sometimes/occasionally on some occasions; rarely/hardly ever very infrequently; never at no time. These are not fixed percentages.
I usually work from home.
We often review difficult decisions together, and we always document the reasoning.
I sometimes attend networking events, but I rarely stay until the end.
I hardly ever check work email on vacation, and I never take work calls during family dinners.

2. be + frequency adverb

Usage: Put the frequency adverb after be.
I am occasionally in the office.

3. every now and then / from time to time

Usage: Describe occasional events with these similar phrases; beginning or end position is natural. Occasionally can also appear before a main verb. These phrases can occur at the beginning or end of a clause.
Every now and then, I attend an industry meetup.
I attend industry meetups from time to time.

4. How often ...?

Usage: Ask about frequency; answer with a frequency phrase or rate.
How often do you travel for work? — About once a month.

column2: tend to + verb · In general/Generally/In most cases, + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe a tendency while allowing exceptions.

1. tend to + verb

Usage: Describe characteristic behavior while allowing exceptions. A tendency does not specify an exact frequency or exclude exceptions.
I tend to focus better when I have a clear deadline.

2. In general/Generally/In most cases, + clause

Usage: Introduce a generalization rather than a claim about every case.
In general, shorter meetings are easier to schedule.
Generally, shorter meetings are easier to schedule.
In most cases, a written update is enough.

column2: The main reason + clause + is that + clause · One reason for + noun/V-ing + is that + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Give an explanation.

1. The main reason + clause + is that + clause

Usage: Name the most important reason; follow is that with its explanation.
The main reason I chose this job is that I can work with an international team.

2. One reason for + noun/V-ing + is that + clause

Usage: Introduce one contributing reason; for takes a noun or V-ing.
One reason for the delay is that the requirements changed.
One reason for recording meetings is that colleagues can catch up later.

column2: because/since/as + clause · because of/due to + noun/V-ing
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Give a cause.

1. because/since/as + clause

Usage: Give a reason with a complete clause; since/as can also have time meanings. Because makes the cause explicit; use it if since/as could be misunderstood as time.
We postponed the launch because the tests failed.
Since everyone is here, we can start.
As everyone is here, we can start.

2. because of/due to + noun/V-ing

Usage: Give a reason with a noun phrase or V-ing, rather than a bare subject–verb clause.
We postponed the launch because of the failed tests.
The delay was due to a supplier shortage.
We made fewer errors because of double-checking the totals.

column2: clause, so + result · As a result/Therefore/Consequently, + clause · That is why + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Present a result or conclusion.

1. clause, so + result

Usage: Join the cause and result in one sentence; this is common in conversation.
The trains were canceled, so we drove.

2. As a result/Therefore/Consequently, + clause

Usage: Introduce a consequence or logical conclusion; use a sentence boundary or semicolon where needed. As a result emphasizes consequence; therefore often emphasizes reasoning; consequently is more formal. These uses overlap.
The trains were canceled. As a result, we drove.
Every request needs a token. This request has none; therefore, it will be rejected.
The supplier closed its factory. Consequently, production stopped.

3. That is why + clause

Usage: Explain why the previously named outcome happened.
The buses stop running at ten. That is why I booked a taxi.

column2: Given/Considering + noun/that-clause · Based on + evidence · In light of + facts · On that basis, + conclusion
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Present the grounds for a judgment or recommendation.

1. Given/Considering + noun/that-clause

Usage: Bring relevant circumstances into your reasoning; given and considering often overlap.
Given our budget, we should start small.
Given that we have only two weeks, we should reduce the scope.
Considering that we have only two weeks, we should reduce the scope.
Considering our budget, we should start small.

2. Based on + evidence

Usage: Name the evidence or criteria used to reach your judgment; a what-clause also works. According to instead attributes information to a source; it does not itself state your inference.
Based on the benchmarks, I would choose Model A.
On the basis of the benchmarks, I would choose Model A.
Based on what you have told me, the smaller team sounds like a better fit.

3. In light of + facts

Usage: Highlight relevant facts that inform a judgment or reassessment.
In light of the recent failures, we should reconsider the design.

4. On that basis, + conclusion

Usage: Refer back to grounds already stated and give the resulting decision.
The model failed our security tests. On that basis, we rejected it.

column2: One possible explanation is that + clause · It might have something to do with + noun · X has nothing to do with Y
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Suggest an explanation without presenting it as established.

1. One possible explanation is that + clause

Usage: Propose an explanation without presenting it as established.
One possible explanation is that users cannot find the search button.

2. It might have something to do with + noun

Usage: Suggest a connection that still needs investigation.
It might have something to do with the cached credentials.

3. X has nothing to do with Y

Usage: Deny a connection; this is a stronger claim than proposing a possible explanation.
The crash has nothing to do with your change; it started before you deployed.

column2: The cause of X is Y · What is causing + noun?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Identify or ask about the cause of a problem or event.

1. The cause of X is Y

Usage: Identify a cause; distinguish it from a symptom or possible explanation.
The cause of the timeout was a blocked connection; the slow interface was a symptom.

2. What is causing + noun?

Usage: Ask which factor is producing the problem or event.
What is causing the sudden increase in response time?

column2: (in order) to + verb · so that + subject + can/could + verb · The goal is to + verb · be designed to + verb
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Explain purpose.

1. (in order) to + verb

Usage: Express the actor's purpose; in order to makes it explicit, and in an effort to stresses the attempt. An effort does not guarantee success. In diving in an effort to avoid boats, in belongs to in an effort to, not to dive in.
I muted notifications to concentrate.
I muted notifications in order to concentrate.
I muted notifications in an effort to concentrate.

2. so that + subject + can/could + verb

Usage: State a purpose while explicitly naming who should benefit or act.
I shared the recording so that colleagues in other time zones could watch it.

3. The goal is to + verb

Usage: Name an intended objective, without claiming it was achieved.
The goal of the trial is to identify confusing steps.

4. be designed to + verb

Usage: Explain intended function; design does not guarantee success.
The interface is designed to make common tasks easier.

column2: clause, but + clause · Although/Though/Even though + clause, main clause · Despite/In spite of + noun/V-ing, main clause · statement. However, statement. · clause, though
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Something happened even though another fact might make you expect otherwise. These forms can express the same message after restructuring.

1. clause, but + clause

Usage: Join contrasting clauses. But also has broader contrast uses beyond an unexpected outcome.
I was tired, but I finished the review.

2. Although/Though/Even though + clause, main clause

Usage: Use a complete subject–verb clause; even though emphasizes the unexpected result.
Although I was tired, I finished the review.
Though I was tired, I finished the review.
Even though I was tired, I finished the review.

3. Despite/In spite of + noun/V-ing, main clause

Usage: Use a noun or V-ing: despite my exhaustion / in spite of being tired. A complete clause requires the fact that. Never use despite of.
Despite being tired, I finished the review.
In spite of being tired, I finished the review.
Despite my exhaustion, I finished the review.
Despite the fact that I was tired, I finished the review.

4. statement. However, statement.

Usage: Introduce a contrasting statement after a period or semicolon; often more formal than but.
I was tired. However, I finished the review.
I was tired; however, I finished the review.

5. clause, though

Usage: Add a conversational contrast at the end. Although and even though cannot occupy this position.
I was tired. I finished the review, though.

column2: That said/Still/Even so/Nevertheless, + clause · While it is true that + clause, main clause · X may be true, but Y
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Acknowledge a point before limiting its implications.

1. That said/Still/Even so/Nevertheless, + clause

Usage: Qualify a preceding point or stress what remains true despite it; nevertheless is more formal.
The tool saves time. That said, we still need to check its output.
The tool sometimes misses errors. Still, it saves time.
The tool sometimes misses errors. Even so, it saves time.
The tool sometimes misses errors. Nevertheless, it saves time.

2. While it is true that + clause, main clause

Usage: Explicitly concede a point before stating a limitation.
While it is true that the tool saves time, it still needs supervision.

3. X may be true, but Y

Usage: Concede that X may be true while maintaining Y; may need not express uncertainty here.
The tool may be useful, but it cannot replace a careful review.

column2: clause, whereas/while + clause · On the one hand, + clause; on the other hand, + clause · One advantage/disadvantage of + noun/V-ing + is that + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Use these expressions to contrast facts or weigh the benefits and drawbacks of an option.

1. clause, whereas/while + clause

Usage: Contrast two facts; while can also express time.
I prefer written feedback, whereas my manager prefers a call.
I prefer written feedback, while my manager prefers a call.

2. On the one hand, + clause; on the other hand, + clause

Usage: Weigh two competing considerations without requiring either to be false.
On the one hand, the job pays well; on the other hand, the hours are unpredictable.

3. One advantage/disadvantage of + noun/V-ing + is that + clause

Usage: Name a benefit or drawback; the flip side introduces another aspect, while the downside names a drawback. The flip side can introduce a positive or negative aspect; comes at the cost of names a sacrifice.
One advantage of remote work is that I avoid a long commute.
One disadvantage is that I miss spontaneous conversations.
Working from home gives me flexibility. The flip side is that I sometimes feel isolated.
On the flip side, I have more time with my family.
The downside is that the simpler design offers fewer options.
Simplicity comes at the cost of customization.

column2: I agree/disagree with + noun · I agree to some extent/up to a point, but + clause · I see your point, but + clause · That is a valid concern · To be fair, + clause · I have a different take on + noun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Acknowledge another viewpoint before responding.

1. I agree/disagree with + noun

Usage: State agreement or disagreement with a person, view, or conclusion.
I agree with your assessment.
I disagree with that conclusion.

2. I agree to some extent/up to a point, but + clause

Usage: Agree partly, then introduce a reservation with but.
I agree to some extent, but a higher salary is not the only priority.
I agree up to a point, but a higher salary is not the only priority.

3. I see your point, but + clause

Usage: Acknowledge someone's reasoning without necessarily accepting their conclusion.
I see your point, but I would still prefer to test it first.

4. That is a valid concern

Usage: Recognize a reasonable concern without necessarily agreeing with every proposed response.
That is a valid concern. We should check who can access the recordings.

5. To be fair, + clause

Usage: Introduce a consideration that deserves recognition.
To be fair, the team had only two days to prepare.

6. I have a different take on + noun

Usage: Offer a different interpretation of the same issue.
I have a different take on the survey results: price may matter more than speed.

column2: X does not necessarily mean Y · Just because + clause + does not mean + clause · X does not guarantee Y
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

One fact alone is not enough to establish a conclusion or ensure an outcome. All three work in this situation: the first two question an inference, and the third emphasizes the lack of certainty.

1. X does not necessarily mean Y

Usage: Say the conclusion is not automatic, rather than saying it is always false. Shape: noun/V-ing + does not necessarily mean + noun/clause.
Compiling successfully does not necessarily mean the program works correctly.

2. Just because + clause + does not mean + clause

Usage: Push back against an assumption using two complete clauses. This expresses essentially the same idea as the first pattern.
Just because the program compiles does not mean it works correctly.

3. X does not guarantee Y

Usage: Deny certainty about an outcome, even when the first fact makes it more likely. Follow guarantee with a noun or that-clause.
Compiling successfully does not guarantee that the program works correctly.

column2: It is not that X; it is (just) that Y · It’s not like + clause · It’s not like + person + to + verb · I am not saying X; I am saying Y · The problem is not X; it is Y
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Correct a possible interpretation by stating the intended distinction.

1. It is not that X; it is (just) that Y

Usage: Reject an assumed reason and give the real one; it's just that can soften a refusal.
It is not that I dislike the idea; it is that we cannot afford it yet.
I’d love to come. It’s just that I have a deadline tomorrow.

2. It’s not like + clause

Usage: Dismiss a worry or assumption: it is not as if that situation were true or likely.
Just ask him. It’s not like he’s going to say no.

3. It’s not like + person + to + verb

Usage: Describe behavior as unusual for the named person.
It’s not like her to miss a deadline. I hope everything is okay.

4. I am not saying X; I am saying Y

Usage: Clarify your intended claim by rejecting a misunderstanding.
I am not saying we should cancel the release; I am saying we should reduce its scope.

5. The problem is not X; it is Y

Usage: Distinguish the real problem from an incorrectly identified one.
The problem is not a lack of effort; it is a lack of clear priorities.

column2: If anything, + clause
column3:
1. If anything, + clause

Usage: Use this to suggest that the opposite interpretation, or a stronger version of your point, is more accurate.
The change hasn’t simplified the process. If anything, it has made it more confusing.
I don’t think remote work has reduced my productivity. If anything, I get more done.
The trip didn’t make me less interested in living abroad. If anything, it strengthened that interest.

column2: In terms of + noun/V-ing · in this/that regard/respect
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Limit an evaluation to one aspect, measure, or activity.

1. In terms of + noun/V-ing

Usage: Name the aspect, measure, or activity you are evaluating.
In terms of cost, the second proposal is more practical.
In terms of reducing emissions, improving public transportation may have the greatest impact.
In terms of long-term health, regular exercise matters more than short-term weight loss.

2. in this/that regard/respect

Usage: Refer back to an aspect already clear from context; this/that and regard/respect often overlap. In that sense instead refers to an interpretation, rather than simply to an aspect already named.
Model A uses less memory. In this regard, it has an advantage.
In that regard, it has an advantage.
The revised interface is easier to navigate. In this respect, it is an improvement.
In that respect, it is an improvement.

column2: What I need/value/like most is + noun/clause · What matters most is + noun/clause · What I struggle with most is + noun/V-ing
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Put the focus at the end of the sentence.

1. What I need/value/like most is + noun/clause

Usage: Focus on what you need, value, or like; is introduces the important information.
What I need most is uninterrupted time to finish the analysis.
What I value most is that the team shares feedback openly.
What I like most is the freedom to choose how I work.

2. What matters most is + noun/clause

Usage: Identify the most important consideration.
What matters most is whether we can maintain the system.

3. What I struggle with most is + noun/V-ing

Usage: Identify the activity or issue you find most difficult.
What I struggle with most is explaining complicated ideas briefly.

column2: The thing is, + clause
column3:
1. The thing is, + clause

Usage: Use this in conversation to introduce the key fact or complication that the listener needs to understand.
I would like to live downtown. The thing is, I cannot afford the rent there.
The job sounds interesting. The thing is, the commute would take almost two hours.
We could postpone the event. The thing is, several speakers have already booked their flights.

column2: What I mean is + clause · What I am trying to say is + clause · That is not what I meant · In other words/To put it simply, + clause · Sorry, I meant to say + correction
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Clarify or reformulate a message.

1. What I mean is + clause

Usage: State your intended meaning more explicitly.
What I mean is that we need a smaller first release.

2. What I am trying to say is + clause

Usage: Repair or clarify an explanation you are trying to give.
What I am trying to say is that the deadline depends on the requirements.

3. That is not what I meant

Usage: Reject a misunderstanding, then explain your actual meaning.
That is not what I meant. I was asking whether the estimate includes testing.

4. In other words/To put it simply, + clause

Usage: Restate a point; to put it simply specifically promises a simpler version.
The service has no spare capacity. In other words, it cannot handle more traffic.
To put it simply, the faster option uses more memory.

5. Sorry, I meant to say + correction

Usage: Correct your own wording or information.
Sorry, I meant to say Thursday, not Tuesday.

column2: For example/For instance, + clause · such as/like + noun/V-ing
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Illustrate a general point with a specific case.

1. For example/For instance, + clause

Usage: Introduce a specific illustration as a sentence; both openings work.
Small changes can help. For example, we could shorten the form.
Small changes can help. For instance, we could remove optional fields.

2. such as/like + noun/V-ing

Usage: Introduce examples within a noun phrase; like is also natural in conversation.
I enjoy activities such as hiking and taking photographs.
I enjoy activities like hiking and taking photographs.

column2: In fact/Actually, + clause
column3:
1. In fact/Actually, + clause

Usage: Add a fact that strengthens or corrects what was just said or assumed. In fact often reinforces a claim; actually often corrects an expectation. Both can correct a claim, and neither simply means for example. Actually can sound confrontational when correcting someone, depending on tone.
The trip was not expensive. In fact, it cost less than staying home that week.
I thought the office was closed. Actually, it is open until six.
I expected the task to be easy. In fact, it took all afternoon.
I expected the task to be easy. Actually, it took all afternoon.

column2: Also, + clause · In addition/Furthermore, + clause · Another thing is that + clause · not only X but also Y
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Add a related point.

1. Also, + clause

Usage: Add a related point in everyday conversation or writing.
The apartment is quiet. Also, it is close to the station.

2. In addition/Furthermore, + clause

Usage: Add a related point; furthermore sounds more formal than in addition.
The policy reduces paperwork. In addition, it makes decisions easier to track.
The policy reduces paperwork. Furthermore, it improves transparency.

3. Another thing is that + clause

Usage: Add another consideration conversationally.
Another thing is that we need a backup plan.

4. not only X but also Y

Usage: Emphasize two contributions and keep their grammatical shapes parallel.
The change not only reduced latency but also cut our hosting costs.

column2: First/First of all, + clause · Then/Next/After that, + clause · Finally, + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Put steps or points in a clear order.

1. First/First of all, + clause

Usage: Introduce the first step or point.
First, reproduce the issue. Then, check the logs. Finally, test the proposed fix.
First of all, confirm the address. Next, choose a delivery time. After that, check the total.

2. Then/Next/After that, + clause

Usage: Move to a subsequent step; these forms organize the sequence.
First, reproduce the issue. Then, check the logs. Finally, test the proposed fix.
First of all, confirm the address. Next, choose a delivery time. After that, check the total.

3. Finally, + clause

Usage: Introduce the last step or point.
First, reproduce the issue. Then, check the logs. Finally, test the proposed fix.

column2: The main point is that + clause · The bottom line is that + clause · At the end of the day, + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Highlight the central message or practical conclusion.

1. The main point is that + clause

Usage: Identify the central message you want understood.
The main point is that users need a clear way to recover their accounts.

2. The bottom line is that + clause

Usage: Emphasize the practical conclusion or decisive consideration.
The bottom line is that we cannot support two versions indefinitely.

3. At the end of the day, + clause

Usage: State what ultimately matters after other considerations; avoid overusing this conversational phrase.
At the end of the day, the client cares more about reliability than new features.

column2: To sum up/In summary/In conclusion/Overall, + clause · Long story short, + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Summarize or give an overall assessment.

1. To sum up/In summary/In conclusion/Overall, + clause

Usage: Summarize, close an argument, or assess the whole picture; in conclusion is more formal.
To sum up, the proposal is feasible but needs more testing.
In summary, the proposal is feasible but needs more testing.
In conclusion, the evidence supports a limited trial.
Overall, response times improved even though costs increased slightly.

2. Long story short, + clause

Usage: Skip story details and give the outcome; this is casual.
Long story short, we missed the connection and spent an extra night in Denver.

column2: base verb + object/complement · Do not/Don’t + base verb · Make sure (that) + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Give instructions with an understood you as the subject.

1. base verb + object/complement

Usage: Give a direct instruction with an understood you. Please can soften the instruction.
Save a local copy before you close the page.

2. Do not/Don’t + base verb

Usage: Tell someone not to act; contractions are normal in conversation.
Do not share the link outside the team.
Don’t share the link outside the team.

3. Make sure (that) + clause

Usage: Ask someone to ensure a condition holds; the following clause uses its ordinary tense.
Make sure the attachment opens before you send the message.

column2: Speaking of + noun, + clause · Going back to + topic, + clause · Anyway, as I was saying, + clause · Now that you mention it, + clause · One thing I forgot to mention is + noun/clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Move between topics clearly.

1. Speaking of + noun, + clause

Usage: Introduce a topic related to something just mentioned.
Speaking of travel, have you booked your flight?

2. Going back to + topic, + clause

Usage: Return to an earlier topic.
Going back to your question about cost, we have two options.

3. Anyway, as I was saying, + clause

Usage: Resume a point interrupted by another turn or topic.
Anyway, as I was saying, we need to confirm the venue.

4. Now that you mention it, + clause

Usage: Introduce something prompted by the other person's remark.
Now that you mention it, I noticed the same error yesterday.

5. One thing I forgot to mention is + noun/clause

Usage: Add information you omitted earlier.
One thing I forgot to mention is that the hotel offers a free shuttle.

column2: Can I jump in for a second? · Let me finish + noun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Ask to take a turn or keep your turn long enough to finish.

1. Can I jump in for a second?

Usage: Ask to take a brief turn in a discussion.
Can I jump in for a second? I have a question about the timeline.

2. Let me finish + noun

Usage: Ask to finish your current point; tone can make this sound firm.
Let me finish this point, and then I would like to hear your view.

column2: Let me think for a second · I have never really thought about + noun/wh-clause · I am not sure how to answer that · It’s hard to say + wh-/whether-clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Acknowledge that you need thinking time or do not yet have an answer.

1. Let me think for a second

Usage: Ask for a little time to formulate your response.
Let me think for a second. There may be another way to approach this.

2. I have never really thought about + noun/wh-clause

Usage: Acknowledge that you have not considered the topic before.
I have never really thought about how cities should fund public art.

3. I am not sure how to answer that

Usage: Say you cannot yet give a useful answer.
I am not sure how to answer that without seeing the results.

4. It’s hard to say + wh-/whether-clause

Usage: Say an answer is difficult to determine; follow with a question-word or whether-clause.
It’s hard to say whether prices will drop next year.

column2: To be honest, + clause · I have to say/admit, + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Use these only when you are genuinely being candid or admitting something; do not use them as empty fillers.

1. To be honest, + clause

Usage: Introduce a candid view or admission rather than using the phrase as an empty filler.
To be honest, I would not choose to live in such a crowded area.
To be honest, I had expected the course to be easier.
To be honest, convenience matters more to me than having a large home.

2. I have to say/admit, + clause

Usage: Say stresses a frank judgment; admit concedes something unexpected or difficult to acknowledge.
I have to say, the neighborhood is livelier than I expected.
I have to admit, the course was harder than I expected.

column2: simple present · am/is/are + V-ing · Do/Does + subject + base verb? · Am/Is/Are + subject + V-ing?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Choose between general/habitual and current/temporary situations, in statements and questions.

1. simple present

Usage: Describe a habit, fact, or stable situation; state verbs normally use this form.
I work with overseas clients.
The server handles requests automatically.
I need more time; I do not know the answer yet.

2. am/is/are + V-ing

Usage: Describe an activity in progress or a temporary situation.
I am working with a new client this week.
The server is handling a large request right now.

3. Do/Does + subject + base verb?

Usage: Ask about a routine or general situation; after does use the base verb.
Does she work remotely?

4. Am/Is/Are + subject + V-ing?

Usage: Ask about a current or developing situation.
Is she working remotely today?
Is your English improving? — Ask about progress now.

column2: I think + clause · I am thinking about/of + noun/V-ing
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Distinguish holding an opinion from actively considering an idea.

1. I think + clause

Usage: Express an opinion; opinion think normally uses a simple form.
I think the plan is realistic.
What do you think of the offer?

2. I am thinking about/of + noun/V-ing

Usage: Describe actively considering an option, rather than merely holding a view.
I am thinking about changing the plan.
Are you thinking of accepting it?

column2: be + adjective · be being + behavior adjective
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Use be for a state or characteristic; be being highlights current behavior.

1. be + adjective

Usage: Describe a state or characteristic; temporary states do not automatically take being.
She is usually patient, but she is being unusually impatient today.
I am tired after the trip.

2. be being + behavior adjective

Usage: Highlight current behavior with adjectives such as careful or impatient.
She is usually patient, but she is being unusually impatient today.
I am being careful because the floor is slippery.

column2: be always/constantly + V-ing
column3:
1. be always/constantly + V-ing

Usage: Comment on repeated behavior, often with irritation, surprise, or appreciation. This is not simply the neutral statement that something happens every time. A simple form is better for an unemotional routine.
The printer is always breaking down right before a deadline.
She is constantly finding ways to make new colleagues feel welcome.

column2: simple past · have/has + past participle · Have you ever ...? · have/has not ... yet
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Relate events to a finished past time or look back from the present.

1. simple past

Usage: Locate an event in a finished past time; recent-event simple past also overlaps with the perfect in casual AmE.
I submitted the report yesterday.
I worked there from 2021 to 2023.
Did you finish yet? — Both are common in AmE.
I already checked the address.
I just started learning to drive.

2. have/has + past participle

Usage: Look back from now at experience, a present result, or an unfinished period.
I have submitted the report, so we can discuss it now.
I have worked here since 2023.
I have not seen her in ages, but we still exchange messages.
I have already checked the address.
I have just started learning to drive.
Has your English improved? — Ask about the result by now.

3. Have you ever ...?

Usage: Ask about experience at any time up to now; never gives a negative answer.
Have you ever spoken at a conference?
I have never spoken at one before.

4. have/has not ... yet

Usage: Ask whether an expected action is completed; use have not ... yet for an incomplete one.
Have you finished yet?

column2: have/has + noun · have + object + state/condition
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Use main-verb have for possession, relationships, availability, activities, and an object's current condition. Have got is a conversational alternative for current possession. Distinguish these uses from auxiliary have + past participle and causative have + person + base verb.

1. have/has + noun

Usage: Describe possession, relationships, or conditions. Have got is a common conversational alternative for current possession; use had for past possession. Have can be progressive when it describes activities, such as eating a meal.
I have a spare charger.
I've got a spare charger.
Do you have any allergies? — No, I don't.
I had a food allergy as a child.
We're having lunch now.

2. have + object + state/condition

Usage: Describe the object's present state or availability using have + object + complement. Left means remaining, ready means prepared, and on silent describes a device setting. This is not the causative pattern have + person + base verb.
We have three exercises left.
How many exercises do we have left?
I have the documents ready, and she has her phone on silent.

column2: have/has + past participle · have/has been + V-ing · for + duration · since + starting point
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Choose a focus on result, state, or activity, and express duration or a starting point.

1. have/has + past participle

Usage: Emphasize a result, count, or state; know normally stays in the simple perfect. Own, like know, normally takes the simple form rather than the continuous.
I have reviewed three proposals.
I have lived here for two years.
I have known her for a decade.

2. have/has been + V-ing

Usage: Emphasize an activity or its duration up to now; live/work often allow either perfect form.
I have been reviewing proposals all morning.
I have been living here for two years.
How long have you been working on this?
I have been working on it since Monday.

3. for + duration

Usage: Measure a length of time; the duration can accompany either suitable perfect form.
I have lived here for two years.
I have been living here for two years.
I have known her for a decade.

4. since + starting point

Usage: Identify the starting point of a continuing period.
How long have you been working on this?
I have been working on it since Monday.

column2: The first/last time + past clause, + clause · This is the first time + present perfect · When was the last time + past clause?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Distinguish narrating an occasion from counting experience up to now.

1. The first/last time + past clause, + clause

Usage: Narrate a particular earlier occasion. After a past was, had done is available when looking back from that past occasion.
The first time I led a meeting in English, I prepared far too many notes.
The last time I visited, the museum was closed for repairs.

2. This is the first time + present perfect

Usage: Relate the current experience to all earlier occasions with present perfect.
This is the first time I have handled the entire release myself.

3. When was the last time + past clause?

Usage: Ask when the most recent occurrence happened, using the simple past.
When was the last time you took a full week off?

column2: It has been + duration + since + past clause · How long has it been since + past clause?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Measure the time from an earlier event to now.

1. It has been + duration + since + past clause

Usage: Give the elapsed duration from an earlier event to now.
It has been six months since I last took a vacation.

2. How long has it been since + past clause?

Usage: Ask how much time has elapsed since the event.
How long has it been since you visited your family?

column2: used to + base verb · would + base verb for repeated past actions · be/get used to + noun/V-ing
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Used to describes a past habit or state that no longer holds.

1. used to + base verb

Usage: Describe a former habit or state that no longer holds.
I used to live downtown, and I used to walk to work.

2. would + base verb for repeated past actions

Usage: Describe repeated past actions after establishing the past setting; not normally a past state.
When I lived downtown, I would stop at the same café every morning.

3. be/get used to + noun/V-ing

Usage: Be used to means familiar with; get used to means becoming familiar. To takes a noun or V-ing.
I am used to presenting online, but I am still getting used to speaking to a large audience.

column2: was/were + V-ing + when + past event · While + past continuous, + past continuous
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Set an activity in progress as background to an event, or describe two simultaneous activities.

1. was/were + V-ing + when + past event

Usage: Set an activity in progress as background to a past event; interruption is inferred from context.
I was reviewing the proposal when the client called.
We were discussing the budget when the meeting ended.

2. While + past continuous, + past continuous

Usage: Describe two activities happening at the same time in the past.
While I was cooking dinner, my roommate was setting the table.

column2: simple past · had + past participle · had been + V-ing
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Narrate past events, or look back from a past reference point.

1. simple past

Usage: Narrate past events without automatically marking one as earlier than another past reference point. Do not use past perfect merely because an event happened a long time ago.
I sent the proposal and then called the client.
She ate before the meeting.
After I finished the report, I sent it.

2. had + past participle

Usage: Look back from a past moment to an earlier event; just/barely can emphasize a short gap. In I'd just sat down, I'd means I had; in I'd ask, it means I would.
I had just sent the proposal when the client called.
I’d barely fallen asleep when the alarm went off.
She was not hungry because she had eaten before the meeting.
By the time I sent the report, I had checked every figure.

3. had been + V-ing

Usage: Look back at an activity that had continued up to a past moment.
I had been waiting for an hour when the clinic finally called my name.

column2: be about to + verb + when + event · was/were going to + verb, but + clause · meant to + verb, but + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

About to means an action is imminent; it does not guarantee that another event prevents it.

1. be about to + verb + when + event

Usage: Describe an imminent action and an event at that point; prevention is not automatic.
I was about to leave when the courier arrived, so I waited.

2. was/were going to + verb, but + clause

Usage: State an earlier plan or expectation, then explain what changed.
We were going to meet in person, but her flight was canceled.

3. meant to + verb, but + clause

Usage: State an intention and explain why it was not carried out.
I meant to reply yesterday, but I could not find the attachment.

column2: will not/would not + base verb
column3:
1. will not/would not + base verb

Usage: Describe refusal or failure to cooperate. Won’t can concern a person or a machine now; wouldn’t can report refusal or a failure in the past. Context distinguishes this from a prediction or imagined situation.
I have asked twice, but she will not discuss the deadline.
The car would not start, so we took the bus.

column2: As soon as/Once/The moment + clause, + main clause · right after + noun/clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Link events in sequence.

1. As soon as/Once/The moment + clause, + main clause

Usage: Link events: as soon as/the moment emphasize immediacy; once emphasizes reaching a stage. For a future time clause, use a present form rather than will for the expected event.
As soon as I get the results, I will call you.
Once we have approval, we can choose a launch date.
The moment I saw the warning, I stopped the test.

2. right after + noun/clause

Usage: Describe the short interval after an event; use a noun or a clause.
I called her right after the meeting.
I called her right after the meeting ended.

column2: by + deadline · until + endpoint · not ... until + time/clause · It was not until X that Y
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Distinguish a completion deadline, continuation, and a delayed occurrence.

1. by + deadline

Usage: Set the latest time for completion, rather than a period of continuation.
I will finish the review by Friday.

2. until + endpoint

Usage: Describe continuation up to an endpoint.
I will keep reviewing applications until Friday.

3. not ... until + time/clause

Usage: Delay an action until the stated time or condition. Use a present form in a future until-clause.
I will not send the report until you approve it.

4. It was not until X that Y

Usage: Emphasize when a delayed event finally happened.
It was not until I checked the logs that I understood the failure.

column2: By the time + clause, + perfect form
column3:
1. By the time + clause, + perfect form

Usage: Use a past perfect form for a completed state before a past event and a future perfect form for completion by a future event.
By the time the meeting started, the team had resolved the main issue.
By the time I reached the station, the last train had already left.
By the time the new line opens, the city will have completed the surrounding roadwork.

column2: will + base verb · be going to + base verb · present continuous + future time · will be + V-ing · simple present for a timetable
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Express a prediction, plan, arrangement, activity in progress, or timetable. These forms overlap; they are not rigid one-to-one categories.

1. will + base verb

Usage: Make a promise, prediction, or decision made at the moment of speaking.
I will send you the notes tonight; I promise.

2. be going to + base verb

Usage: State an existing intention or a prediction based on present evidence.
I am going to take a week off after the release.

3. present continuous + future time

Usage: Present a future arrangement.
I am meeting the client at ten tomorrow.

4. will be + V-ing

Usage: Describe an activity in progress at a future time.
At ten tomorrow, I will be meeting with the client, so I may not answer.

5. simple present for a timetable

Usage: State a scheduled service or timetable.
The train leaves at seven tomorrow morning. — A scheduled service.

column2: Whenever/Every time + clause, + clause · when/if + clause, + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Whenever and every time describe repeated occasions.

1. Whenever/Every time + clause, + clause

Usage: Describe repeated occasions; whenever and every time overlap.
Whenever I travel, I save a copy of my reservation offline.
Every time I travel, I do the same thing.

2. when/if + clause, + clause

Usage: When treats an event as expected; if leaves it conditional. General rules can allow both. Use a present form in a future when/if clause.
When I get home tonight, I will send the photos.
If I get home early enough, I will join the call.

column2: At first, + clause; eventually/in the end, + clause · Over time, + clause · Over the past + period, + present perfect
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Contrast an initial situation with a later outcome.

1. At first, + clause; eventually/in the end, + clause

Usage: Contrast the initial situation with a later or final outcome.
At first, I found the schedule exhausting; eventually, I adjusted.
We considered several options. In the end, we stayed with the original design.

2. Over time, + clause

Usage: Describe gradual development across time.
Over time, I became more comfortable asking questions.

3. Over the past + period, + present perfect

Usage: Connect a period ending now with the present perfect.
Over the past year, our response times have improved considerably.

column2: still + verb · not ... anymore/any longer · no longer + verb · already/yet
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe whether a situation continues or an expected change has happened.

1. still + verb

Usage: Say that a situation continues.
I still work remotely.
The printer is still broken.

2. not ... anymore/any longer

Usage: Say that an earlier situation has ended; use a negative verb with anymore/any longer. Adverbial anymore is commonly one word in AmE.
I do not work remotely anymore.
We do not use that system any longer.

3. no longer + verb

Usage: Say that a situation has ended without another negative verb.
I no longer work remotely.

4. already/yet

Usage: Already marks completion by now; yet asks about or negates an expected change.
Have you sent the draft yet? — I already sent it.
It has not been fixed yet.

column2: at the beginning/end of + noun · in the beginning/end
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Distinguish a point within a named period from an initial situation or final outcome.

1. at the beginning/end of + noun

Usage: Identify a point within a named period, event, or object.
We will review the results at the end of the month.

2. in the beginning/end

Usage: Describe an initial situation or eventual outcome; do not add of after in the end.
In the beginning, we met every day. In the end, we settled on weekly updates.

column2: What happened was (that) + clause
column3:
1. What happened was (that) + clause

Usage: Use this to introduce the event that explains a situation, especially in a spoken story.
What happened was that my flight was canceled at the last minute.
What happened was, we took the wrong exit and ended up in another town.
What happened was that the landlord sold the building, so everyone had to move.

column2: You will not believe what happened · So there’s this + noun + clause · All of a sudden/Out of nowhere, + clause · The next thing I knew, + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Introduce a surprising story or an abrupt event.

1. You will not believe what happened

Usage: Invite attention before a surprising story.
You will not believe what happened on the way to the airport.

2. So there’s this + noun + clause

Usage: Introduce a new person or thing in a casual story.
So there’s this guy on my team who answers every email in thirty seconds.

3. All of a sudden/Out of nowhere, + clause

Usage: All of a sudden emphasizes suddenness; out of nowhere emphasizes an unexpected appearance or event.
All of a sudden, the lights went out.
Out of nowhere, a dog ran across the road.

4. The next thing I knew, + clause

Usage: Skip to a rapid or surprising development in the story.
The next thing I knew, everyone was helping us push the car.

column2: Luckily/Fortunately/Unfortunately, + clause · To make matters worse, + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Evaluate whether events were fortunate or unfortunate.

1. Luckily/Fortunately/Unfortunately, + clause

Usage: Evaluate an event as fortunate or unfortunate; luckily and fortunately overlap.
Luckily, someone had turned my wallet in.
Fortunately, someone had turned my wallet in.
Unfortunately, our train was canceled.

2. To make matters worse, + clause

Usage: Add a further problem to an already bad situation.
The flight was canceled. To make matters worse, the hotel was full.

column2: Surprisingly, + clause · I could not believe + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Express surprise about an event.

1. Surprisingly, + clause

Usage: Mark an event as unexpected.
Surprisingly, the repair took only ten minutes.

2. I could not believe + clause

Usage: Express a strong personal reaction, without literally denying what happened.
I could not believe how quickly everyone offered to help.

column2: almost/nearly + verb · almost/nearly all/every + noun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Say an action came close to happening or a quantity was close to complete.

1. almost/nearly + verb

Usage: Describe coming close to an event; almost missing means you caught the train. Almost finishing, in contrast, means some work remained unfinished.
I almost missed the last train, but I got on just before the doors closed.
I nearly missed the last train, but I made it.

2. almost/nearly all/every + noun

Usage: Describe a quantity close to the whole, using a plural group or every + singular noun.
Almost all the reviewers agreed.
Nearly every reviewer agreed.

column2: If + present, + present/will/can/may · as long as/provided that + clause · only if + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Use an open condition for general rules or real possibilities.

1. If + present, + present/will/can/may

Usage: State a general rule or a real future possibility, normally with a present form after if.
If I skip lunch, I lose concentration.
If I finish early, I will join you.

2. as long as/provided that + clause

Usage: State a requirement; provided that is more formal than as long as.
You can work remotely as long as you are available for the meeting.
We can proceed provided that the client approves the budget.

3. only if + clause

Usage: State a necessary condition; it does not guarantee the outcome.
I will accept the offer only if the hours are flexible.

column2: unless + clause · if not, + clause · otherwise, + clause · in that case/if that’s the case, + clause · That’s not the case
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Unless usually means if ...

1. unless + clause

Usage: Usually express if ... not; check the meaning instead of substituting mechanically.
Unless the weather improves, we will move the event indoors.

2. if not, + clause

Usage: Negate a clear condition from the preceding question or statement.
Can you send it today? If not, tomorrow morning is fine.

3. otherwise, + clause

Usage: State what follows if a preceding requirement is not met.
Please save a copy; otherwise, you could lose your changes.

4. in that case/if that’s the case, + clause

Usage: Respond to the situation just described; both expressions work here.
The venue is unavailable? In that case, we should meet online.
If that’s the case, we should meet online.

5. That’s not the case

Usage: Say that the described situation is not true.
A: I heard the office is closing. B: That’s not the case; it’s just moving to the fourth floor.

column2: Even though + fact, + clause · Even if + possible case, + clause · whether or not/no matter what/how + clause · It doesn’t matter + wh-/if-clause · regardless of + noun/V-ing/whether-clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Make an outcome independent of a circumstance while preserving the distinction between fact and possibility.

1. Even though + fact, + clause

Usage: Treat the contrasting circumstance as a fact.
Even though the task is difficult, I will try it.

2. Even if + possible case, + clause

Usage: Treat it as a possible condition, without asserting it is true.
Even if the task is difficult, I will try it.

3. whether or not/no matter what/how + clause

Usage: Say the result is independent of both alternatives or of what/how something happens.
Whether or not they approve the proposal, we need to document the risks.
No matter what happens, I will keep you informed.
No matter how busy I am, I make time for a short walk.

4. It doesn’t matter + wh-/if-clause

Usage: State that a variation does not affect the result, using a complete sentence.
It doesn't matter whether they approve it; we still need to document the risks.
It doesn't matter which framework you use, as long as the tests pass.

5. regardless of + noun/V-ing/whether-clause

Usage: Use a noun, V-ing, or whether-clause; a bare subject–verb statement does not follow regardless of.
We need to document the risks regardless of their decision.
All participants need a ticket, regardless of attending online or in person.
We will publish the results regardless of whether the findings support our hypothesis.

column2: in case + clause · just in case · in case of + noun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe a precaution with in case: prepare before you know whether the event will happen.

1. in case + clause

Usage: Describe a precaution before knowing whether an event will happen; compare if as a condition. Use a present form for a future event after in case.
I saved a local copy in case the connection fails.
If the connection fails, I will switch to the local copy.

2. just in case

Usage: Leave the anticipated event unstated because context makes it clear.
I do not expect rain, but I brought a jacket just in case.

3. in case of + noun

Usage: Give an instruction for the event named by a noun phrase.
In case of a power outage, use the stairs.

column2: What if + clause? · Let’s say/Suppose + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Invite someone to consider a hypothetical scenario.

1. What if + clause?

Usage: Raise a hypothetical worry or propose an option.
What if the client changes the requirements?
What if we start with a smaller trial?

2. Let’s say/Suppose + clause

Usage: Establish an imagined case for discussion.
Let’s say we have only two weeks.
Suppose we have only two weeks. What would you cut?

column2: depend on + noun/whether/how-clause · Depending on + noun/wh-clause, + main clause · Whether + clause + depends on + noun/wh-clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Use depend on to name what determines an answer or outcome.

1. depend on + noun/whether/how-clause

Usage: Name the factor or unresolved question that determines the outcome.
The timeline depends on whether the client approves the design.
It depends on how much testing we need.

2. Depending on + noun/wh-clause, + main clause

Usage: Introduce a variable that changes which action is appropriate. This names a variable affecting the outcome, not personal dependence on someone.
Depending on the weather, we may move the dinner inside.

3. Whether + clause + depends on + noun/wh-clause

Usage: Make the yes-or-no outcome the subject, then name what determines it.
Whether we travel this weekend depends on how much work remains.

column2: If + past form, + would/could + base verb · If + subject + were to + verb, + would + base verb · Without + noun, + would/could + base verb
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Imagine a present or future situation as hypothetical or remote.

1. If + past form, + would/could + base verb

Usage: Imagine a remote present or future case; the past form need not refer to past time. Were is standard for hypothetical be; was also occurs in conversation. Could describes an imagined possibility or ability.
If I had more time, I would take a longer trip.
What would you do if you were in my position?
If I were you, I would ask for the details in writing.

2. If + subject + were to + verb, + would + base verb

Usage: Present a future possibility as especially hypothetical, often in a sensitive discussion.
If the company were to cut the budget, which project would you keep?

3. Without + noun, + would/could + base verb

Usage: Express an absent condition and its imagined consequence.
Without clear requirements, we could spend weeks solving the wrong problem.

column2: If + had + past participle, + would/could have + past participle · If + had + past participle, + would + base verb + now
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Imagine a different past and its consequence.

1. If + had + past participle, + would/could have + past participle

Usage: Imagine a different past and a past consequence; could have expresses a possibility. Without + noun can replace a clear condition; preserve the time of its imagined consequence.
If we had left earlier, we would have caught the train.
Without your help, I could not have finished the application.

2. If + had + past participle, + would + base verb + now

Usage: Imagine a different past with a consequence that belongs to now.
If I had accepted that offer, I would live in Chicago now.

column2: I hope + clause · I wish + past form · I wish + had + past participle · I wish + would + verb
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Express desired outcomes, unreal wishes, or regret about the past.

1. I hope + clause

Usage: Express a desired outcome that may be true or become true.
I hope the interview goes well.
I hope you enjoyed the trip.

2. I wish + past form

Usage: Express an unreal or unsatisfactory present; could can name an unavailable ability or option.
I wish I had more time to travel.
I wish I could join you, but I have to work.

3. I wish + had + past participle

Usage: Regret a past situation by imagining an alternative past.
I wish I had asked about the schedule before accepting.

4. I wish + would + verb

Usage: Express a desired change, often in another person's behavior. This is a desired change rather than merely a neutral prediction.
I wish they would tell us about changes earlier.

column2: could have + past participle · should/should not have + past participle
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Could have can describe an unrealized possibility or a possible explanation; context determines which.

1. could have + past participle

Usage: Describe an unused possibility or a possible explanation; context determines which.
I could have taken a taxi, but I decided to walk. — An unused option.
The message could have gone to spam. — A possible explanation.

2. should/should not have + past participle

Usage: Evaluate a past choice or express regret; should have can also express expected completion.
I should have checked the address.
I should not have rushed the review.

column2: must/might/cannot + base verb · must/might/could not have + past participle · should + base verb
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Distinguish inference, possibility, and expectation.

1. must/might/cannot + base verb

Usage: Draw a current inference, allow a possibility, or rule it out. Must here can express an inference rather than an obligation.
She must be busy; she has not answered.
She might be busy, but I am not sure.
That cannot be the final version; it still has comments in it.

2. must/might/could not have + past participle

Usage: Place the inference or possibility in the past with have + past participle.
They must have missed the email.
They might have missed the email.
He could not have sent it yesterday; his account was still locked.

3. should + base verb

Usage: Predict an expected event; should have predicts expected completion by a reference time.
The package should arrive soon.
The package should have arrived by now.

column2: plan/decide/hope/agree/promise + to + verb · decide against + noun/V-ing · think about + V-ing
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

These verbs can take to + base verb for an intended action; each verb still keeps its own meaning.

1. plan/decide/hope/agree/promise + to + verb

Usage: Name an intended action after these verbs; each main verb keeps its own meaning. Do not assume every verb permits both to and V-ing complements.
We plan to expand the trial, but we have not agreed to a date.
I decided to apply.
I hope to finish this week, and I promised to send an update tomorrow.

2. decide against + noun/V-ing

Usage: Reject an option; against takes a noun or V-ing.
I decided against applying.

3. think about + V-ing

Usage: Consider an activity without committing to it.
I have been thinking about taking a course before I decide.

column2: have to/have got to/need to/must + verb · do not have to/do not need to + verb · did not have to + verb · be going to have to + verb · cannot/must not + verb · be supposed to + verb · be supposed to be + adjective/noun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe necessity, lack of necessity, prohibition, and expectations.

1. have to/have got to/need to/must + verb

Usage: Express necessity; have got to is conversational, while have to works across tenses.
I have to submit the form today.
I need to submit it today.
I must submit it today.
I have got to leave soon; the last train is at ten.

2. do not have to/do not need to + verb

Usage: Remove necessity: the action is optional, rather than prohibited.
You do not have to attend.
You do not need to attend. — Attendance is optional.

3. did not have to + verb

Usage: Say an action was unnecessary in the past; You didn't have to! can thank someone for a kindness.
I didn’t have to pay for parking because the meter was broken.
You didn’t have to bring anything, but thank you!

4. be going to have to + verb

Usage: Announce a coming necessity, often an unwelcome one, relatively gently.
I’m going to have to leave a little early today.

5. cannot/must not + verb

Usage: Prohibit an action; this is different from not having to do it.
You cannot share that password.
You must not share it. — It is prohibited.

6. be supposed to + verb

Usage: Describe an expectation, rule, or arrangement; was supposed to alone does not prove failure.
We are supposed to check in by six.
I was supposed to lead the meeting, and I did.

7. be supposed to be + adjective/noun

Usage: Report what people say about something's quality or identity.
That new taco place is supposed to be really good.

column2: should + verb · might want to + verb · had better + verb · would be better off + V-ing · Have you tried + V-ing?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Give advice.

1. should + verb

Usage: Give a direct recommendation; use a base verb without to.
You should ask which expenses are covered.

2. might want to + verb

Usage: Soften a recommendation.
You might want to save a copy before changing the settings.

3. had better + verb

Usage: Give a warning about an important consequence; this can sound pushy for a small suggestion. Had better, like should, takes a base verb without to.
We had better leave now, or we will miss the last train.

4. would be better off + V-ing

Usage: Say an option would leave someone in a better position; use V-ing.
You’d be better off asking HR directly.

5. Have you tried + V-ing?

Usage: Suggest a possible solution by asking whether it has been tried.
Have you tried restarting the router?

column2: might as well/may as well + base verb
column3:
1. might as well/may as well + base verb

Usage: Choose a sensible available option when there is no compelling reason to do something else. Might as well and may as well overlap; might as well is a natural conversational choice. This is not simply a prediction that you might act.
We are already downtown, so we might as well visit the museum.
The download will take an hour. We may as well get lunch while we wait.

column2: It is time (for + person) to + verb · It is (about) time + subject + past form
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Say an action should happen now.

1. It is time (for + person) to + verb

Usage: Neutrally signal that an action should happen now.
It is time for us to leave.

2. It is (about) time + subject + past form

Usage: Suggest an action is overdue; the past form refers to now, not a past event.
It is time we left.
It is about time they fixed the broken elevator.

column2: prefer + noun/V-ing + to + noun/V-ing · would prefer to + verb · would rather + base verb + than + base verb · instead of + noun/V-ing · rather than + parallel alternative
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Express a preference or describe the alternative chosen.

1. prefer + noun/V-ing + to + noun/V-ing

Usage: Express a preference; to in prefer A to B and in preference to is a preposition, so an action takes V-ing. In preference to is formal; prefer A to B, choose A over B, and rather than are often more conversational.
I prefer working from home to commuting every day.
We used reusable containers in preference to disposable ones.
They chose to repair the device in preference to replacing it.

2. would prefer to + verb

Usage: Express a desired current choice with to + base verb. Prefer often states a general preference; would prefer/would rather often state a current choice, with overlap.
I would prefer to meet online.

3. would rather + base verb + than + base verb

Usage: Express a preference with a base verb after would rather, without to.
I would rather meet online than drive across town.

4. instead of + noun/V-ing

Usage: Name the option not taken; of takes a noun or V-ing.
We met online instead of driving across town.

5. rather than + parallel alternative

Usage: Contrast parallel alternatives; repair and replace are parallel base verbs here.
We chose to repair the system rather than replace it.

column2: like/love/hate + V-ing / to + verb · would like/love + to + verb
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Both -ing and to can express general likes and dislikes, especially in AmE.

1. like/love/hate + V-ing / to + verb

Usage: Describe general likes/dislikes; V-ing and to often overlap, with to also useful for a chosen routine. Do not turn this tendency into a rigid enjoyment-versus-duty distinction.
I love working with a small team.
I love to work with a small team.
I like to check the agenda before a meeting. — A preferred routine.

2. would like/love + to + verb

Usage: Express a particular wish with to + base verb.
I would like to discuss the offer before I decide.
I would love to join you for dinner.

column2: Either one works for me · What are our options for + noun/V-ing? · Which would you recommend?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Discuss a choice among options.

1. Either one works for me

Usage: Accept either of two available choices.
We could meet Tuesday or Thursday. Either one works for me.

2. What are our options for + noun/V-ing?

Usage: Ask what choices are available before selecting one.
What are our options for reducing the cost?

3. Which would you recommend?

Usage: Ask for someone's judgment about the best choice.
Which would you recommend for someone who travels frequently?

column2: be willing/unwilling to + verb
column3:
1. be willing/unwilling to + verb

Usage: Describe whether someone is prepared to do something. Willing does not necessarily mean enthusiastic; unwilling describes a lack of willingness, not inability. Use can/be able to when the issue is ability.
I am willing to adjust the schedule if we can keep the deadline.
They were unwilling to share the data without permission.

column2: be worth + noun/V-ing · There is no point in + V-ing · It makes sense to + verb
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Evaluate whether an action offers enough value or serves a purpose.

1. be worth + noun/V-ing

Usage: Evaluate value; worth takes a noun or V-ing, not a to-infinitive.
Is the upgrade worth the extra cost?
Is it worth upgrading now?

2. There is no point in + V-ing

Usage: Say an action lacks a useful purpose.
There is no point in collecting feedback if nobody reads it.

3. It makes sense to + verb

Usage: Say an action is reasonable in this context, without claiming it is the only option. Reasonable in context does not necessarily mean morally right.
It makes sense to test a smaller version first.
Does it make sense to renew for another year?

column2: can/be able to + verb · could + verb · managed to + verb · could not + verb + in time · cannot seem to + verb
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe ability and actual success.

1. can/be able to + verb

Usage: Express ability; finally can mark the end of a delay or obstacle.
I can work remotely now.
I am able to work remotely now.
I can finally access the portal, but I cannot seem to upload the attachment.

2. could + verb

Usage: Describe general past ability.
When I was younger, I could study for hours without a break.

3. managed to + verb

Usage: Emphasize actual success on a particular difficult occasion; was able to also works.
I managed to recover the file.
I was able to recover the file.

4. could not + verb + in time

Usage: Describe a particular failure to act before the deadline.
I could not finish the application in time.

5. cannot seem to + verb

Usage: Describe difficulty achieving an action despite trying.
I can finally access the portal, but I cannot seem to upload the attachment.

column2: try to + verb · try + V-ing
column3:
