Shared idea / comparison

Try to emphasizes an attempt; try doing presents an action as a method or experiment.

1. try to + verb

Usage: Emphasize the attempt to perform the action. The forms can overlap when an attempted action also tests a solution; neither guarantees success.
I tried to restart the laptop, but it would not respond.

2. try + V-ing

Usage: Propose an action as an experiment or possible method; success is not guaranteed.
Try restarting the laptop; that may fix it.

column2: mean to + verb · mean + V-ing
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Mean to expresses intention; mean doing describes what something entails.

1. mean to + verb

Usage: Express intention; did not mean to acknowledges an unintended action.
I did not mean to interrupt you.

2. mean + V-ing

Usage: Describe what a choice entails or requires.
Accepting this role would mean moving to another city.

column2: need + V-ing · need to be + past participle
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe an action that needs to be performed on the subject.

1. need + V-ing

Usage: Describe an action needed on the subject; this V-ing has a passive meaning.
The report needs updating.

2. need to be + past participle

Usage: Express the same passive requirement explicitly; compare we need to update for the actor's action.
The report needs to be updated.
We need to update the report before the meeting.

column2: remember/forget + to + verb · remember/forget + V-ing
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Remember/forget to points to an action you need to perform.

1. remember/forget + to + verb

Usage: Remember to perform a needed action, or fail to do it because you forgot.
I remembered to attach the file.
I forgot to lock the door.

2. remember/forget + V-ing

Usage: Recall an earlier experience, or say its memory will never leave you.
I remember attaching the file.
I will never forget meeting her.

column2: stop + V-ing · stop + to + verb
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Stop doing ends an activity.

1. stop + V-ing

Usage: End the named activity.
I stopped checking email during dinner. — I no longer do that.

2. stop + to + verb

Usage: Pause another activity in order to perform the named action.
I stopped to check an urgent email. — I paused what I was doing.

column2: regret + V-ing · regret to say/inform + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Regret doing looks back at an action with sorrow.

1. regret + V-ing

Usage: Look back at an action with sorrow.
I regret sending that message before checking the facts.

2. regret to say/inform + clause

Usage: Formally introduce unwelcome news; ordinary I'm sorry often sounds less distant.
We regret to inform you that your application was unsuccessful.

column2: go on + V-ing · go on + to + verb
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Distinguish continuing the same activity from moving to a new one.

1. go on + V-ing

Usage: Continue the same activity after a pause.
She paused for questions, then went on explaining the same process.

2. go on + to + verb

Usage: Move to a different subsequent activity or stage.
After explaining the problem, she went on to propose a solution.

column2: have trouble/difficulty + V-ing · have trouble with + noun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe something you find hard to do.

1. have trouble/difficulty + V-ing

Usage: Name a difficult action with V-ing, without to. Having trouble describes a current difficulty.
I have trouble explaining this briefly.
I have difficulty explaining this briefly.

2. have trouble with + noun

Usage: Name the thing causing difficulty after with.
I am having trouble with the payment page.

column2: be done + V-ing / with + noun · still need to + verb
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Report what is finished and what remains.

1. be done + V-ing / with + noun

Usage: Describe completion with done doing/done with; done with can also express wanting no further involvement.
I am done checking the figures.
I am done with the spreadsheet.

2. still need to + verb

Usage: Name an action that remains unfinished or necessary.
I still need to write the summary before I can send it.

column2: It takes + (person +) time/effort + to + verb · spend + time/money + on + noun / V-ing · How much longer will + clause?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Takes describes the time or effort required; spend makes the person or organization the subject.

1. It takes + (person +) time/effort + to + verb

Usage: Make the required time or effort the subject with it takes.
It takes me an hour to prepare the report.
How long does it take to prepare the report?

2. spend + time/money + on + noun / V-ing

Usage: Make the person/organization the subject; use on before a noun, usually no on before V-ing after time.
I spend an hour preparing the report.
The company spent a large part of its budget on training.

3. How much longer will + clause?

Usage: Ask about the remaining duration, rather than the total duration.
How much longer will the repairs take?

column2: be busy + V-ing · be busy with + noun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Say an activity or task is occupying your time.

1. be busy + V-ing

Usage: Name the activity occupying someone's time, using V-ing directly.
I am busy preparing for tomorrow’s presentation.

2. be busy with + noun

Usage: Name the task or person occupying someone after with.
She is busy with a customer right now.

column2: have/get a chance to + verb · give + person + a chance/the opportunity to + verb · Have you had a chance to + verb?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe an opportunity or politely ask about progress.

1. have/get a chance to + verb

Usage: Describe an available opportunity; get can mean it becomes available.
I finally got a chance to discuss the proposal with her.

2. give + person + a chance/the opportunity to + verb

Usage: Say who provides an opportunity and who performs the action.
The placement gave me the opportunity to work with customers directly.
It gave me a chance to handle real customer requests.

3. Have you had a chance to + verb?

Usage: Politely ask about progress without assuming the person had time to act. It can sound gentler than Have you done it?, but tone and context still matter.
Have you had a chance to look at the estimate?

column2: Could you + verb? · I was wondering if you could + verb · Would it be possible to + verb? · Could I ask you a favor? · I would be grateful if you could + verb
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Make a request.

1. Could you + verb?

Usage: Make a normal polite request; name the action and deadline clearly.
Could you send me the revised estimate by Thursday?

2. I was wondering if you could + verb

Usage: Soften the approach; was wondering need not refer to a past request.
I was wondering if you could review the opening paragraph.

3. Would it be possible to + verb?

Usage: Ask about feasibility; context can leave the actor implicit.
Would it be possible to move the appointment to next week?

4. Could I ask you a favor?

Usage: Introduce a request, then say specifically what help you want.
Could I ask you a favor? Could you check the address before I book?

5. I would be grateful if you could + verb

Usage: Make a more formal request, often in correspondence.
I would be grateful if you could confirm the booking by Friday. — A more formal request.

column2: Can/Could I + verb? · Do you mind if + present clause? · Would you mind + V-ing? · Is it okay if + clause? · Would you mind if + past clause?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Ask permission or request an action.

1. Can/Could I + verb?

Usage: Ask permission for your own action.
Can I use this seat?
Could I use this seat?

2. Do you mind if + present clause?

Usage: Ask whether your proposed action would cause an objection; No normally grants permission. Go ahead or Sure makes your response clearer than an isolated yes/no.
Do you mind if I record the call? — No, go ahead.

3. Would you mind + V-ing?

Usage: Ask the other person to act; use V-ing, not a clause describing your action.
Would you mind closing the window? — Sure, no problem.

4. Is it okay if + clause?

Usage: Check whether your proposed action is acceptable.
Is it okay if I send the draft tomorrow morning?

5. Would you mind if + past clause?

Usage: Politely ask permission; the past form can describe a request about now.
Would you mind if I opened the window? — A polite request about now, despite the past form.

column2: Do you want me to + verb? · Do you need a hand with + noun? · What would you like me to + verb?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Offer help or ask which action the other person wants.

1. Do you want me to + verb?

Usage: Offer to do a specific action; me is the person who would do it.
Do you want me to book the room?

2. Do you need a hand with + noun?

Usage: Offer help with a task or thing; need a hand is conversational.
Do you need a hand with your luggage?

3. What would you like me to + verb?

Usage: Ask which action the other person wants you to perform.
What would you like me to check first?

column2: Are you free + time/to + verb? · Does + time + work for you? · Could we move + event + to + time? · I can’t make it (to + event) · Can we make it + time? · When will you be ready to + verb? · Do you have any plans for + time?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Check availability, propose a time, reschedule, or ask about readiness.

1. Are you free + time/to + verb?

Usage: Check availability, rather than price.
Are you free tomorrow afternoon?
Are you free to talk for ten minutes?

2. Does + time + work for you?

Usage: Ask whether a proposed time is suitable.
Does three o’clock work for you?

3. Could we move + event + to + time?

Usage: Reschedule a named event to a new time.
Could we move the meeting to Friday?

4. I can’t make it (to + event)

Usage: Say you cannot attend or arrive at the event.
Sorry, I can’t make it to the team lunch.

5. Can we make it + time?

Usage: Propose a different meeting time.
Can we make it Thursday instead?

6. When will you be ready to + verb?

Usage: Ask when someone will be prepared to act.
When will you be ready to share the first draft?

7. Do you have any plans for + time?

Usage: Ask about existing plans, often before proposing something.
Do you have any plans for the weekend?

column2: Do you want to/Would you like to + verb? · How about + noun/V-ing? · Why don’t we + verb? · Let’s + verb
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Invite someone or suggest a joint action.

1. Do you want to/Would you like to + verb?

Usage: Invite someone to an activity; would you like to is a polite alternative.
Do you want to get dinner after the conference?
Would you like to get dinner after the conference?

2. How about + noun/V-ing?

Usage: Propose an option with a noun or V-ing.
How about meeting somewhere near your office?

3. Why don’t we + verb?

Usage: Suggest a joint action; use a base verb after we.
Why don’t we split the work and compare notes tomorrow?

4. Let’s + verb

Usage: Make a conversational suggestion; should ... sometime is friendly but does not fix a date.
Let’s take a short break.
We should go hiking sometime.

column2: go + recreational activity in -ing
column3:
1. go + recreational activity in -ing

Usage: Describe participating in activities such as hiking, shopping, swimming, or skiing. This is a conventional activity pattern, not permission to put any verb after go in -ing form.
We went hiking after the conference.
Would you like to go swimming this weekend?

column2: That would be great, thanks · I’m good, thanks · Thanks for asking, but + clause · I’d love to, but + clause · I would rather not + verb
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Accept or decline an offer or invitation.

1. That would be great, thanks

Usage: Accept an offer and acknowledge the help.
That would be great, thanks. I could use some help with the setup.

2. I’m good, thanks

Usage: Politely decline a small offer such as coffee or help.
A: Want some more coffee? B: I’m good, thanks.

3. Thanks for asking, but + clause

Usage: Thank someone before declining an invitation or offer.
Thanks for asking, but I already have plans that evening.

4. I’d love to, but + clause

Usage: Warmly decline an invitation, then explain the obstacle.
I’d love to, but I already have plans that evening.

5. I would rather not + verb

Usage: State a preference not to act, without needing an invented excuse.
I would rather not join the group photo.

column2: Please do not + verb · I need you to + verb · I need + noun + from + person
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Set a boundary or state what you need from someone.

1. Please do not + verb

Usage: Set a boundary with a direct negative instruction.
Please do not share this outside the team.

2. I need you to + verb

Usage: State the action you require another person to perform.
I need you to let me finish before responding.

3. I need + noun + from + person

Usage: Name the information or thing you need from someone.
I need a clear answer from you before I can make plans.

column2: Sorry for/about + noun · Sorry for + V-ing · That was my mistake
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Apologize and acknowledge responsibility.

1. Sorry for/about + noun

Usage: Apologize for a situation or problem; about commonly names the situation.
I am sorry about the confusion.

2. Sorry for + V-ing

Usage: Apologize for your action with V-ing.
I am sorry for sending the wrong link.

3. That was my mistake

Usage: Accept responsibility and, when needed, state a repair. Sorry to hear that instead expresses sympathy, without necessarily accepting responsibility.
That was my mistake. I will send the corrected version now.

column2: I appreciate + noun/V-ing/how-clause · Thank you for + noun/V-ing
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Express thanks.

1. I appreciate + noun/V-ing/how-clause

Usage: Take the appreciated thing/action directly, without for; a how-clause can name the appreciated manner. Object-form subjects such as you taking are natural conversationally.
I appreciate your patience.
I appreciate you taking the time to explain.
I appreciate how carefully you explained the options.

2. Thank you for + noun/V-ing

Usage: Use for before the thing or action you are thanking someone for.
Thank you for checking the figures.

column2: How have you been? · How is + event/day + going? · How is + task + coming along? · What have you been up to? · How was + event?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Open a conversation.

1. How have you been?

Usage: Ask about someone's life or well-being over a recent period.
How have you been? It has been a while since we last talked.

2. How is + event/day + going?

Usage: Ask how an ongoing experience or event is developing.
How is your first week going?

3. How is + task + coming along?

Usage: Ask about progress on a task or project.
How is the new website coming along?

4. What have you been up to?

Usage: Ask about recent activities, rather than only health.
What have you been up to since you moved?

5. How was + event?

Usage: Ask about a finished experience or event.
How was your trip to Los Angeles?

column2: I think/suppose/guess/hope so · I do not think so · I suppose/guess/hope not · I am afraid so/not
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Respond to a yes-or-no proposition without restating it.

1. I think/suppose/guess/hope so

Usage: Use so to stand for a positive proposition rather than repeating it.
Will the office be open? — I think so.
Will the office be open? — I suppose so.
Will the office be open? — I guess so.
Will the replacement arrive today? — I hope so.

2. I do not think so

Usage: Give a negative response with think; use do not think so.
Will the meeting run late? — I do not think so.

3. I suppose/guess/hope not

Usage: Give a negative reply with suppose/guess/hope not.
Will the meeting run late? — I suppose not.
Will the meeting run late? — I guess not.
Will the meeting run late? — I hope not.

4. I am afraid so/not

Usage: Politely give an unwelcome answer; afraid here need not express fear.
Do we need to start again? — I am afraid so.
Do we need to start again? — Can we recover the original file? — I am afraid not.

column2: What do you think of/about + noun? · How do you feel about + noun/V-ing?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Invite a view or reaction.

1. What do you think of/about + noun?

Usage: Ask for an opinion; think of/about commonly overlap here.
What do you think of the new office?
What do you think about the new office?

2. How do you feel about + noun/V-ing?

Usage: Ask for an attitude or reaction, which need not be emotional.
How do you feel about working abroad?

column2: I am glad/relieved that + clause · I am glad/relieved to + verb
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Express happiness or relief, using a complete situation or an action.

1. I am glad/relieved that + clause

Usage: Name the situation in a that-clause: glad expresses happiness; relieved means a worry has eased.
I am glad that you enjoyed the visit.
I am relieved that everyone got home safely.

2. I am glad/relieved to + verb

Usage: Use to + verb for an action with the same understood subject.
I am glad to hear that you enjoyed the visit.
I am relieved to be home after that flight.

column2: I am worried/concerned that + clause · I am worried/concerned about + noun/V-ing · It concerns me that + clause · My concern is that + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Express worry and identify its cause.

1. I am worried/concerned that + clause

Usage: Identify the worrying situation using a complete clause; worried/concerned overlap.
I'm worried that we're promising more than we can deliver.
I'm concerned that we're promising more than we can deliver.

2. I am worried/concerned about + noun/V-ing

Usage: Identify the topic or action causing worry using about + noun/V-ing.
I'm worried about missing the deadline.
I'm concerned about missing the deadline.

3. It concerns me that + clause

Usage: Make the worrying situation the cause of your concern with it concerns me that.
It concerns me that nobody explained the change.

4. My concern is that + clause

Usage: Use the noun concern to introduce the issue you are worried about. As far as I am concerned instead introduces a viewpoint.
My concern is that users could lose access to their accounts.

column2: I feel + adjective + when + clause · It bothers me that/when + clause · I love it/hate it/can’t stand it when + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe how a situation affects you.

1. I feel + adjective + when + clause

Usage: Name your emotional reaction and the situation that produces it. Describe the behavior/situation without assuming you know another person's intentions.
I feel left out when decisions are made without me.

2. It bothers me that/when + clause

Usage: Name a situation that causes annoyance, distress, or worry.
It bothers me that nobody explained the change.
It bothers me when people interrupt before I have finished.

3. I love it/hate it/can’t stand it when + clause

Usage: Express liking or strong dislike of a situation; have had enough of marks reaching your limit.
I love it when the whole team is involved in a decision.
I can’t stand it when people interrupt before I’ve finished.
I’ve had enough of being interrupted.

column2: I can see why + clause · Do you want to talk about it? · I am sorry to hear that + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Acknowledge another person’s experience and offer support.

1. I can see why + clause

Usage: Recognize why someone reacts as they do, without endorsing every reaction.
I can see why you are frustrated; the instructions changed twice.

2. Do you want to talk about it?

Usage: Offer space to discuss the experience.
Do you want to talk about it, or would you prefer some time alone?

3. I am sorry to hear that + clause

Usage: Express sympathy rather than accepting responsibility for causing the problem.
I am sorry to hear that your trip was canceled.

column2: be comfortable/uncomfortable + V-ing · be comfortable/uncomfortable with + noun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe whether an activity or situation feels acceptable or manageable.

1. be comfortable/uncomfortable + V-ing

Usage: State how acceptable or manageable an activity feels, using V-ing directly. Uncomfortable can express a boundary or hesitation rather than inability. Getting comfortable describes growing confidence.
I am not comfortable sharing that information.
I am getting more comfortable speaking up in meetings.

2. be comfortable/uncomfortable with + noun

Usage: State how acceptable a proposal or situation feels, using with + noun.
Are you comfortable with the proposed schedule?

column2: It was great talking to you · I should get going · Let’s keep in touch
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Close a conversation politely.

1. It was great talking to you

Usage: Acknowledge that you enjoyed the conversation.
It was great talking to you. I enjoyed hearing about your work.

2. I should get going

Usage: Politely signal that you need to leave.
I should get going; I have an early meeting tomorrow.

3. Let’s keep in touch

Usage: Express interest in future contact without setting a specific plan.
Let’s keep in touch. I will send you the article we discussed.

column2: I work as/for/on + noun · I have + duration + of experience in/with + noun · My role involves/involved + V-ing
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Introduce your work precisely.

1. I work as/for/on + noun

Usage: Use as for your role, for for your employer/client, and on for your project.
I work as a software engineer for a small company, mainly on internal tools.

2. I have + duration + of experience in/with + noun

Usage: Name your duration and area of experience; in and with can overlap depending on the area.
I have five years of experience in backend development and three years of experience with distributed systems.

3. My role involves/involved + V-ing

Usage: Describe the activities included in your role.
My previous role involved coordinating releases across three teams.

column2: be responsible for + noun/V-ing · My contribution was to + verb · I + action, which + result
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Explain responsibility and contribution.

1. be responsible for + noun/V-ing

Usage: Identify a duty or accountability; it does not always mean personally causing an outcome.
I was responsible for reviewing deployment plans.

2. My contribution was to + verb

Usage: Name your specific contribution rather than only listing responsibilities.
My contribution was to automate the repetitive checks.

3. I + action, which + result

Usage: Link a concrete action to its result; which can summarize the preceding action.
I shortened the approval process, which reduced the average waiting time by two days.

column2: Where are we with + task? · Could you give me an update on + task? · I will keep you posted on + noun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Request or promise progress information.

1. Where are we with + task?

Usage: Ask where a task stands, rather than asking its physical location.
Where are we with the data migration?

2. Could you give me an update on + task?

Usage: Politely request current progress information.
Could you give me an update on the customer interviews?

3. I will keep you posted on + noun

Usage: Promise further updates as information becomes available.
I will keep you posted on the launch date.

column2: Here is what we agreed on · The next step is to + verb
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Summarize a decision and its immediate follow-through.

1. Here is what we agreed on

Usage: Summarize the actual agreement.
Here is what we agreed on: the first release will support email login only.

2. The next step is to + verb

Usage: Name the immediate next action; add an owner/deadline when relevant.
The next step is to confirm who owns the approval.

column2: We are blocked by + noun · We need more time to + verb
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Explain an obstacle or request more time.

1. We are blocked by + noun

Usage: Identify the dependency that prevents progress.
We are blocked by the missing test credentials.

2. We need more time to + verb

Usage: State the time requirement and explain the reason when requesting a change.
We need more time to verify the migration before we commit to a date.

column2: Just a heads-up: + clause · I (just) wanted to let you know/check/ask + clause · Just a quick question: + question
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Give advance notice or open a short work message without sounding demanding.

1. Just a heads-up: + clause

Usage: Give advance notice of something relevant; heads-up is conversational and common at work.
Just a heads-up: the maintenance window has moved to Friday.

2. I (just) wanted to let you know/check/ask + clause

Usage: Soften the introduction to current information, a check, or a request.
I wanted to let you know that I will be offline tomorrow morning.
I just wanted to check whether Thursday still works for you.

3. Just a quick question: + question

Usage: Introduce a brief question in a low-pressure way.
Just a quick question: are the slides due today or tomorrow?

column2: I would appreciate your feedback on + noun · Could you tell me what I could improve?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Ask for an assessment that helps you revise your work.

1. I would appreciate your feedback on + noun

Usage: Ask for an assessment of a specific piece of work.
I would appreciate your feedback on the revised timeline.

2. Could you tell me what I could improve?

Usage: Ask what to improve; the embedded question keeps statement word order.
Could you tell me what I could improve in the opening paragraph?

column2: I am writing to + verb · I am writing about/regarding/in response to + noun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

State the purpose of an email or letter.

1. I am writing to + verb

Usage: State the action or purpose of your message using to + verb.
I am writing to ask whether the workshop is open to remote participants.

2. I am writing about/regarding/in response to + noun

Usage: Name the topic, or the earlier message prompting your response; regarding is more formal than about.
I am writing about the duplicate charge.
I am writing regarding the duplicate charge.
I am writing in response to your request for feedback.

column2: I am following up on + noun · Please let me know + if/whether/wh-clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Refer back to an earlier request and specify the information you need.

1. I am following up on + noun

Usage: Refer back to an earlier request, estimate, or matter.
I am following up on the estimate you sent last week.

2. Please let me know + if/whether/wh-clause

Usage: Specify the information you want; keep statement order after whether or a question word.
Please let me know whether the price includes installation.
Please let me know when you expect to finish.

column2: Something went wrong with + noun · X is not working properly · It only happens when + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe an observable problem and the conditions that trigger it.

1. Something went wrong with + noun

Usage: Identify the part of a process where a failure occurred.
Something went wrong with the upload; half the files are missing.

2. X is not working properly

Usage: Describe something as malfunctioning; add the actual observed behavior when useful.
The search filter is not working properly.

3. It only happens when + clause

Usage: State the circumstances that trigger the problem.
It only happens when I switch accounts.

column2: Can you walk me through + noun? · Let me walk you through + noun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Ask for or offer a step-by-step explanation.

1. Can you walk me through + noun?

Usage: Ask for an explanation in steps.
Can you walk me through the steps that led to the error?

2. Let me walk you through + noun

Usage: Offer an explanation in steps.
Let me walk you through how we estimated the cost.

column2: That did not solve/fix + noun · X solved/fixed + noun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Report whether an attempted remedy worked.

1. That did not solve/fix + noun

Usage: Report that an attempted remedy failed and identify the remaining problem.
That did not solve the problem; the same error appears after I sign in.

2. X solved/fixed + noun

Usage: Report a successful remedy; solve/fix overlap for many practical problems.
Restarting the service fixed the connection issue.

column2: The problem with + noun/V-ing + is that + clause · A possible solution to + noun + is to + verb · One way to + verb + is to + verb
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Move from a problem to a response or method.

1. The problem with + noun/V-ing + is that + clause

Usage: Identify the weakness of a process, thing, or activity.
The problem with the current process is that nobody owns the final decision.

2. A possible solution to + noun + is to + verb

Usage: Propose a response to the named problem.
A possible solution to the delay is to assign one reviewer.

3. One way to + verb + is to + verb

Usage: Describe a possible method without claiming it is the only one.
One way to reduce misunderstandings is to summarize decisions in writing.

column2: There is a risk of + V-ing
column3:
1. There is a risk of + V-ing

Usage: Use this to describe a possible harmful or unwanted result.
There is a risk of losing public trust if the process is not transparent.
There is a serious risk of widening the gap between urban and rural communities.
Without regular maintenance, there is a risk of the equipment failing unexpectedly.

column2: Compared with/to + noun, + clause · in terms of + aspect · be about the same · differ in + aspect · What makes X better than Y?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Set a comparison and its dimension.

1. Compared with/to + noun, + clause

Usage: Establish the reference point of a comparison; compare like with like.
Compared with the old design, the new one is easier to maintain.
Compared to the old design, the new one is easier to maintain.

2. in terms of + aspect

Usage: Name the dimension of evaluation or comparison.
They are about the same in terms of cost, but they differ in reliability.
I do not see much difference between the two plans.

3. be about the same

Usage: Describe approximate equality on the specified dimension.
They are about the same in terms of cost.

4. differ in + aspect

Usage: Name the dimension on which the two things differ.
They differ in reliability.

5. What makes X better than Y?

Usage: Ask which feature gives one option an advantage.
What makes this option better than the other one?

column2: much/far/slightly/a little + comparative + than · any/no + comparative
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Place these words before a comparative to show whether the difference is large or small.

1. much/far/slightly/a little + comparative + than

Usage: Show how large or small a difference is by modifying a comparative.
Public transportation is far more affordable than owning a car.
It is much cheaper than driving every day.
The revised proposal is slightly less expensive than the original one.
The second explanation was a little clearer than the first.

2. any/no + comparative

Usage: Ask whether there is any improvement or state that there is none.
Is the connection any faster now? — No, it is no faster than before.

column2: twice/three times as + adjective/adverb + as · twice/three times the + size/number/amount + of
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Compare quantities by a multiplier.

1. twice/three times as + adjective/adverb + as

Usage: Compare by a multiplier; as long measures duration/length and as many measures count. Avoid ambiguous comparisons such as twice smaller.
The new battery lasts twice as long as the old one.
This year we received three times as many applications as last year.

2. twice/three times the + size/number/amount + of

Usage: Name the measured quantity explicitly with the size/number/amount of.
The new office is twice the size of the old one.

column2: as + adjective/adverb + as · not as + adjective/adverb + as · comparative + than expected · as + adjective/adverb + as possible/you can
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Compare equality, a lower degree, or a result against expectations.

1. as + adjective/adverb + as

Usage: Express equality on a particular quality.
The smaller room is as quiet as the larger one, but it is not as bright.

2. not as + adjective/adverb + as

Usage: Say something has a lower degree of a quality.
The smaller room is as quiet as the larger one, but it is not as bright.
It was not as difficult as it seemed.

3. comparative + than expected

Usage: Compare the actual result with an earlier expectation.
The task was easier than I expected.

4. as + adjective/adverb + as possible/you can

Usage: Ask for the greatest feasible degree; possible and you can often overlap.
Please explain the problem as clearly as possible.
Please explain it as clearly as you can.

column2: the + superlative + noun · one of the + superlative + plural noun · the + superlative + noun + I have ever + past participle
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Identify an extreme within a relevant group.

1. the + superlative + noun

Usage: Identify the extreme within the relevant group.
This is the most practical option within our budget.

2. one of the + superlative + plural noun

Usage: Identify one member of an extreme group; use a plural noun after one of the.
She is one of the most reliable people I have worked with.

3. the + superlative + noun + I have ever + past participle

Usage: Compare with your experience up to now using ever + present perfect.
That was the best meal I have ever had on a flight.

column2: too + adjective/adverb + to + verb · adjective/adverb + enough + to + verb · enough + noun + to/for
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Too describes exceeding a useful limit; enough describes reaching the required amount or degree.

1. too + adjective/adverb + to + verb

Usage: Say a useful limit has been exceeded; too does not simply mean very.
The room is too small to hold everyone.

2. adjective/adverb + enough + to + verb

Usage: Say the required degree is reached; enough follows the adjective/adverb.
The room is large enough to hold everyone.
She explained it slowly enough for everyone to follow.

3. enough + noun + to/for

Usage: Say the required amount is available; enough precedes the noun, and for can name the purpose/person.
We have enough time to test it, and two days should be enough for the review.

column2: so + adjective/adverb (that + clause) · such + (a/an +) noun phrase (that + clause)
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Use so before an adjective/adverb and such before a noun phrase.

1. so + adjective/adverb (that + clause)

Usage: Intensify an adjective/adverb, optionally introducing its result with that. Use so much/many before quantities.
The application process was so complicated that many people gave up.
She explained it so clearly that we finished in minutes.

2. such + (a/an +) noun phrase (that + clause)

Usage: Intensify a noun phrase; include a/an with a singular count noun.
It was such a convincing presentation that the committee approved the proposal immediately.
It was such a useful explanation.

column2: even + focused phrase · even + comparative
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Highlight an unexpected inclusion or a further change in degree.

1. even + focused phrase

Usage: Place even near the unexpected person, thing, or action. This focus-marker use is separate from clause-introducing even though/even if.
Even the manager had trouble finding the setting. — The manager was an unexpected person to have trouble.
She even checked the links in the footnotes. — An unexpected extra action.

2. even + comparative

Usage: Emphasize a further change in degree.
The new interface is even easier to use than the previous version.

column2: only + focused phrase · not all/every + noun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Limit a claim precisely.

1. only + focused phrase

Usage: Limit the claim; moving only changes what is restricted.
Only Maya reviewed the draft.
Maya reviewed only the draft. — Who reviewed versus what she reviewed.

2. not all/every + noun

Usage: Allow at least one exception; compare none, which excludes every member.
Not all the changes were useful.
None of the changes were useful. — Some exceptions versus zero useful changes.

column2: There’s only so much … / There are only so many …
column3:
1. There’s only so much … / There are only so many …

Usage: Emphasize that resources, capacity, or tolerance have a limit. Use much with uncountable nouns or without a stated noun; use many with plural countable nouns.
There’s only so much we can do without access to the source code.
There’s only so much time we can spend investigating this issue.
There are only so many tasks we can handle at once.

column2: The more/less + clause, the more/less + clause · As + quantity + changes, + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe linked changes.

1. The more/less + clause, the more/less + clause

Usage: Highlight two changes that vary together with a paired comparative.
The more clearly we define the task, the less time we spend revising it.
The longer I work without a break, the harder it is to concentrate.

2. As + quantity + changes, + clause

Usage: Link a change in quantity to another change without automatically proving causation.
As the number of users increases, the average response time rises.

column2: get/become + adjective/comparative · comparative and comparative · more and more + adjective/noun · a growing number of + plural noun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe a developing state or trend.

1. get/become + adjective/comparative

Usage: Describe a developing state; get is often conversational and become is neutral.
The evenings are getting colder.
The evenings are becoming colder.

2. comparative and comparative

Usage: Describe a continuing trend by repeating a short comparative.
The process is getting easier and easier.

3. more and more + adjective/noun

Usage: Use more and more with longer adjectives or an increasing quantity of a noun.
The requirements are becoming more and more complicated.
More and more people are choosing to work remotely.

4. a growing number of + plural noun

Usage: Describe an increasing count; a growing number of + plural noun takes a plural verb.
A growing number of employees are choosing flexible schedules.

column2: increase/decrease by + amount · increase/decrease from X to Y · an increase/decrease in + variable
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Distinguish the amount of change from its starting and ending levels.

1. increase/decrease by + amount

Usage: Use by for the amount of change; to alone names the final level, not the change. A change from 20% to 30% is ten percentage points, or a 50% relative increase.
The price increased by ten dollars.
The fee decreased by ten dollars.
Compare: the price increased to sixty dollars names the final level, not the amount of change.

2. increase/decrease from X to Y

Usage: Use from for the starting level and to for the ending level.
The price increased from fifty to sixty dollars.
The fee decreased from sixty to fifty dollars.

3. an increase/decrease in + variable

Usage: Use in to identify which variable changed.
There has been a decrease in the number of complaints.

column2: account for/make up + share + of + whole · fraction/percentage + of + group
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe part of a total.

1. account for/make up + share + of + whole

Usage: Express what portion of the whole something represents; account for/make up overlap numerically. A large/big/substantial/considerable/sizable share is a considerable portion; significant can emphasize size or importance. A large share need not exceed half; a majority does. Larger compares portions; largest identifies the biggest.
Rent accounts for/makes up a substantial share of my monthly expenses.

2. fraction/percentage + of + group

Usage: Use of to identify the group the fraction/percentage comes from.
About 40% of the respondents work remotely.
Three out of four participants preferred the shorter form.

column2: The chart/table shows + noun/wh-clause · The figures for + group + verb
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Introduce what a visual or data set represents.

1. The chart/table shows + noun/wh-clause

Usage: Explain what the chart represents with a noun or question-word clause. The frame does not establish a cause; describe only what the data support.
The chart shows how average commuting time changed over five years.

2. The figures for + group + verb

Usage: Name the group or measure whose figures you are describing.
The figures for remote workers remained stable throughout the period.

column2: the number of + plural count noun · the amount of + uncountable noun · a number of + plural count noun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

The number of measures a count and takes a singular verb; the amount of measures an uncountable quantity and also takes a singular verb.

1. the number of + plural count noun

Usage: Describe a count; the number of ... takes a singular verb.
The number of applications has increased, but the amount of available funding has not.

2. the amount of + uncountable noun

Usage: Describe an uncountable quantity; the amount of ... takes a singular verb.
The number of applications has increased, but the amount of available funding has not.

3. a number of + plural count noun

Usage: Mean several; a number of ... takes a plural verb.
A number of applicants have asked for feedback.

column2: about/roughly + number · more or less + quantity/description · at least/no less than + number · at most/no more than + number
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Give an estimate or bound.

1. about/roughly + number

Usage: Give an approximate number; about and roughly overlap.
About forty people attended.
Roughly forty people attended.

2. more or less + quantity/description

Usage: Give an approximate quantity or broadly accurate description.
The task took more or less an hour.
The two versions are more or less identical.

3. at least/no less than + number

Usage: Set a minimum; no less than can emphasize a surprisingly large amount. A bound need not be the exact amount.
We need at least three reviewers; no fewer would be enough.
No less than fifty people volunteered.

4. at most/no more than + number

Usage: Set a maximum; no more than can emphasize a small amount.
The visit will take at most two hours.
The visit will take no more than two hours.

column2: few/a few + plural count noun · a couple of + plural count noun · little/a little + uncountable noun · fewer/less + noun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Few/little emphasizes scarcity; a few/a little emphasizes that some is available.

1. few/a few + plural count noun

Usage: Few emphasizes scarcity; a few emphasizes that some countable items exist.
Few applicants had relevant experience.
A few applicants had relevant experience.

2. a couple of + plural count noun

Usage: Mean two, or loosely a small number in conversation.
A couple of applicants had worked in healthcare.

3. little/a little + uncountable noun

Usage: Little emphasizes scarcity; a little emphasizes some available uncountable quantity.
We have little time left.
We have a little time left.

4. fewer/less + noun

Usage: Use fewer for countable items and less for amounts, including measurements treated as amounts.
We received fewer complaints and spent less time answering them.
The repair took less than two hours.

column2: much + uncountable noun · many + plural count noun · a lot of/lots of/plenty of + noun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Choose a quantity expression that matches countability.

1. much + uncountable noun

Usage: Use much with uncountable amounts, especially in questions/negatives or after too/so. Plain affirmative much often sounds formal.
Do we have much time?

2. many + plural count noun

Usage: Use many with plural countable nouns.
Do we have many options?
There is plenty of room, but there are too many chairs near the door.

3. a lot of/lots of/plenty of + noun

Usage: A lot of/lots of work with either noun type; plenty of means enough or more than enough.
We have a lot of work and lots of unanswered questions.
There is plenty of room, but there are too many chairs near the door.

column2: all/most/some + noun · all/most/some of + determiner/pronoun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Without of, refer to a group directly.

1. all/most/some + noun

Usage: Name a group directly without selecting from an already specified group.
Most people prefer clear instructions.

2. all/most/some of + determiner/pronoun

Usage: Use of before a determiner/pronoun; all can omit of before a determiner, but not an object pronoun.
Most of the people we interviewed preferred a shorter form.
All of us contributed, and some of our suggestions were accepted.
All my notes are online.
All of my notes are online.

column2: both + plural noun · either/neither + singular noun · both/either/neither of + identified pair
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe two choices: both includes the two; either selects one or the other; neither excludes both.

1. both + plural noun

Usage: Include two members, using a plural noun after both.
Both options work.

2. either/neither + singular noun

Usage: Select either one or exclude both; use a singular noun after either/neither.
Either option is acceptable.
Neither option requires a subscription.

3. both/either/neither of + identified pair

Usage: Select from an identified pair; use of before a determiner or object pronoun. Agreement after either/neither of varies; singular is the cautious formal choice.
Both of us can drive, so either of us can take you.
Neither of these plans includes support.

column2: some/any + noun · someone/anyone · something/anything
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Refer to unspecified amounts, people, or things.

1. some/any + noun

Usage: Some commonly introduces an amount; any appears in questions/negatives and can mean whichever.
I bought some fruit, but I did not buy any bread.
Choose any seat.

2. someone/anyone

Usage: Refer to an unspecified person; any is common in an open condition.
If anyone needs help, ask someone at the front desk.

3. something/anything

Usage: Refer to an unspecified thing; something is natural in an offer expecting an available option.
Would you like something to drink?
Do you have anything without caffeine?

column2: no + noun · not ... any + noun · none of + identified group
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Express zero quantity.

1. no + noun

Usage: Put no directly before a noun to express zero.
There are no seats left.

2. not ... any + noun

Usage: Express the same zero quantity with a negative verb and any. Do not add another negative for the same negation in standard English.
There are not any seats left.

3. none of + identified group

Usage: Select zero members of an identified group.
None of the proposals addressed the main concern.

column2: all (of) the + noun · the whole + singular count noun · every + singular count noun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Distinguish a complete amount, a complete individual thing, and every member or occasion.

1. all (of) the + noun

Usage: Describe the complete amount or period; all also works with uncountable nouns.
I read all of the report.
We need all the information before deciding.
I worked all day yesterday.

2. the whole + singular count noun

Usage: Describe one complete countable thing or period.
I read the whole report.

3. every + singular count noun

Usage: Describe each member or repeated occasion; every day differs from all day.
I work from home every day.

column2: each + singular noun · every + singular noun · each of + group · every one of + group
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Each draws attention to individual members; every includes all members of a group.

1. each + singular noun

Usage: Focus on individual members; each can refer to a pair.
Each reviewer has a copy.

2. every + singular noun

Usage: Include every member; every normally involves more than two and can express frequency.
Every reviewer has a copy.

3. each of + group

Usage: Use each of before an identified group or object pronoun.
Each of the two proposals has a clear advantage.
I checked every one of the attachments; each of them opened correctly.

4. every one of + group

Usage: Include every individual in the group; use every one of, not every of.
I checked every one of the attachments; each of them opened correctly.

column2: Do/Does/Did + subject + base verb? · be/auxiliary/modal + subject ...? · Who/What + verb ...?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Choose question structure according to the verb/helper and whether the question word is the subject.

1. Do/Does/Did + subject + base verb?

Usage: Invert do/does/did for ordinary simple-tense questions; the main verb stays in its base form.
How does the system work?
Why did you decide to leave?
Who did you ask for help?

2. be/auxiliary/modal + subject ...?

Usage: Invert be or the existing auxiliary/modal instead of adding do.
Where is the entrance?
Have they confirmed?
Can we start?

3. Who/What + verb ...?

Usage: When who/what is the subject, normally do not add do.
Who changed the settings?
What happened to the original plan?

column2: How come + subject + verb? · Why + auxiliary + subject + verb?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Ask for a reason.

1. How come + subject + verb?

Usage: Ask for a reason conversationally, using statement word order.
How come the deadline changed?
How come she is leaving early?

2. Why + auxiliary + subject + verb?

Usage: Ask the same kind of reason question with normal question word order.
Why did the deadline change?
Why is she leaving early?

column2: Do you know/Could you tell me + wh-word + subject + verb? · I wonder + wh-clause/if/whether-clause · Do you happen to know + noun?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Use statement word order inside an indirect question.

1. Do you know/Could you tell me + wh-word + subject + verb?

Usage: Keep statement order inside an indirect question after do you know/could you tell me.
Could you tell me where the meeting is?
Do you know when it starts?

2. I wonder + wh-clause/if/whether-clause

Usage: Present an unresolved question, using a question word or if/whether without inversion.
I have been wondering how this feature works.
I wonder whether the office is open tomorrow.

3. Do you happen to know + noun?

Usage: Soften a question about whether someone knows a person or item.
Do you happen to know the new project manager?

column2: positive statement, negative auxiliary + pronoun? · negative statement, positive auxiliary + pronoun?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Use a question tag to invite confirmation.

1. positive statement, negative auxiliary + pronoun?

Usage: Invite confirmation with a negative tag after a positive statement; match the helper. A falling voice often expects agreement; a rising voice asks more openly. After I am, the common tag is aren't I.
The meeting starts at ten, doesn’t it?
I am next, aren’t I?

2. negative statement, positive auxiliary + pronoun?

Usage: Use a positive tag after a negative statement; answer according to the actual fact.
You have not sent it yet, have you? — Yes, I have; I sent it this morning.

column2: do/does/did not + base verb · be/auxiliary/modal + not · never/nobody/nothing + affirmative verb
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Form a negative with the first helper; ordinary simple-tense main verbs need do/does/did.

1. do/does/did not + base verb

Usage: Add do/does/did for a simple-tense negative and keep the base verb. Negative contractions are normal in everyday AmE.
I do not understand the error.
She did not receive the message.

2. be/auxiliary/modal + not

Usage: Negate the first existing helper instead of adding do.
The document is not ready, and I have not checked the figures.

3. never/nobody/nothing + affirmative verb

Usage: Use one negative meaning in standard English; never/nobody/nothing do not need an extra not.
Nobody replied.
I did not hear anything.
I never received a reply.

column2: There is/are + noun · There is/are + noun + V-ing · There seems to be + noun · There used to be + noun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Introduce the existence or presence of something.

1. There is/are + noun

Usage: Introduce existence/presence; match is/are to the noun in careful English. Plural there's occurs casually, but is not the careful model here.
There is a problem with the estimate.
There are two problems with the estimate.

2. There is/are + noun + V-ing

Usage: Introduce a noun doing something; the V-ing modifier needs no second are.
There are more and more people using AI at work.

3. There seems to be + noun

Usage: Introduce an impression about something's existence.
There seems to be a misunderstanding.

4. There used to be + noun

Usage: Describe something that existed in the past but no longer does.
There used to be a bookstore on this corner.

column2: There is/are + new thing · It is + known thing’s description · It is + weather/time/distance
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Introduce existence with there, or describe an identified thing, weather, time, or distance with it.

1. There is/are + new thing

Usage: Introduce the presence of a new thing.
There is a café downstairs. It is open until eight.
It is raining, and there is water coming through the roof.

2. It is + known thing’s description

Usage: Describe something already identified with it.
There is a café downstairs. It is open until eight.

3. It is + weather/time/distance

Usage: Use it as the subject for weather, time, or distance.
It is raining, and there is water coming through the roof.
It is almost noon, and it is about two miles to the station.

column2: a/an + singular count noun · the + identified noun · plural/uncountable noun for a general class
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Use a/an for one nonspecific countable member and the when the listener can identify which one.

1. a/an + singular count noun

Usage: Introduce one nonspecific countable member; a/an follows sound, not spelling. A singular count noun normally needs an article or another determiner, such as my/this.
I spoke to a recruiter. The recruiter asked about my current role.
She is an engineer at a university, and she has a useful perspective.

2. the + identified noun

Usage: Refer to a noun the listener can identify from context or a following description.
I spoke to a recruiter. The recruiter asked about my current role.
Software can save time, but the software we bought is difficult to use.

3. plural/uncountable noun for a general class

Usage: Discuss a general plural or uncountable class without an article.
Software can save time, but the software we bought is difficult to use.

column2: a piece/item/unit/container of + uncountable noun · a pair of + plural item
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Count an amount with a suitable unit rather than giving an uncountable noun an arbitrary plural.

1. a piece/item/unit/container of + uncountable noun

Usage: Count an uncountable quantity using a suitable unit; some nouns also allow countable servings.
She gave me two pieces of advice and a useful piece of information.
I need a bottle of water and a pair of scissors.
We ordered two coffees.
I do not drink much coffee.

2. a pair of + plural item

Usage: Count a two-part item as a pair, with the item itself in its conventional plural.
I need a bottle of water and a pair of scissors.

column2: at school/work · in college/bed/prison · go to school/work/bed · at/in the + specific place
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Some institutional activities use no article, while a specific building or object often takes the.

1. at school/work

Usage: Describe participation in school/work without an article. These are conventional combinations, not a no-article rule for every place.
My daughter is at school. I am at the school to meet her teacher.
She is in college, and her brother is at work.

2. in college/bed/prison

Usage: Use conventional article-free states; AmE normally says in the hospital for a patient.
She is in college, and her brother is at work.
I went to bed early, but my phone was under the bed.
He is in the hospital recovering from surgery.

3. go to school/work/bed

Usage: Describe the destination/activity without an article in these fixed combinations.
I went to bed early, but my phone was under the bed.
He is in the hospital recovering from surgery.

4. at/in the + specific place

Usage: Use the for an identified building or object, such as the school or the bed.
My daughter is at school. I am at the school to meet her teacher.
I went to bed early, but my phone was under the bed.
He is in the hospital recovering from surgery.

column2: noun + noun · noun + of + contents · number-unit + noun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Use a noun before another noun to identify its type or purpose; the first noun is usually singular, with conventional exceptions.

1. noun + noun

Usage: Put a noun before another noun to identify type/purpose; the first noun is usually singular.
We need a coffee cup.
The customer support team handles account questions.

2. noun + of + contents

Usage: Use of to name a container's contents.
We need a cup of coffee. — A kind of container versus its contents.

3. number-unit + noun

Usage: Use a singular unit in a measurement before a noun; a duration after the verb normally has a plural unit.
It is a two-week course.
The course lasts two weeks.

column2: singular subject + singular verb · plural subject + plural verb · each/every + singular noun · one of + plural noun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Choose the verb form from the actual subject, not a nearby noun.

1. singular subject + singular verb

Usage: Match the verb to the singular head of the subject, not a nearby plural noun.
The list of requirements is on the shared drive.
Reading long reports takes practice.

2. plural subject + plural verb

Usage: Use a plural verb for plural subjects; two distinct activities joined by and normally count as plural.
The requirements are on the shared drive.
Reading and writing are different skills.

3. each/every + singular noun

Usage: Each/every before a singular noun normally takes a singular verb.
Each reviewer has access to the file.

4. one of + plural noun

Usage: One of takes a plural group noun but normally a singular verb because the subject is one.
One of the reviewers has raised a concern.

column2: possessive determiner + noun · possessive pronoun · a friend/colleague of mine/yours/hers/ours/theirs
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Use my/your/their before a noun and mine/yours/theirs when the noun is not repeated.

1. possessive determiner + noun

Usage: Use my/your/their before a noun, rather than mine/yours/theirs.
Is this your charger? — No, mine is on the desk.

2. possessive pronoun

Usage: Use mine/yours/theirs when the noun is not repeated.
Is this your charger? — No, mine is on the desk.

3. a friend/colleague of mine/yours/hers/ours/theirs

Usage: Identify one of someone's friends/colleagues using a possessive form after of.
A colleague of mine recommended the course.

column2: subject + verb + reflexive pronoun · each other/one another
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

A reflexive points back to the subject; each other and one another describe reciprocal actions.

1. subject + verb + reflexive pronoun

Usage: Point back to the subject, or emphasize who acted; do not replace an ordinary me with myself.
I taught myself the basics, then asked a colleague to check my work.
We introduced ourselves and helped each other find our seats.
I checked the original figures myself.

2. each other/one another

Usage: Express reciprocal actions between people, rather than actions directed back at the subject.
We introduced ourselves and helped each other find our seats.

column2: person/organization + ’s + noun · plural ending in s + ’ + noun · the + part + of + whole
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Express possession, association, or a part–whole relationship.

1. person/organization + ’s + noun

Usage: Use possessive 's with a person/organization or irregular plural; it also works with time expressions. Do not impose a rigid living-versus-nonliving possessive rule; the alternatives overlap.
The company’s policy changed after the employees’ feedback.
Today’s meeting starts at ten.
The children’s coats are beside the entrance.

2. plural ending in s + ’ + noun

Usage: Put the apostrophe after final plural s, as in employees' feedback.
The company’s policy changed after the employees’ feedback.
Today’s meeting starts at ten.

3. the + part + of + whole

Usage: Name a part of a whole; of is also useful with longer noun phrases.
The cover of the report lists the authors.

column2: my/your/their own + noun · a/an + noun + of my/your/their own
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Emphasize that something belongs or is assigned to that person, often rather than being shared or borrowed.

1. my/your/their own + noun

Usage: Emphasize possession or personal authorship before the noun.
I would like my own desk.
She writes her own presentations instead of using a template.

2. a/an + noun + of my/your/their own

Usage: Emphasize that someone has an individual thing of their own.
I would like a desk of my own.

column2: on my/your/their own · by myself/yourself/themselves
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Say someone is alone or does something without help.

1. on my/your/their own

Usage: Describe being alone or acting without help; context determines which.
I live on my own.
She completed the application on her own.

2. by myself/yourself/themselves

Usage: Express the same broad alone/without-help meanings with a reflexive after by.
I live by myself.
She completed the application by herself.

column2: adjective + noun · be/look/seem + adjective · verb + adverb · adverb + adjective
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Choose adjectives/adverbs according to what they describe.

1. adjective + noun

Usage: Describe a noun with an adjective placed before it.
She gave a clear explanation.

2. be/look/seem + adjective

Usage: Describe the subject's quality after a linking verb; looks good, not looks well for appearance.
The design looks good, and the system works well.

3. verb + adverb

Usage: Describe how an action is performed with an adverb; works well, not works good in the standard model. Not all adverbs end in -ly: fast/hard can be adverbs, while hardly means almost not.
She explained it clearly.
The design looks good, and the system works well.
The unusually long meeting ended surprisingly quickly.

4. adverb + adjective

Usage: Modify an adjective with an adverb, as in unusually long.
The unusually long meeting ended surprisingly quickly.

column2: feeling adjective in -ed · feeling-causing adjective in -ing
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

With paired adjectives such as bored/boring and confused/confusing, -ed describes the experienced feeling; -ing describes what causes it.

1. feeling adjective in -ed

Usage: Describe an experienced feeling with the -ed adjective. This is a meaning contrast, not a tense rule.
The instructions were confusing, so I was confused.
I am interested in the project.
It was an exhausting week, and everyone felt exhausted.

2. feeling-causing adjective in -ing

Usage: Describe what causes the feeling with the -ing adjective; people can also be interesting or boring.
The instructions were confusing, so I was confused.
I am interesting to talk to. — The second describes how other people may experience talking to me.
It was an exhausting week, and everyone felt exhausted.

column2: opinion + size/age/color/material + noun
column3:
1. opinion + size/age/color/material + noun

Usage: Put descriptive adjectives in a conventional order rather than simply translating their order from another language. Opinion usually comes before factual properties; common sequences include size, age, color, origin, and material. Use only the adjectives the listener needs.
They rented a comfortable new apartment.
I keep my notes in a small blue leather notebook.

column2: pretty/fairly/really/quite + adjective · not quite + adjective
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Adjust the strength of a description.

1. pretty/fairly/really/quite + adjective

Usage: Modify the strength of a description without memorizing a fixed intensity ranking. Pretty is conversational; fairly often sounds moderate; really intensifies. In AmE, quite can be strong, but adjective, tone, and context affect its force.
The instructions are pretty clear.
The instructions are fairly clear. — The second can sound more restrained.
The final result was really impressive.
The final result was quite impressive.

2. not quite + adjective

Usage: Mean not completely rather than simply not.
The draft is not quite ready.

column2: verb + direct object · verb + object + preposition phrase · give/send + person + thing / thing + to + person
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

A verb determines the shape of its complements; do not add a preposition by translating from Mandarin.

1. verb + direct object

Usage: Follow a verb with the object shape it permits: discuss the plan, without an inserted about.
We discussed the plan with the client.
I explained the plan to the client.

2. verb + object + preposition phrase

Usage: Name a recipient/other relation with its preposition; explain the plan to someone.
We discussed the plan with the client.
I explained the plan to the client.

3. give/send + person + thing / thing + to + person

Usage: Give/send allow two object orders; buy can take a for-phrase. Do not generalize these options to every verb.
I sent Maya the report.
I sent the report to Maya.
I bought her a ticket.
I bought a ticket for her.

column2: subject + verb + object + manner/place/time
column3:
1. subject + verb + object + manner/place/time

Usage: Use this as a practical default order, not an absolute rule. Normally keep an ordinary object close to its verb, then add how, where, or when. A time phrase can move to the front to establish the setting. Frequency adverbs follow their own positions.
I explained the problem clearly during the meeting.
We reviewed the proposal at the office yesterday.
Yesterday, we reviewed the proposal at the office.

column2: subject + also/already/probably + main verb · be/first auxiliary + adverb
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Place common middle-position adverbs where they modify the verb phrase.

1. subject + also/already/probably + main verb

Usage: Put these adverbs before an ordinary main verb; probably often precedes a negative contraction.
We also need a backup plan.
I probably will not finish today.
I probably won’t finish today.

2. be/first auxiliary + adverb

Usage: Put them after be or the first auxiliary.
The backup is already available.
She has already sent the draft, and we can probably review it today.

column2: verb + object + to + verb
column3:
1. verb + object + to + verb

Usage: Use this when the object is understood to perform or experience the following action or state. The meaning comes from the main verb: ask requests, tell directs, allow permits, cause produces a result, and expect anticipates. Common verbs include ask, tell, advise, remind, allow, enable, encourage, convince, persuade, force, want, need, and expect. Use not before to to negate the following action.
I asked her to check the figures, and she told me to revise the estimate.
The new tool allows us to test changes faster.
The outage caused us to postpone the release.
We expected the client to agree, but I could not convince her to accept the revised terms.

column2: make/let/have + person + base verb · have/get + object + past participle · want/need + object + past participle · get + person + to + verb · be made to + verb
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Distinguish causing someone to act from arranging or requiring an action on an object.

1. make/let/have + person + base verb

Usage: Make causes/forces, let permits, and have arranges an action; use a base verb without to.
The delay made us reconsider the schedule.
My supervisor let me work from home.
I had the technician check my laptop.

2. have/get + object + past participle

Usage: Make the object the recipient of the action; this can describe an arranged service or an unwanted experience.
I had my laptop checked.
I got my laptop checked.
I had my wallet stolen while I was traveling.

3. want/need + object + past participle

Usage: Describe an action you want or need completed on the object.
The manager wants all applications checked by Friday.
We need the figures verified.

4. get + person + to + verb

Usage: Name the person you bring to perform an action; get takes to here.
I got the technician to check the wiring.

5. be made to + verb

Usage: Passive make requires to, even though active make uses a base verb.
We were made to wait outside.

column2: help + person + (to) + verb
column3:
1. help + person + (to) + verb

Usage: Help allows a base verb with or without to. The person named after help performs the action. Cannot help doing is a different expression meaning you cannot stop yourself.
The examples helped me understand the rule.
The examples helped me to understand the rule.
Could you help us move the meeting to a quieter room?

column2: prevent/stop/keep + person + from + V-ing
column3:
1. prevent/stop/keep + person + from + V-ing

Usage: Describe blocking or stopping an action. Use an -ing form after from. Keep someone from doing blocks the action; keep someone doing makes it continue.
A clear agenda prevents us from wasting time on unrelated issues.
Noise kept me from sleeping; an urgent problem kept me working.

column2: consider/find + object + adjective · regard/see/treat + object + as + adjective/noun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Express an evaluation, classification, perspective, or finding.

1. consider/find + object + adjective

Usage: Express a judgment/finding with an adjective; consider/deem can also take a noun or to be, and find can take to be. Deem expresses a judgment more formally. Passive forms include be considered/deemed (to be) + adjective/noun and be found to be + adjective/noun.
We consider the proposal risky.
The proposal is considered risky.
The proposal is considered to be risky.
The pilot is considered a success.
The pilot is considered to be a success.
The committee deemed the proposal impractical.
The proposal was deemed impractical.
The pilot was deemed to be a success.
Users found the instructions confusing.
The instructions were found to be confusing.
The message was found to be a hoax.

2. regard/see/treat + object + as + adjective/noun

Usage: Express a perspective or treatment with as; passive forms retain as.
I regard clear documentation as essential.
Clear documentation is regarded as essential.
She is widely regarded as an excellent engineer.
I see the examples as a useful starting point.
The clinic treated the case as urgent.

column2: make/keep + object + adjective
column3:
1. make/keep + object + adjective

Usage: Describe causing or maintaining a state. Make introduces the resulting condition; keep maintains it. The adjective describes the object, not how the subject performs the action.
The examples made the task clearer.
Please keep the exit clear.

column2: call/name/elect + object + name/role noun
column3:
1. call/name/elect + object + name/role noun

Usage: Assign a description, name, or role to an object or person. The noun after the object identifies that object. Articles depend on the complement: a descriptive category often takes a/an, while a unique appointed role may have no article.
Critics called the plan a mistake.
The team named the platform Atlas, and the committee elected Maya chair.

column2: verb + object + place/state phrase · find/leave + object + past participle
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Use the final phrase to show where the object is placed, where it ends up, or what situation it is left in.

1. verb + object + place/state phrase

Usage: Show where the object is placed, sent, or left, or what role/state it receives.
Please put the signed forms on my desk.
The manager left me in charge of the office.
The company sent everyone home early.

2. find/leave + object + past participle

Usage: Describe the object's discovered or resulting state with a past participle.
We found the side door locked and left it closed.

column2: perception verb + object + base verb / V-ing
column3:
1. perception verb + object + base verb / V-ing

Usage: Use the base verb for a complete event and V-ing for an action observed in progress.

Common perception verbs include see, hear, watch, notice, and feel.
I watched the train leave the station.
When I entered, I saw two students discussing the results.
We heard someone knock on the door, then heard people talking outside.

column2: verb + object + V-ing
column3:
1. verb + object + V-ing

Usage: Use this when the object is involved in an ongoing action or situation. The object belongs to the main verb, and the V-ing part describes what that object is doing or experiencing.

Common verbs include catch, find, keep, leave, and have.
Security caught him entering a restricted area.
The delay kept us waiting for nearly two hours.
The announcement had everyone talking.

column2: It is + adjective + for + person + to + verb · find/make it + adjective + to + verb · It is + adjective + of + person + to + verb
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

For names the performer of an evaluated action.

1. It is + adjective + for + person + to + verb

Usage: Name who performs the evaluated action using for.
It is difficult for new employees to ask for help.

2. find/make it + adjective + to + verb

Usage: Find it expresses your evaluation; make it expresses what causes the activity's difficulty or possibility. It stands for the following action and cannot simply be omitted.
I find it useful to summarize the decision.
A template makes it easier to write the summary.

3. It is + adjective + of + person + to + verb

Usage: Evaluate a person's behavior or character with of, as in kind of you.
It was kind of you to stay and help.

column2: thing/person + be + easy/hard/difficult/safe + to + verb
column3:
1. thing/person + be + easy/hard/difficult/safe + to + verb

Usage: Evaluate an action involving the subject. The subject fills an object role in the infinitive: this tool is easy to use means using this tool is easy. Do not repeat that object. Keep a required final preposition, as in easy to work with.
The report is difficult to understand.
It is difficult to understand the report.
The new manager is easy to work with.
The water is safe to drink. — Do not add it after drink.

column2: V-ing clause + singular verb · To + verb + is + complement · What + clause + is + complement
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Use an action or a what-clause as the subject.

1. V-ing clause + singular verb

Usage: Make an activity the subject; a single V-ing activity normally takes a singular verb.
Putting related expressions together helps me compare them.

2. To + verb + is + complement

Usage: Make an infinitive the subject; an it ... to version is often easier in conversation.
To change the deadline now would create confusion.
It would create confusion to change the deadline now.

3. What + clause + is + complement

Usage: Make the thing/idea described by a what-clause the subject.
What she proposed is a shorter review cycle.

column2: enjoy/avoid/consider/finish/keep + V-ing · feel like/cannot help + V-ing
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

These verbs and expressions select an -ing action.

1. enjoy/avoid/consider/finish/keep + V-ing

Usage: Follow these verbs directly with V-ing; their meanings differ even though their complements match. A future intended action does not automatically require to instead of V-ing.
I enjoy discussing ideas, but I avoid interrupting people.
We are considering changing the schedule; we have not decided yet.
I finished reviewing the draft, but she kept adding comments.

2. feel like/cannot help + V-ing

Usage: Feel like expresses inclination; cannot help expresses a reaction/action you find difficult to avoid.
I feel like taking a walk.
I cannot help wondering whether we missed something.

column2: suggest/recommend + V-ing / suggest/recommend (that) + subject + base verb · It is important/essential that + subject + base verb
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Recommend an activity or require someone to act.

1. suggest/recommend + V-ing / suggest/recommend (that) + subject + base verb

Usage: Recommend an activity with V-ing or name its actor in a base-verb that-clause; no -s after he/she here.
Health experts recommend limiting the amount of added sugar in children's diets.
I suggest that the city expand the late-night bus service.
The doctor recommended that Maya reduce her working hours for a few weeks.

2. It is important/essential that + subject + base verb

Usage: Express a requirement with a base-verb that-clause, including be.
It is essential that each participant be informed before the schedule changes.

column2: preposition + (subject +) V-ing
column3:
1. preposition + (subject +) V-ing

Usage: Use V-ing when an action follows a preposition such as after, before, by, without, despite, about, for, in, of, or on. This also applies to prepositional to in look forward to, object to, be used to, be committed to, contribute to, admit to, and be opposed to. By + V-ing describes a method, whereas to + verb can describe a purpose. These prepositions can also take noun phrases: I look forward to the trip. Insert a subject before V-ing when you need to name who performs the action.
You can improve your pronunciation by recording yourself.
The workshop ended without anyone asking a question.
We look forward to hearing the committee's final decision.

column2: ... + subject + V-ing
column3:
1. ... + subject + V-ing

Usage: Use this when the V-ing situation has its own named performer. Object-form pronouns are common in conversation; possessive forms such as his waiting are more formal.
I do not mind him waiting outside.
She left without me noticing.
Residents objected to the company collecting their personal information.

column2: being + past participle · (not) having + past participle · having been + past participle/V-ing/adjective/noun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe passive or earlier actions in complements; this card does not teach deletion of clauses.

1. being + past participle

Usage: Use a passive V-ing complement when the subject receives the action.
I dislike being interrupted during a presentation.

2. (not) having + past participle

Usage: Mark an earlier event explicitly; not having negates it.
She regretted not having applied earlier.
She admitted having ignored the warning.

3. having been + past participle/V-ing/adjective/noun

Usage: Preserve an earlier passive event, ongoing activity, state, or identity; these forms can sound formal. These perfect complements can sound more formal/explicit than simple V-ing; this card does not teach deletion of clauses.
They objected to the data having been shared without consent.
I remember him having been working there for several years by that point.
She regretted having been so impatient.
He mentioned having been a volunteer before joining the staff.
