column2: be/get + past participle · be being + past participle · have/has been + past participle · modal + be + past participle
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Use the passive when the subject receives an action.

1. be/get + past participle

Usage: Make the recipient the subject; get is more conversational and often highlights an event. A past participle can also describe a state; context determines whether an action is being presented.
The team approved the proposal.
The proposal was approved by the team.
My account got locked after several failed attempts.

2. be being + past participle

Usage: Show a passive action in progress.
The application is being reviewed.

3. have/has been + past participle

Usage: Show a completed passive event/result with a perfect form; contrast the active been checking.
The application has been reviewed.
The engineer has been checking the system.
The system has been checked.

4. modal + be + past participle

Usage: Put be + past participle after a modal; negate the modal as required.
The file can be shared internally, but it must not be published.

column2: appear/seem + to be ... / to have + past participle
column3:
1. appear/seem + to be ... / to have + past participle

Usage: Use to be when the apparent situation exists at the same time as the judgment. Use to have + past participle when present evidence suggests an earlier event. Use to have been + V-ing for an earlier continuing activity and to have been + past participle for an earlier passive event.
The server appears to be stable now.
It appears to have recovered overnight.
The process seems to have been running all night.
The database appears to have been corrupted during the update.

column2: say (that) + clause · tell + person + clause · ask + person + if/whether/wh-clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Report speech or questions.

1. say (that) + clause

Usage: Report a statement; say does not take the listener directly as its object. Adjust pronouns/time references to the reporting context. Past reporting verbs often backshift, but still-current information can retain the present.
She said that the deadline had changed.
She said she works remotely; that is still her current arrangement.

2. tell + person + clause

Usage: Report a statement and name its listener directly after tell.
She told me that the deadline had changed.

3. ask + person + if/whether/wh-clause

Usage: Report a question using statement order after if/whether or a question word.
He asked whether I was available and when I could start.

column2: It is said/reported/believed/expected that + clause · subject + be said/reported/believed/expected + to-infinitive
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Report a claim or expectation with less focus on its source.

1. It is said/reported/believed/expected that + clause

Usage: Report a claim or expectation as an impersonal that-clause; this does not guarantee truth.
It is believed that the system is reliable.
It is expected that demand will rise.

2. subject + be said/reported/believed/expected + to-infinitive

Usage: Make the reported subject the subject; use to have + past participle for an earlier event. Use to be + adjective/noun for a state/classification; other verbs follow to directly.
The system is believed to be reliable. It is also believed to be a major improvement over the previous version.
Demand is expected to rise.
The supplier is reported to have missed several deadlines.

column2: noun + who/that/which + clause · noun + whose + noun + clause · place/time + where/when + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Add information about a person, thing, possession, place, or time.

1. noun + who/that/which + clause

Usage: Add identifying information without commas or extra information with commas; that is excluded after a comma. Do not repeat the noun's subject/object role with an extra pronoun inside the relative clause.
The colleague who reviewed my draft noticed a missing assumption.
The proposal that we discussed yesterday needs a clearer budget.
My manager, who works in Boston, will join remotely.

2. noun + whose + noun + clause

Usage: Link the noun with something it possesses; whose can refer to things too. Whose can refer to things as well as people.
I contacted the engineer whose team maintains the service.

3. place/time + where/when + clause

Usage: Add identifying place/time information using where/when.
This is the room where we met.
I remember the day when we first spoke.

column2: plural noun, some/most/none of whom/which + clause
column3:
1. plural noun, some/most/none of whom/which + clause

Usage: Add information about a subset of an already identified group. Use whom for people and which for things after of. This is useful in writing and formal explanations; in conversation, a separate sentence with them is often simpler.
We interviewed twelve applicants, three of whom had led remote teams.
They proposed five changes, most of which were inexpensive.

column2: It is a kind/type of + noun that + clause · It is something/someone that/who + clause · It is used for + V-ing / to + verb · What do you call + description? · What’s the word for + description?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe a category, person, or function when introducing an unfamiliar term or when the exact word is unavailable.

1. It is a kind/type of + noun that + clause

Usage: Define an unfamiliar thing by category and identifying information.
It is a type of sensor that detects changes in air quality.

2. It is something/someone that/who + clause

Usage: Describe a person/thing when the precise term is unavailable.
It is someone who helps new employees settle in.
It is something that warns you when the pressure gets too high.

3. It is used for + V-ing / to + verb

Usage: Describe function; for takes V-ing and to takes a base verb here. Function be used to + verb is different from the past-habit expression used to.
It is used for measuring response times.
It is used to measure response times.

4. What do you call + description?

Usage: Ask for the missing term by describing the thing.
What do you call the thing you plug several chargers into?

5. What’s the word for + description?

Usage: Ask for a missing word with for + a description.
What’s the word for a person who checks facts before an article is published?

column2: consist of + parts · include + item · involve + noun/V-ing
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe how parts relate to a whole.

1. consist of + parts

Usage: State the composition of the whole, rather than merely naming one included member.
The package consists of a camera, a cable, and a carrying case.

2. include + item

Usage: Identify an included member without requiring a complete list.
The package includes a carrying case; other items are included too.

3. involve + noun/V-ing

Usage: Identify an activity or element participating in a process/situation.
The installation involves connecting the camera and configuring the software.

column2: both X and Y · either X or Y · neither X nor Y · X rather than Y
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Coordinate matching grammatical units.

1. both X and Y

Usage: Include both matching items or ideas.
We need both accurate estimates and clear priorities.

2. either X or Y

Usage: Offer two alternatives with parallel grammatical shapes.
We can either meet online or postpone the discussion.

3. neither X nor Y

Usage: Exclude both alternatives; rephrase an awkward mixed subject if agreement becomes unclear. With either/neither subjects, agreement usually follows the nearer subject.
Neither the manager nor the reviewers are available today.

4. X rather than Y

Usage: Prefer or contrast one parallel alternative with another.
I prefer checking the assumptions rather than guessing at a solution.

column2: subject + do/does/did + base verb
column3:
1. subject + do/does/did + base verb

Usage: Use a stressed do, does, or did to emphasize an affirmative statement, often when correcting an assumption or acknowledging a point. The main verb stays in its base form.
I do think AI will change parts of our work.
She does understand the risks; she just disagrees about their likelihood.
We did test the migration, but we missed that edge case.

column2: the fact/idea/claim that + clause · noun + that + relative clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

A content clause states what the fact, idea, or claim is.

1. the fact/idea/claim that + clause

Usage: State the content of a fact, idea, or claim in the that-clause.
The claim that prices had fallen surprised us. — The content of the claim is that prices had fallen.
The fact that everyone agreed does not prove the idea was sound.

2. noun + that + relative clause

Usage: Identify which noun you mean; the noun fills a subject/object role inside the relative clause.
The claim that she made surprised us. — She made the claim; the clause identifies it.

column2: This/That + summary noun + clause · These/Those + plural noun + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Refer back to a previous idea with a noun that accurately summarizes it.

1. This/That + summary noun + clause

Usage: Summarize an earlier idea with an accurate singular noun.
We replaced weekly meetings with written updates. This approach gave everyone more uninterrupted time.

2. These/Those + plural noun + clause

Usage: Refer back to earlier changes/items using an accurate plural noun.
The team shortened the form and removed duplicate questions. These changes reduced completion time.

column2: Could you say/repeat + noun + again? · Could you slow down? · What do you mean by + noun? · Could you clarify + wh-clause?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Request repetition, a slower pace, or an explanation.

1. Could you say/repeat + noun + again?

Usage: Ask to hear the wording again, rather than requesting its meaning.
Could you say the last part again?
Could you repeat the address?

2. Could you slow down?

Usage: Request a slower speaking pace.
Could you slow down a little? I missed the number.

3. What do you mean by + noun?

Usage: Ask what an expression means in this context.
What do you mean by flexible hours?

4. Could you clarify + wh-clause?

Usage: Ask for clarification; keep statement order inside the embedded question.
Could you clarify how the approval process works?

column2: If I understand correctly, + clause · Just to confirm, + clause · So you are saying that + clause? · Does that make sense? · Are we on the same page about + noun?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Check your interpretation or shared understanding before proceeding.

1. If I understand correctly, + clause

Usage: State your interpretation so the other person can check it.
If I understand correctly, the deadline applies only to the first draft.

2. Just to confirm, + clause

Usage: Confirm a specific arrangement or fact before proceeding.
Just to confirm, we are meeting at the downtown office, right?

3. So you are saying that + clause?

Usage: Check your interpretation of the other person's message; neutral tone avoids sounding confrontational.
So you are saying that the existing accounts will keep their settings?

4. Does that make sense?

Usage: Check whether your explanation was clear to the listener.
Does that make sense, or should I go through an example?

5. Are we on the same page about + noun?

Usage: Check shared understanding or agreement about a named issue.
Are we on the same page about the deadline and who will review the draft?

column2: Can you give me an example of + noun? · Could you explain + noun + in plain English? · I do not understand why/how + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Ask for a concrete illustration or a clearer explanation.

1. Can you give me an example of + noun?

Usage: Request a concrete illustration.
Can you give me an example of a situation where this would help?

2. Could you explain + noun + in plain English?

Usage: Ask for clear language without unnecessary jargon.
Could you explain the limitation in plain English?

3. I do not understand why/how + clause

Usage: Name the specific part you do not understand; use statement order after why/how.
I do not understand why the same request produces different results.

column2: How would you say X in English? · Does X sound natural? · Can I use X to mean Y? · What is the difference between X and Y?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Ask about expression, naturalness, meaning, or a contrast.

1. How would you say X in English?

Usage: Ask for a way to express the intended meaning in English.
How would you say “I cannot attend” more politely in English?

2. Does X sound natural?

Usage: Ask whether an expression is natural in a given context.
Does “Could we move the meeting?” sound natural?

3. Can I use X to mean Y?

Usage: Ask whether wording can express your intended meaning.
Can I use “available” to mean that I have time to talk?

4. What is the difference between X and Y?

Usage: Ask for the relevant distinction; how does X compare with Y requests a broader comparison.
What is the difference between “borrow” and “lend”?
How does this expression compare with the other one?

column2: Can/Could I get + noun? · I would like + noun, please · without + ingredient · What does X come with?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Order something or ask what is included.

1. Can/Could I get + noun?

Usage: Place an order using ordinary conversational American English.
Can I get a coffee?
Could I get a coffee?

2. I would like + noun, please

Usage: Place the same order with a polite I would like form.
I would like a coffee, please.

3. without + ingredient

Usage: Request omission of an ingredient.
Can I get the sandwich without mayonnaise?

4. What does X come with?

Usage: Ask which items are included in the order. Included items are different from extras available for an additional charge.
What does the meal come with?

column2: I ordered/asked for X, but I got Y · I have not gotten my + item + yet · Could you + remedy?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Explain a service problem and request a concrete remedy.

1. I ordered/asked for X, but I got Y

Usage: Explain the mismatch between what you requested and what you received.
I ordered a vegetarian meal, but I got the chicken. Could you replace it?
I asked for a room away from the elevator. Could you move me to a quieter one?

2. I have not gotten my + item + yet

Usage: Say an expected item has not arrived yet; gotten is standard AmE here.
I have not gotten my refund yet. Could you check its status?

3. Could you + remedy?

Usage: Request a concrete remedy after explaining the service problem.
I ordered a vegetarian meal, but I got the chicken. Could you replace it?
I have not gotten my refund yet. Could you check its status?
I asked for a room away from the elevator. Could you move me to a quieter one?

column2: Do you have + item + in + size/color? · Is there another + option/time?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Ask what is available or request an alternative.

1. Do you have + item + in + size/color?

Usage: Ask whether an item is available in a particular size or color.
Do you have this jacket in a medium?
Do you have it in blue?

2. Is there another + option/time?

Usage: Ask for a different or additional option, depending on context.
Is there another appointment time on Thursday?

column2: I would like to book/reschedule/cancel + noun
column3:
1. I would like to book/reschedule/cancel + noun

Usage: Manage a reservation or appointment. Name the booking and action clearly. Book creates the reservation; reschedule changes its time; cancel ends it.
I would like to book a table for two.
I would like to reschedule my appointment for next week.
I would like to cancel my reservation for Friday.

column2: How much is it per + unit? · Is this charged by weight?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Clarify the unit price and what determines the charge.

1. How much is it per + unit?

Usage: Ask for the rate for each stated unit.
How much is it per pound?
How much is the rental per day?

2. Is this charged by weight?

Usage: Ask whether weight, rather than a fixed item/container price, determines the charge.
Is the salad charged by weight or by the container?

column2: check bags through to + destination
column3:
1. check bags through to + destination

Usage: Use this when checked luggage is sent onward to a later or final destination. Ask the airline to confirm the arrangement for your particular itinerary.
Will our bags be checked through to Taipei?
Can you check this bag through to Los Angeles?
Our bags were checked through to the final destination.

column2: be coated in/with + substance · be packed in + liquid/container · be served + adjective / with + accompaniment
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe a food or item’s presentation.

1. be coated in/with + substance

Usage: Describe a surface layer; in and with commonly both work.
The cookies are coated in chocolate.
The cookies are coated with chocolate.

2. be packed in + liquid/container

Usage: Identify the surrounding liquid or protective container.
The tuna is packed in olive oil, and the jars are packed in protective boxes.

3. be served + adjective / with + accompaniment

Usage: Describe serving condition with an adjective or an accompaniment with with.
The soup is served hot.
The soup is served with bread.

column2: I have had + symptom + for + duration · It hurts when + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe a symptom, its duration, or the action that causes discomfort.

1. I have had + symptom + for + duration

Usage: State a symptom continuing through a duration up to now.
I have had a headache for two days.

2. It hurts when + clause

Usage: State which action or circumstance causes discomfort.
It hurts when I put weight on my ankle.

column2: I need help with + noun · Could you call + person/service?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Ask for practical or urgent assistance.

1. I need help with + noun

Usage: Ask for assistance with a named task or thing.
I need help with my luggage.

2. Could you call + person/service?

Usage: Ask someone to contact a particular person/service.
Could you call an ambulance? Someone has collapsed.

column2: on the left/right · at the top/bottom · in the middle/center · at the top left/bottom right · in the upper-left/lower-right corner · at/near/along the edge of
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe general positions and boundary areas on a map, diagram, or plan.

1. on the left/right

Usage: Describe the left/right position within the map, diagram, or space.
The entrance is on the left, and the parking lot is on the right.

2. at the top/bottom

Usage: Identify the top/bottom area of the map or object.
The title is at the top, while the scale is at the bottom.

3. in the middle/center

Usage: Describe a central area; at the center is also natural for an exact point.
A courtyard is in the middle of the resort, with a fountain in the center.

4. at the top left/bottom right

Usage: Identify a position combining vertical and horizontal directions.
The office is at the top left, and the playground is at the bottom right.

5. in the upper-left/lower-right corner

Usage: Identify a specific corner using in.
The legend is in the upper-left corner, and the compass is in the lower-right corner.

6. at/near/along the edge of

Usage: At marks the boundary, near proximity to it, and along a path following it.
A gate stands at the edge of the park, several homes are near the edge, and a path runs along the edge.

column2: at + point/site · on + surface/line · in + area/enclosure · located/situated at/on/in · inside/outside/within · at home/work · on a bus/train/plane · in a car/taxi
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe location, using spatial relationships and conventional combinations.

1. at + point/site

Usage: Treat the location as a point or site.
The information booth is at the entrance.

2. on + surface/line

Usage: Describe contact with a surface or position on a line.
The map is on the wall.

3. in + area/enclosure

Usage: Locate something within an area or enclosure.
The café is in the lobby.

4. located/situated at/on/in

Usage: Add location to located/situated; be set amid describes being surrounded by something, often formally. Located is neutral; situated is slightly more formal. Set stays set as a past participle.
The office is located at 120 Main Street, on Fifth Avenue, in Boston.
The cabin is situated at the edge of the lake, on a wooded hillside, in a national park.
The hotel is set amid rolling hills.
We stayed in a cabin set amid pine trees.

5. inside/outside/within

Usage: Distinguish the inside, outside, or permitted boundary of an area.
Equipment must remain inside the marked zone, visitors must wait outside it, and staff must stay within the designated area.

6. at home/work

Usage: Use these conventional locations without an article.
I worked at home while my supervisor was at work.

7. on a bus/train/plane

Usage: Use on for these forms of passenger transportation.
I reviewed the report on the bus, revised it on the train, and emailed it on the plane.

8. in a car/taxi

Usage: Use in for a car/taxi; fixed vehicle conventions supplement the spatial model.
I left my umbrella in the car and remembered it while I was in a taxi.

column2: in + month/year/season/part of day · on + day/date/specific day-part · at + time/noon/night
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Locate events in time with in, on, or at.

1. in + month/year/season/part of day

Usage: Use in with general periods such as months, seasons, and general parts of a day.
The project starts in November.
I usually study in the evening.
Our favorite trail is busiest in summer.

2. on + day/date/specific day-part

Usage: Use on with a named day/date or a particular day's morning/evening; AmE also uses on weekends.
Our kickoff meeting is on Monday.
I have a meeting on Friday evening.
We go hiking on weekends.

3. at + time/noon/night

Usage: Use at with clock times and fixed expressions including noon, midnight, and night.
Our kickoff meeting is at 9:00 a.m.
The system runs scheduled checks at midnight and sends a report at noon.
She often works at night, especially during the busy season.

column2: to the left/right of · next to/beside/right next to · by/near · adjacent to · between/among · around · across from/opposite · in front of/behind · above/below · over/under/beneath · on top of
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Locate something relative to another object or place.

1. to the left/right of

Usage: Compare horizontal positions relative to a reference point.
The elevators are to the left of the entrance, and the restrooms are to the right of it.

2. next to/beside/right next to

Usage: Describe immediately neighboring positions; right next to emphasizes closeness.
The café is next to the bank, a bench is beside the fountain, and the ATM is right next to the door.

3. by/near

Usage: Describe proximity; by can mean beside/near, while near need not mean immediately adjacent.
A bench stands by the river, while several cafés are near the station.

4. adjacent to

Usage: Describe adjacency in a more formal way than next to/beside.
The parking garage is adjacent to the hospital.

5. between/among

Usage: Between presents distinct reference points; among locates something within a group. Between can use more than two reference points when they are treated as distinct.
The café is between the bank and the bookstore, while the statue stands among the trees.

6. around

Usage: Describe surrounding positions; at the front instead identifies part of a larger space. About can also mean around an area, but around is more common for location in AmE.
Guests sat around the table; their host stood at the front of the room.

7. across from/opposite

Usage: Locate something on the other side facing a reference point; both expressions work.
The pharmacy is across from the hotel, and the bus stop is opposite the station.

8. in front of/behind

Usage: Locate something ahead of or behind another object; before an audience is a separate formal use.
Taxis wait in front of the building, while staff parking is behind it.
The speaker stood before a large audience; her colleague waited behind the curtain.

9. above/below

Usage: Compare higher/lower positions without requiring direct vertical alignment or contact.
A sign is above the entrance, a bench is below it, a canopy hangs over it, and several bicycles are stored under it.

10. over/under/beneath

Usage: Describe above/below positions; over/under can emphasize directly vertical or covering relations, and beneath is often more formal.
A sign is above the entrance, a bench is below it, a canopy hangs over it, and several bicycles are stored under it.
A tunnel runs beneath the highway, and a communications antenna sits on top of the building.

11. on top of

Usage: Describe a position on the upper surface of something, often with contact.
A tunnel runs beneath the highway, and a communications antenna sits on top of the building.

column2: north/south/east/west of · northeast/northwest/southeast/southwest of · in northern/southern/eastern/western X · in the north/south/east/west of X · on the northern/southern/eastern/western side of X · at the northern/southern/eastern/western end of X
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe a compass relationship, a region, a side, or an endpoint.

1. north/south/east/west of

Usage: Give a cardinal direction relative to another place. A relative compass direction does not itself say whether the places share a wider region.
The station is north of the mall, the stadium is south of it, the school is east of it, and the park is west of it.

2. northeast/northwest/southeast/southwest of

Usage: Give an intermediate compass direction relative to another place.
The four clinics are northeast, northwest, southeast, and southwest of downtown, respectively.

3. in northern/southern/eastern/western X

Usage: Locate something inside the directional part of a larger named area.
The company has offices in northern, southern, eastern, and western Taiwan.

4. in the north/south/east/west of X

Usage: Express the same regional relation with in the north/south/east/west of.
Most farms are in the north of the county, the vineyards are in the south of the county, the port is in the east of the county, and the industrial district is in the west of the county.

5. on the northern/southern/eastern/western side of X

Usage: Identify a directional side of a site.
The main entrances are on the northern and southern sides of the campus, while the parking areas are on its eastern and western sides.

6. at the northern/southern/eastern/western end of X

Usage: Identify a directional endpoint rather than the entire side.
The trailheads are at the northern and southern ends of the route.
The bridge is at the eastern end of the highway, and a service area is at its western end.

column2: near + noun · close to + noun · nearby · fairly/pretty/relatively close to · not far from · in (fairly) close proximity to · far/quite far/pretty far from · a long way/some distance from · [distance] from or north/south/east/west of X · a [time]-minute walk from · within walking distance of · [time] away by car/train
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe proximity, measured distance, or travel time.

1. near + noun

Usage: Put the nearby reference point directly after near.
The hotel is near the station.

2. close to + noun

Usage: Include to when close has a reference-point complement.
The café is close to the hotel.

3. nearby

Usage: Use nearby without a complement, or before a noun.
There is a pharmacy nearby, and a nearby convenience store stays open all night.

4. fairly/pretty/relatively close to

Usage: Modify the degree of closeness; pretty close is conversational.
The campus is fairly close to downtown.
My apartment is pretty close to campus.
The laboratory is relatively close to the hospital.

5. not far from

Usage: Describe a short distance using a negative far statement.
The station is not far from the campus, my apartment, or the laboratory.

6. in (fairly) close proximity to

Usage: Use a formal alternative to close to; fairly can qualify the closeness.
The clinic is in close proximity to the hospital, and the frog lives in fairly close proximity to water.

7. far/quite far/pretty far from

Usage: Describe a large distance; quite/pretty modify its degree. Pretty far, like pretty close, is conversational AmE.
The airport is far from downtown.
The harbor is quite far from the station.
The village is pretty far from the highway.

8. a long way/some distance from

Usage: Describe separation with a long way or some distance from a place.
The cabin is a long way from town.
The campsite is some distance from the river.

9. [distance] from or north/south/east/west of X

Usage: State a measured distance and, optionally, its compass direction from a reference point.
The hotel is two miles from the airport.
The clinic is one mile north of downtown, the depot is two miles south of it, the station is three miles east of it, and the airport is ten miles west of it.

10. a [time]-minute walk from

Usage: Describe walking duration with a singular unit in the compound adjective.
The office is a ten-minute walk from the subway.

11. within walking distance of

Usage: Say walking is a practical option without giving an exact duration.
Several restaurants are within walking distance of the office.

12. [time] away by car/train

Usage: State travel time and the mode of transportation.
The airport is 30 minutes away by car, while the city center is 20 minutes away by train.

column2: on + street · at + exact address/intersection · on/at the corner of two streets · in the corner of a room · on + floor · at + entrance/exit/end · at the traffic light(s)/next light
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Locate places using streets, addresses, corners, floors, and landmarks.

1. on + street

Usage: Locate a building along a named street.
The café is on Main Street.

2. at + exact address/intersection

Usage: Use at for a precise address or intersection.
The clinic is at 120 Main Street.
Meet me at the intersection of Main Street and First Avenue.

3. on/at the corner of two streets

Usage: Locate a building at the corner of two streets; on and at can both work.
The bank is on the corner of Main and First; at the corner of Main and First is also natural.

4. in the corner of a room

Usage: Use in for an interior corner.
An ATM stands in the corner of the lobby.

5. on + floor

Usage: Use on to identify a building floor.
The office is on the third floor.

6. at + entrance/exit/end

Usage: Treat an entrance, exit, or end as a point.
Meet me at the entrance, not at the rear exit; the bus stop is at the end of the street.

7. at the traffic light(s)/next light

Usage: Identify the traffic light as a turning landmark; the next light is common conversational AmE.
Turn right at the traffic lights or, in common conversational AmE, at the next light.

column2: go/head/walk/drive + compass direction · go/continue straight ahead · go up/down + street · walk/continue along + route · go as far as + landmark · continue until + clause · turn at/onto · take the first/second left/right · on your left/right · just before/after/past
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Give a route as a sequence of clear navigation instructions.

1. go/head/walk/drive + compass direction

Usage: Give a compass direction after the movement verb, without an extra to.
Go north for two blocks, then head east at the park.
Walk south through the plaza.
Drive west toward the highway.

2. go/continue straight ahead

Usage: Tell someone to continue without turning.
Go straight ahead, then continue straight ahead through the intersection.

3. go up/down + street

Usage: Follow a named street; up/down need not mean north/south. Up/down a street does not necessarily mean geographic north/south.
Go up Bridge Street, then go down Queens Road.

4. walk/continue along + route

Usage: Follow the length of a route or feature.
Walk along the river, then continue along the footpath.

5. go as far as + landmark

Usage: Name the landmark that marks how far to continue.
Go as far as the traffic lights.

6. continue until + clause

Usage: Name the event that ends the current instruction using a complete clause.
Continue until you reach the bank.

7. turn at/onto

Usage: Use at for the turning landmark and onto for the street entered.
Turn left at the bank, then turn right at the next traffic light.
Turn left onto Main Street, then turn right onto First Avenue.

8. take the first/second left/right

Usage: Count turning opportunities and name left/right.
Take the first left, followed by the second right.

9. on your left/right

Usage: Locate a destination relative to the traveler's direction.
The pharmacy will be on your left, and the station will be on your right.

10. just before/after/past

Usage: Place a landmark shortly before/after another; past emphasizes having passed it.
The entrance is just before the bridge, the parking lot is just after it, and the hotel is just past the next intersection.

column2: to/toward/from/away from · into/out of · onto/off · across/through · along/past · around · over/under
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe destinations, directions, boundaries, and paths.

1. to/toward/from/away from

Usage: To names a destination, toward a direction, from an origin, and away from increasing separation. Toward is more common in AmE; towards is also correct and more common in British English.
The route runs from the hotel to the station, but you should first walk toward the clock tower.
Move away from the construction site and head toward the bus stop.

2. into/out of

Usage: Describe crossing into or out of an enclosed space.
Go into the lobby and out of the rear exit.

3. onto/off

Usage: Describe movement onto or off a surface/vehicle; the two actions here involve different reference objects.
Step onto the platform, then get off the train at Central Station.

4. across/through

Usage: Describe crossing an open area/surface versus moving within a space from one part to another.
Walk across the street and through the park.

5. along/past

Usage: Follow the length of a feature or move beyond a landmark.
Continue along the river and past the bank.

6. around

Usage: Go round an obstacle or explore different parts of an area; context determines the path.
Go around the construction barrier, and then walk around the campus to explore its different areas.

7. over/under

Usage: Describe a path above or below an obstacle/reference object.
Cross over the footbridge, then pass under the railroad tracks.

column2: upstairs/downstairs · go up/down the stairs · take the elevator to + floor · on the same floor · one floor above/below · down/along/across the hall · at the far end of the hall · through + door · around the corner · the first/second door on your left/right
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Give directions between floors and through a building.

1. upstairs/downstairs

Usage: Locate something on a higher/lower level; no to is needed before upstairs/downstairs.
The conference room is upstairs, while the cafeteria is downstairs.

2. go up/down the stairs

Usage: Name the direction of movement on the stairs.
Go up the stairs to reach reception, or go down the stairs to reach the parking garage.

3. take the elevator to + floor

Usage: Name the destination floor after take the elevator to.
Take the elevator to the third floor.

4. on the same floor

Usage: Say two places occupy the same floor.
The accounting department is on the same floor as the meeting room.

5. one floor above/below

Usage: Compare floor positions with above/below.
The laboratory is one floor above the library and one floor below the rooftop garden.

6. down/along/across the hall

Usage: Follow the hall's length with down/along or cross its width with across.
Walk down the hall, continue along the hall, and then walk across the hall to the waiting area.

7. at the far end of the hall

Usage: Locate something at the distant endpoint of the hall.
The restrooms are at the far end of the hall.

8. through + door

Usage: Describe passing from one side of a doorway to the other.
Go through the glass door.

9. around the corner

Usage: Describe a route or position beyond a corner.
The waiting area is around the corner.

10. the first/second door on your left/right

Usage: Identify a door by sequence and its side relative to the traveler.
The office is the first door on your left; the meeting room is the second door on your right.

column2: go + number of blocks · continue for + number of blocks · merge onto + road/highway · stay in + lane · keep/bear left/right · take + exit · get on/off the highway · at the fork · make a U-turn · take the first/second exit at the roundabout
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Give road-navigation instructions and distances in blocks.

1. go + number of blocks

Usage: Give a distance in blocks directly after go.
Go two blocks.

2. continue for + number of blocks

Usage: Give the length of a continued segment with for.
Continue for another three blocks.

3. merge onto + road/highway

Usage: Enter and join traffic on the named road/highway.
Merge onto Interstate 95.

4. stay in + lane

Usage: Tell someone which lane to remain in.
Stay in the right lane.

5. keep/bear left/right

Usage: Give a left/right path instruction; bear commonly describes a gentler direction change or branch.
Keep left at the tunnel entrance, but keep right after the bridge.
Bear left when the road divides; later, bear right toward downtown.

6. take + exit

Usage: Identify the exit to use.
Take Exit 12.

7. get on/off the highway

Usage: Describe entering or leaving the highway.
Get off the highway at the service area, then get on the highway again after your break.

8. at the fork

Usage: Identify the branch point where the road divides.
At the fork, follow the road on the right.

9. make a U-turn

Usage: Reverse travel direction with a U-turn.
If you miss the entrance, make a U-turn at the next intersection.

10. take the first/second exit at the roundabout

Usage: Count exits from the entry point at the roundabout.
Take the first exit at the roundabout for downtown or the second exit for the airport.

column2: get on/off + bus/train · board + bus/train · take + bus/train to/toward + place · ride for + number of stops · get off at + stop/station · transfer at + station · transfer/change to + line · catch/miss + bus/train · northbound/southbound/eastbound/westbound
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe using public transportation, including stops, transfers, and travel direction.

1. get on/off + bus/train

Usage: Use get on/off with the vehicle; add at to identify the stop.
Get on the bus outside the hotel and get off the bus downtown.
Get on the train at Central Station and get off the train at Riverside.

2. board + bus/train

Usage: Use board with a direct vehicle object, without on.
Board the train at Central Station; passengers can also board the bus outside the terminal.

3. take + bus/train to/toward + place

Usage: Use to for the destination or toward for the service's direction.
Take the train to City Hall, or take Bus 22 toward Riverside.

4. ride for + number of stops

Usage: Give the number of stops to remain on the vehicle.
Ride for three stops.

5. get off at + stop/station

Usage: Name the stop where the passenger should leave the vehicle.
Get off at Union Station.

6. transfer at + station

Usage: Name the station where the transfer happens.
Transfer at Central Station.

7. transfer/change to + line

Usage: Name the new line after transfer/change to.
Transfer to the Red Line.
You can also say: change to the Red Line.

8. catch/miss + bus/train

Usage: Describe reaching a service in time or failing to board it.
We managed to catch the bus, but we nearly missed the train.

9. northbound/southbound/eastbound/westbound

Usage: Specify the vehicle's direction of travel with a bound compound adjective.
Take the northbound train in the morning and the southbound train home.
The eastbound bus goes downtown, while the westbound bus goes toward the airport.

column2: How do I get to ...? · Could you tell me how to get to ...? · Do you know where ... is? · Which way is ...? · Where exactly is ...? · Where is the nearest ...? · Is there a ... near here? · Is this the way to ...? · Am I going in the right direction? · How far is ...? · Is it within walking distance? · How long does it take to get there? · Could you show me on the map?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Use these neutral, polite questions to ask for directions or confirm a route.

1. How do I get to ...?

Usage: Ask for a route to the destination. Excuse me makes an opening request to a stranger more polite.
Excuse me, how do I get to the train station?

2. Could you tell me how to get to ...?

Usage: Politely request directions with an embedded infinitive phrase.
Could you tell me how to get to City Hall?

3. Do you know where ... is?

Usage: Ask whether someone knows the location; keep is after the subject in the embedded question.
Do you know where the nearest pharmacy is?

4. Which way is ...?

Usage: Ask which direction leads to a place.
Which way is downtown?

5. Where exactly is ...?

Usage: Request a more precise location.
Where exactly is the information booth?

6. Where is the nearest ...?

Usage: Ask for the closest example of a place/service.
Where is the nearest subway station?

7. Is there a ... near here?

Usage: Ask whether a place/service exists nearby.
Is there a convenience store near here?

8. Is this the way to ...?

Usage: Confirm whether the current route leads to the destination.
Is this the way to the airport?

9. Am I going in the right direction?

Usage: Confirm whether you are traveling in the correct direction.
Am I going in the right direction?

10. How far is ...?

Usage: Ask about distance rather than travel duration.
How far is the museum from here?

11. Is it within walking distance?

Usage: Ask whether walking is a practical option.
Is it within walking distance?

12. How long does it take to get there?

Usage: Ask about the travel duration.
How long does it take to get there?

13. Could you show me on the map?

Usage: Request a visual indication on the map.
Could you show me on the map?

column2: What order number are you on?
column3:
1. What order number are you on?

Usage: Use this to ask which numbered order staff have reached in a queue. It asks about their progress, not specifically whether your own order is ready.
What order number are you on right now?
What number are you on? My order is 44.
What order number are you on? We’ve been waiting for about twenty minutes.

column2: ... + (that/who/whom/which/when/where/why) + subject + verb
column3:
... + (that/who/whom/which/when/where/why) + subject + verb

This card focuses on deleting exactly one optional word. Usually every other word stays in place. If a preposition comes immediately before the deleted word, move the preposition to the end first.

1

In these patterns, the joining word can disappear when another subject and verb follow:

think/say/believe/know/find + that + subject + verb
→ remove that

I believe that public transportation should be more affordable.
→ I believe public transportation should be more affordable.

be sure/glad/afraid + that + subject + verb
→ remove that

I am glad that the city has expanded the bus network.
→ I am glad the city has expanded the bus network.

noun + that/who/whom/which + subject + verb
→ remove that/who/whom/which

The report that the auditors released identified three control failures.
→ The report the auditors released identified three control failures.

The neighborhood that many families moved into has become more diverse.
→ The neighborhood many families moved into has become more diverse.

day + when / place + where / reason + why + subject + verb
→ remove when/where/why

I remember the day when we first met.
→ I remember the day we first met.

The place where we first met is now a community center.
→ The place we first met is now a community center.

The main reason why many families moved was the high cost of living.
→ The main reason many families moved was the high cost of living.

2

Do not remove only one word in these forms:

that/who/which + verb directly
→ do not remove only that/who/which

The report that identified three control failures was released yesterday.
≠ The report identified three control failures was released yesterday.

, who/which ... ,
→ do not remove only who/which

The new policy, which took effect in January, has reduced waiting times.
≠ The new policy, took effect in January, has reduced waiting times.

whose + noun
→ do not remove whose

Students whose families have low incomes may qualify for financial assistance.
≠ Students families have low incomes may qualify for financial assistance.

3

Do not leave a preposition directly before an empty space:

preposition + whom/which + subject + verb
→ subject + verb + preposition

The city in which I grew up has changed considerably.
→ The city I grew up in has changed considerably.

≠ The city in I grew up has changed considerably.

column2: noun/linker + (subject + be) + V-ing/past participle/adjective/PP
column3:
noun/linker + (subject + be) + V-ing/past participle/adjective/PP

This card deletes a subject together with am/is/are/was/were. The remaining words must clearly describe another noun or subject.

1

noun + who/that/which + am/is/are/was/were + description
→ noun + description

The students who are studying abroad often become more independent.
→ The students studying abroad often become more independent.

The data that were collected in rural areas reveal a significant gap in health care.
→ The data collected in rural areas reveal a significant gap in health care.

The bridge that is being repaired connects two residential areas.
→ The bridge being repaired connects two residential areas.

Communities that are in remote areas often lack reliable public transportation.
→ Communities in remote areas often lack reliable public transportation.

The next issue that is to be discussed concerns affordable housing.
→ The next issue to be discussed concerns affordable housing.

, who/which + am/is/are/was/were + description,
→ , description,

The new library, which was funded by local donations, opened last month.
→ The new library, funded by local donations, opened last month.

2

while/when/if/although/even though + subject + am/is/are/was/were + description
→ while/when/if/although/even though + description

While she was a student, she worked part-time at a local clinic.
→ While a student, she worked part-time at a local clinic.

If it is necessary, the policy can be revised next year.
→ If necessary, the policy can be revised next year.

Although it was designed for small towns, the program was adopted nationwide.
→ Although designed for small towns, the program was adopted nationwide.

Even though she was nervous, Maya gave a clear presentation.
→ Even though nervous, Maya gave a clear presentation.

When the removed subject names a person or thing, it must refer to the subject of the main sentence. Impersonal phrases such as if necessary and if possible are also normal.

While Maya was studying, her phone rang.
≠ While studying, her phone rang.

The shortened sentence incorrectly makes her phone the understood subject of studying.

3

After a noun, the remaining words must fit naturally directly after that noun.

An adjective with extra information can often remain:

eligible for financial aid
responsible for the project
available to local residents

Applicants who are eligible for financial aid should apply online.
→ Applicants eligible for financial aid should apply online.

A noun normally cannot remain directly after another noun:

The volunteers who are doctors can provide medical care.
≠ The volunteers doctors can provide medical care.

A short adjective normally moves before the noun:

The measures that are expensive may be difficult to maintain.
≠ The measures expensive may be difficult to maintain.

The measures that are expensive may be difficult to maintain.
→ The expensive measures may be difficult to maintain.

A complete main sentence cannot lose its subject and be:

That policy is expensive.
≠ Expensive.

column2: noun + V-ing / while/when + V-ing
column3:
noun + V-ing / while/when + V-ing

Use this change when the noun performs a current or general action and the exact tense is not important.

1

noun + who/that/which + active verb
→ noun + V-ing

Students who live abroad often become more independent.
→ Students living abroad often become more independent.

Policies that affect low-income families should be evaluated carefully.
→ Policies affecting low-income families should be evaluated carefully.

, who/which + active verb,
→ , V-ing,

The survey, which covers more than 2,000 households, provides useful data on housing costs.
→ The survey, covering more than 2,000 households, provides useful data on housing costs.

noun + who/that + do/does not + verb
→ noun + not + V-ing

Applicants who do not meet the income requirement will not qualify.
→ Applicants not meeting the income requirement will not qualify.

2

while/when + subject + active verb
→ while/when + V-ing

While they wait for the bus, they often check their phones.
→ While waiting for the bus, they often check their phones.

When you compare the two proposals, you should consider their long-term costs.
→ When comparing the two proposals, you should consider their long-term costs.

The person understood after while or when must also perform the main action.

3

Do not use ordinary V-ing when it would remove meaning carried by a modal:

who + can/may/must/will/should + verb ≠ V-ing

Employees who can work from home may choose a more affordable place to live.
≠ Employees working from home may choose a more affordable place to live.

Can work describes an ability or option. Working describes what the employees are actually doing.

Applicants who must provide additional evidence will receive an email.
≠ Applicants providing additional evidence will receive an email.

Must provide describes a requirement. Providing describes what the applicants are actually doing.

column2: Having + past participle / Having been + ..., main clause
column3:
Having + past participle / Having been + ..., main clause

Having + ... can shorten a whole clause about a situation earlier than the main situation. It does not mechanically replace every has, have, or had phrase.

1

For an earlier completed action:

because/after/once + subject + has/have/had + past participle
→ having + past participle

Because Maya has completed the required training, she is eligible to apply.
→ Having completed the required training, Maya is eligible to apply.

After the researchers had completed the safety inspection, they reopened the laboratory.
→ Having completed the safety inspection, the researchers reopened the laboratory.

Has/have uses the present as its reference point. Had uses a past reference point. Having has no tense of its own; the main sentence supplies the time.

When after or once already makes the order clear, the full clause may use the simple past:

because/after/once + subject + completed simple-past action
→ having + past participle

After the committee reviewed all the evidence, it rejected the proposal.
→ Having reviewed all the evidence, the committee rejected the proposal.

2

Keep negative, passive, and continuing meanings in the shortened form:

has/have/had not + past participle
→ not having + past participle

Because she had not received enough information, Maya postponed her decision.
→ Not having received enough information, Maya postponed her decision.

has/have/had (not) been + past participle
→ (not) having been + past participle

Because the proposal has been revised, it now addresses the main concerns.
→ Having been revised, the proposal now addresses the main concerns.

has/have/had (not) been + V-ing
→ (not) having been + V-ing

Because Maya had been working from home for several months, she found it difficult to return to the office.
→ Having been working from home for several months, Maya found it difficult to return to the office.

Having completed describes an earlier completed action. Having been working describes activity continuing over an earlier period and does not necessarily say that the activity was completed.

3

The subject of the main sentence must refer to the same person or thing as the subject removed from the earlier clause.

After the city had raised parking fees, many commuters began using public transportation.
≠ Having raised parking fees, many commuters began using public transportation.

The shortened sentence incorrectly says that the commuters raised the parking fees.

These forms are mainly useful in formal writing. In everyday conversation, a full after, because, or once clause is often more natural.

column2: (for + person +) to + verb / wh-word + to + verb
column3:
(for + person +) to + verb / wh-word + to + verb

To + verb commonly describes an action that is needed, possible, planned, or performed for a purpose. It does not normally describe a completed fact.

1

Choose the form according to who will perform the action:

action for an understood person → noun + to + verb

I have three reports that I need to finish before Friday.
→ I have three reports to finish before Friday.

We need somewhere where we can stay for two nights.
→ We need somewhere to stay for two nights.

action for a named person → noun + for + person + to + verb

She prepared a short guide that new employees could use.
→ She prepared a short guide for new employees to use.

noun receives the action → noun + to be + past participle

The city published a list of buildings that inspectors will examine this year.
→ The city published a list of buildings to be examined this year.

The application lists several forms that must be completed.
→ The application lists several forms to be completed.

Use the passive form when the person performing the action is unimportant or already clear. To be completed presents the forms as a required task, but it does not state the force of must as explicitly. Keep must when the obligation itself is important.

2

For a purpose, keep the person who will perform the purpose action:

same subject + so that + same subject + can/could + verb
→ same subject + to + verb

Maya enrolled in an evening course so that she could improve her academic writing.
→ Maya enrolled in an evening course to improve her academic writing.

so that + different subject + can/could + verb
→ for + subject + to + verb

The city built a playground so that children could exercise safely.
→ The city built a playground for children to exercise safely.

The city built a playground so that children could exercise safely.
≠ The city built a playground to exercise safely.

The incorrect sentence suggests that the city will exercise.

3

the first/next/last/only + noun + who/that + verb
→ the first/next/last/only + noun + to + verb

Nadia was the first student who completed the survey.
→ Nadia was the first student to complete the survey.

Norway was the only country that met the target that year.
→ Norway was the only country to meet the target that year.

4

who/what/where/when/how + subject + should/can + verb
→ who/what/where/when/how + to + verb

whether + subject + should + verb
→ whether + to + verb

The person making the choice or performing the action must be clear from context.

I was not sure what I should include in the introduction.
→ I was not sure what to include in the introduction.

We have not decided where we should hold the meeting.
→ We have not decided where to hold the meeting.

The committee must determine how it can reduce unnecessary spending.
→ The committee must determine how to reduce unnecessary spending.

We have not decided whether we should apply for additional funding.
→ We have not decided whether to apply for additional funding.

Maya asked what Daniel should include in the report.
≠ Maya asked what to include in the report.

The shortened sentence would normally make Maya, not Daniel, the person choosing what to include.

Do not make the same change with why:

I do not understand why I should wait.
≠ I do not understand why to wait.

5

Do not use to + verb for a completed fact:

A policy that reduced emissions was expanded nationwide.
≠ A policy to reduce emissions was expanded nationwide.

The first sentence says that the policy actually reduced emissions. The second describes its purpose, not its actual result.

column2: do/auxiliary/modal/to + (repeated action)
column3:
do/auxiliary/modal/to + (repeated action)

When an action or description is already clear, keep only the small word that carries its tense, negative, ability, or other meaning.

1

Choose the small word that remains:

ordinary verb → do/does/did
can/could/may/might/will/would/should/must + repeated action → keep the modal
has/have/had + repeated words → keep has/have/had
am/is/are/was/were + description/action → keep am/is/are/was/were
verb + to + repeated action → keep to

Maya works remotely, and Daniel works remotely too.
→ Maya works remotely, and Daniel does too.
→ Maya works remotely, and so does Daniel.

Maya cannot attend the workshop, and Daniel cannot attend it either.
→ Maya cannot attend the workshop, and Daniel cannot either.
→ Maya cannot attend the workshop, and neither can Daniel.

Maya has submitted her application, and Daniel has submitted his application too.
→ Maya has submitted her application, and Daniel has too.

The downtown clinic is overcrowded, and the suburban clinic is overcrowded too.
→ The downtown clinic is overcrowded, and the suburban clinic is too.

I did not attend the workshop, although I had planned to attend it.
→ I did not attend the workshop, although I had planned to.

In American English, have meaning possession normally uses do:

have/has + possession → do/does

Maya has flexible working hours, and Daniel has flexible working hours too.
→ Maya has flexible working hours, and Daniel does too.

2

The same omission works in comparisons and concise coordination:

than + subject + small word

Housing costs have risen faster in the city than they have risen in nearby towns.
→ Housing costs have risen faster in the city than they have in nearby towns.

subject + verb + information, and subject + different information

The city invested two million dollars in buses, and the county invested one million dollars in bike lanes.
→ The city invested two million dollars in buses, and the county one million dollars in bike lanes.

The second structure is concise and slightly formal. Repeating the verb is usually more natural in everyday conversation.

3

Do not omit the action when the result could be misunderstood:

The manager asked Maya to revise the report, and Daniel did too.

This could be misread as Daniel also asking Maya or Daniel revising the report. Repeat the intended action when the shorter sentence is unclear.

column2: known event + who/what/where/when/why/how
column3:
known event + who/what/where/when/why/how

When a full event is already known, English can leave only the information that is still missing or newly supplied.

1

known event + who/what/where/when/why/how + repeated clause
→ keep only who/what/where/when/why/how

Someone approved the proposal, but I do not know who approved it.
→ Someone approved the proposal, but I do not know who.

Maya bought something for the office, but she did not say what she bought.
→ Maya bought something for the office, but she did not say what.

They held the meeting somewhere off campus, but I do not know where they held it.
→ They held the meeting somewhere off campus, but I do not know where.

The policy will take effect sometime this year, but we have not been told when it will take effect.
→ The policy will take effect sometime this year, but we have not been told when.

The application was rejected for some reason, but no one explained why it was rejected.
→ The application was rejected for some reason, but no one explained why.

The repairs will cost a certain amount, but we do not know how much they will cost.
→ The repairs will cost a certain amount, but we do not know how much.

2

A direct answer can contain only the new information:

Who submitted the final report?
Maya submitted the final report.
→ Maya.

Where will the meeting take place?
The meeting will take place in the main conference room.
→ In the main conference room.

Did the council approve the proposal?
Yes, the council approved the proposal.
→ Yes.

3

Keep enough words when the remaining question word could refer to more than one event:

Maya told Daniel that the meeting had been canceled, but I do not know when.

This could mean when Maya told Daniel or when the meeting was canceled.

→ I do not know when Maya told Daniel.
→ I do not know when the meeting was canceled.

column2: number/quantity + (repeated noun) / adjective + one/ones
column3:
number/quantity + (repeated noun) / adjective + one/ones

When a noun is already clear, a number or quantity word can often stand without repeating that noun.

1

number + repeated count noun → number
some/any/many/few/a few/several/more/most/fewer/enough/all/both/each/either/neither + repeated count noun → quantity word
some/any/much/little/a little/more/most/less/enough/all + repeated mass noun → quantity word
none of + the + repeated noun → none

We needed five volunteers, but only three volunteers arrived.
→ We needed five volunteers, but only three arrived.

Several proposals were submitted, but only a few proposals met the requirements.
→ Several proposals were submitted, but only a few met the requirements.

The city needs more affordable housing, but it does not have enough affordable housing.
→ The city needs more affordable housing, but it does not have enough.

Both solutions were expensive, but neither solution was practical.
→ Both solutions were expensive, but neither was practical.

The committee reviewed five proposals, but none of the proposals met the safety standard.
→ The committee reviewed five proposals, but none met the safety standard.

2

When an adjective remains, use one or ones instead of leaving the adjective alone:

adjective + repeated singular count noun → adjective + one
adjective + repeated plural count noun → adjective + ones

The larger apartment is expensive, so we chose the smaller apartment.
→ The larger apartment is expensive, so we chose the smaller one.

The city replaced the older buses but kept the newer buses.
→ The city replaced the older buses but kept the newer ones.

3

Repeat the noun when the remaining number or quantity would be unclear:

I ordered two reports and three application forms, but they sent only one.

One could mean one report or one application form.

→ They sent only one report.
→ They sent only one application form.

column2: (predictable opening words) + casual statement/question
column3:
(predictable opening words) + casual statement/question

In casual American conversation, texts, and notes, predictable words at the beginning can disappear when the meaning remains obvious.

1

Common informal statements:

I hope ... → Hope ...
it/that sounds/looks/seems ... → Sounds/Looks/Seems ...
I am sorry ... → Sorry ...
I am + V-ing → V-ing
there is no need ... → No need ...
it is + adjective + to ... → Adjective + to ...

I hope you have a safe trip.
→ Hope you have a safe trip.

That sounds good to me.
→ Sounds good to me.

I am sorry I missed your call.
→ Sorry I missed your call.

I am heading home now.
→ Heading home now.

There is no need to bring anything.
→ No need to bring anything.

It is good to see you again.
→ Good to see you again.

2

Common informal questions:

do you want/need ...? → Want/Need ...?
did you + verb ...? → verb ...?
are you + V-ing ...? → You + V-ing ...? / V-ing ...?
have you + past participle ...? → Past participle ...?
is everything ...? → Everything ...?

Do you want some coffee?
→ Want some coffee?

Did you get home okay?
→ Get home okay?

Are you coming with us?
→ You coming with us?
→ Coming with us?

Have you finished the report?
→ Finished the report?

Is everything okay?
→ Everything okay?

3

Use these shortened openings only when the missing subject and meaning are obvious.

Heading home now. See you soon.

This is natural in a text message. In formal or academic writing, write the complete sentence:

I am heading home now.

Avoid a shortened opening when it could hide important information:

Need more funding.

This does not clearly identify who needs the funding. In formal writing, name the subject:

The public transportation system needs more funding.

column2: It is + focused person/thing + that/who + clause · What + subject + did + was + (to) + verb
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Highlight the person, thing, or action that answers an implicit contrast.

1. It is + focused person/thing + that/who + clause

Usage: Put focus on a person/thing that answers an implicit contrast. This changes focus without necessarily changing the event; do not use clefts merely to make every sentence emphatic.
It was the missing permission that caused the failure, not the file size.
It was Maya who noticed the discrepancy.

2. What + subject + did + was + (to) + verb

Usage: Put focus on the action; the base verb can occur with or without to after was.
What we did was compare the two logs line by line.
What we did was to compare the two logs line by line.

column2: whether X or Y · whether + clause + or not
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Use whether to present alternatives or an unresolved yes-or-no question.

1. whether X or Y

Usage: Present alternatives; whether to can introduce the choice between actions.
We need to decide whether to repair the laptop or replace it.

2. whether + clause + or not

Usage: Leave a yes-or-no question unresolved; keep statement word order inside the clause. Whether or not can also introduce a condition-independent outcome; I do not know whether ... instead leaves the answer unresolved.
I do not know whether she will attend or not.
The answer depends on whether we can finish the tests.

column2: as if/as though + clause
column3:
1. as if/as though + clause

Usage: Describe an appearance or manner through a comparison. As if and as though usually overlap. An ordinary present form can describe a plausible impression; a past form can signal an imagined or unreal comparison. The construction does not guarantee that the comparison is true.
He talks as if he knows everyone.
He talks as though he knows everyone.
She treated me as if I were a complete stranger.
It looks as if the rain has stopped.

column2: like + noun · as + role/function noun · as + subject + verb
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Use like for similarity and as + noun for an actual role or function.

1. like + noun

Usage: Compare something with a similar thing without necessarily assigning it that role.
I work like a mentor. — An actual role versus similar behavior.
We used a box as a table; it looked like a shipping crate.

2. as + role/function noun

Usage: Assign an actual role or function, rather than mere resemblance.
I work as a mentor.
We used a box as a table; it looked like a shipping crate.

3. as + subject + verb

Usage: Express in the way that or refer to earlier words; like I said is a conversational alternative. Conversational like + clause also occurs; like I said is one common example.
Leave the settings as they are.
As I said earlier, the default works for most users.

column2: start/begin + to + verb / V-ing
column3:
1. start/begin + to + verb / V-ing

Usage: Start and begin often allow either to + verb or an -ing form with little practical difference. With verbs of understanding and knowing, a to-infinitive is usually the natural choice. After a progressive starting/beginning form, a to-infinitive often avoids an awkward sequence of -ing forms.
I started checking the figures.
I started to check the figures.
I am starting to notice recurring problems.
I am beginning to understand why the review takes so long.

column2: X matters more to + person + than Y · choose X over Y
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Compare priorities or state a choice.

1. X matters more to + person + than Y

Usage: Compare how important two things are to someone.
Flexibility matters more to me than a prestigious job title.

2. choose X over Y

Usage: State the option chosen or preferred, without calling the other option bad.
I would choose a shorter commute over a slightly higher salary.

column2: would rather + person + past form · would rather + person + had + past participle
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

State a preference about another person's present/future or past action.

1. would rather + person + past form

Usage: Prefer another person's present/future action, using a past form to mark the preference. For your own action, use would rather + base verb instead.
I would rather you sent the draft tomorrow, after you have checked it.
I would rather you did not share my number.

2. would rather + person + had + past participle

Usage: Prefer a different past action that did not happen, using past perfect.
I would rather you had told me before inviting everyone.

column2: When/Why/How + do you think + subject + verb?
column3:
1. When/Why/How + do you think + subject + verb?

Usage: Ask for someone’s judgment about a question. Invert do you think, but keep statement word order in the following clause. This differs from a direct question such as When can we start?
When do you think we can finish the review?
Why do you think the client rejected the proposal?
How do you think we should explain the delay?

column2: for + duration · during + noun · while + clause · before/after + noun/clause/V-ing
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

For measures duration; during names the period in which something happens; while introduces a simultaneous situation.

1. for + duration

Usage: Measure the duration with for.
I waited for twenty minutes during the lunch break.

2. during + noun

Usage: Name the period within which the event happens with during.
I waited for twenty minutes during the lunch break.

3. while + clause

Usage: Describe a simultaneous situation using a complete clause.
I took notes while she explained the process.

4. before/after + noun/clause/V-ing

Usage: Locate an event before/after another with a noun, clause, or V-ing; keep the V-ing actor clear.
I checked the address before the trip.
I checked the address before I left.
I checked the address before leaving.

column2: as/while + clause · just as + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe overlapping events.

1. as/while + clause

Usage: Describe overlapping actions; while can avoid ambiguity with causal as.
As we walked to the station, we discussed the proposal.
While we walked to the station, we discussed the proposal.

2. just as + clause

Usage: Emphasize the exact moment another event happened.
Just as I opened the document, my laptop shut down.

column2: on time · in time for + noun / to + verb
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Distinguish meeting a schedule from arriving early enough for a purpose.

1. on time

Usage: Mean at the scheduled or expected time. The same arrival can be both on time and in time.
The train arrived on time, exactly as scheduled.

2. in time for + noun / to + verb

Usage: Mean early enough for an event or purpose; just in time means almost too late.
We arrived in time for the opening talk.
We arrived in time to hear the opening talk.

column2: verb + particle + noun / verb + noun + particle · verb + pronoun + particle · verb + preposition + object
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Place objects according to whether the verb is separable or prepositional.

1. verb + particle + noun / verb + noun + particle

Usage: With a separable phrasal verb, put a noun object before or after the particle.
Please turn off the alarm.
Please turn the alarm off.
I picked up the parcel and brought it back.

2. verb + pronoun + particle

Usage: Put an ordinary pronoun object between a separable verb and its particle.
Please turn it off.
I picked up the parcel and brought it back.

3. verb + preposition + object

Usage: With a prepositional verb, keep the object after the preposition; it cannot move between verb and preposition. This is a lexical property of the verb: not every short word after a verb is movable.
We need to look into the issue.
We need to look into it.

column2: with + object + V-ing/past participle/adjective/phrase
column3:
1. with + object + V-ing/past participle/adjective/phrase

Usage: Add background circumstances with a named subject. Use -ing when that subject performs an ongoing action, a past participle when it receives an action or is in a resulting state, and an adjective or phrase for a condition. The background subject can differ from the main subject.
With everyone working remotely, we needed a clearer handoff process.
With the budget approved, we could book the venue.
With the office empty and the lights off, the building felt unfamiliar.

column2: lead to/result in + outcome · result from/stem from + cause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Connect a cause with an outcome in either direction.

1. lead to/result in + outcome

Usage: Start with the cause and name its outcome; these prepositions take nouns or V-ing.
Poor maintenance can result in costly repairs.
Poor maintenance can lead to costly repairs.
The new scheduling system resulted in shorter waiting times.
Skipping tests can lead to shipping avoidable bugs.

2. result from/stem from + cause

Usage: Start with the outcome and name its cause/origin. Stem from names an origin; boil down to instead identifies the essential issue.
Many workplace conflicts result from unclear expectations.
Many workplace conflicts stem from unclear expectations.

column2: come to a conclusion/decision/agreement
column3:
1. come to a conclusion/decision/agreement

Usage: Describe reaching a judgment or shared outcome after thought or discussion. The nouns keep their own meanings: conclusion concerns what you believe, decision what you choose, and agreement a shared position or arrangement.
After checking the logs, we came to the conclusion that the timeout was unrelated.
The team came to a decision about which design to adopt.
We came to an agreement on how to divide the work.

column2: come to a halt/stop · come to an end
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe movement or an activity ending.

1. come to a halt/stop

Usage: Describe movement or a process stopping; halt/stop often overlap.
Traffic came to a halt when the tunnel closed.
Traffic came to a stop when the tunnel closed.

2. come to an end

Usage: Describe an event or period reaching its endpoint.
The partnership came to an end after its funding was withdrawn.

column2: come to realize/understand/believe (that) + clause
column3:
1. come to realize/understand/believe (that) + clause

Usage: Describe developing an understanding or belief over time or through experience. Here to introduces a verb, not a noun. The new understanding may arrive gradually or after a decisive experience.
I gradually came to realize that clear feedback prevents larger problems.
After working with the team, I came to understand why the review takes so long.
I came to believe that a smaller first release would be more useful.

column2: have an impact/effect on + target · contribute to + outcome · play a role in + process · be associated with + noun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Distinguish influence, contribution, participation, and association.

1. have an impact/effect on + target

Usage: Name the target affected by the influence.
The schedule change had an effect on attendance.

2. contribute to + outcome

Usage: Identify a partial cause or contribution, not necessarily the sole cause.
Unclear instructions contributed to the delay.

3. play a role in + process

Usage: Describe involvement or influence within a process.
Training plays a role in improving consistency.

4. be associated with + noun

Usage: Identify a connection without claiming that the relationship is causal.
Higher satisfaction was associated with greater flexibility; that alone does not prove a causal relationship.

column2: have access to + noun
column3:
1. have access to + noun

Usage: Say someone can reach, obtain, or use something. Access does not itself mean ownership, affordability, or permission to share it further.
Employees have access to the recordings after each session.
Do you have access to the original report?

column2: can/cannot afford + noun/to + verb
column3:
1. can/cannot afford + noun/to + verb

Usage: Describe whether money, time, or another cost is manageable. Cannot afford to can express that the consequences would be unacceptable, even when money is not involved.
I cannot afford a larger apartment.
We cannot afford to delay the launch again.

column2: work well for + person/purpose
column3:
1. work well for + person/purpose

Usage: Say something suits a person or purpose. The expression concerns suitability, not whether the person works well. A solution can work well for one person and poorly for another.
The flexible schedule works well for parents with young children.
This approach works well for small teams, but it becomes difficult to coordinate at scale.

column2: turn into + result · turn + object + into + result
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe transformation.

1. turn into + result

Usage: Make the thing undergoing the transformation the subject.
The conversation turned into a debate.

2. turn + object + into + result

Usage: Make the agent causing the transformation the subject, followed by the changing object.
We turned the empty room into a workspace.

column2: shift toward/away from + noun/V-ing
column3:
1. shift toward/away from + noun/V-ing

Usage: Describe a change in direction, attention, or emphasis without implying a complete transformation. Toward names the emerging focus; away from names what receives less attention.
My role is shifting toward planning and mentoring.
The discussion shifted away from assigning blame and toward finding a solution.

column2: stand clear of + hazard · stay clear of + person/thing/problem
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Stand clear tells someone to move or stay out of a hazard’s immediate path, especially in announcements.

1. stand clear of + hazard

Usage: Tell someone to remain out of a physical hazard's path, often in an announcement.
Please stand clear of the closing doors.

2. stay clear of + person/thing/problem

Usage: Describe avoiding a physical danger or involvement in something problematic.
Stay clear of the edge of the platform.
I try to stay clear of office gossip.

column2: get + benefit/amount + out of + experience
column3:
1. get + benefit/amount + out of + experience

Usage: Use this to describe the benefit, enjoyment, or value gained from an activity or experience. Get the most out of emphasizes gaining as much as possible.
I got a lot out of the design review.
What do you hope to get out of this course?
I want to get as much out of the trip as I can.

column2: Me too · Me neither · So do I/So am I · Neither do I/Neither am I
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Say that the same positive or negative statement is true for you.

1. Me too

Usage: Give a casual reply saying the positive statement is also true for you.
A: I’m exhausted after that flight. B: Me too.

2. Me neither
