Usage: Give a casual reply saying the negative statement is also true for you; me either also occurs in casual AmE.
A: I don’t really enjoy networking events. B: Me neither.
A: I’ve never been to Chicago. B: Me neither.

3. So do I/So am I

Usage: Use so + matching helper + subject for a positive reply, as in So am I.
A: I’m exhausted after that flight. B: So am I.

4. Neither do I/Neither am I

Usage: Use neither + matching helper + subject for a negative reply, as in Neither do I/have I. Match the original helper: do for ordinary present verbs, am for be, did for past, and have/can when already used.
A: I don’t really enjoy networking events. B: Neither do I.
A: I’ve never been to Chicago. B: Neither have I.

column2: How about you? · What about you? · And you?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Pass the turn back after you answer a question so the conversation keeps going.

1. How about you?

Usage: Return the question to the other speaker after answering.
I’m from Taipei, but I’ve been living in Seattle for two years. How about you?

2. What about you?

Usage: Do the same job as how about you in this turn-returning use.
I usually work from home on Fridays. What about you?

3. And you?

Usage: Give a shorter return question in a simple exchange such as a greeting.
A: How’s it going? B: Pretty good, thanks. And you?

column2: Right. · I see. · That makes sense. · Fair enough. · Exactly. · Totally.
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Show that you are following or agreeing while someone explains something.

1. Right.

Usage: Signal that you follow the explanation; agreement is not required.
A: So the cache only refreshes every ten minutes. B: Right. That explains the outdated numbers.

2. I see.

Usage: Signal understanding of the explanation, without necessarily endorsing it.
A: We’re waiting for legal approval before the launch. B: I see. That makes sense.

3. That makes sense.

Usage: Say the explanation seems logical to you.
A: We’re waiting for legal approval before the launch. B: I see. That makes sense.

4. Fair enough.

Usage: Accept someone's reason, even if you might have chosen differently.
A: We’re waiting for legal approval before the launch. B: Fair enough. Let’s not rush it.

5. Exactly.

Usage: Express strong agreement or precise confirmation.
A: The real issue is that nobody owns the onboarding process. B: Exactly.

6. Totally.

Usage: Express strong agreement casually.
A: The real issue is that nobody owns the onboarding process. B: Totally.

column2: Really? · Seriously? · No way! · You’re kidding! · Oh, nice! · Oh no!
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

React briefly to someone’s news to show interest and invite them to continue.

1. Really?

Usage: Show interest or surprise; a flat tone can instead signal doubt.
A: My connecting flight got canceled. B: Really? What happened?

2. Seriously?

Usage: React with stronger surprise or disbelief.
A: They moved the launch up by two weeks. B: Seriously? Do we even have time to test it?

3. No way!

Usage: React with strong surprise; this need not express a literal refusal.
A: I finally got an offer from that startup. B: No way! That’s amazing.

4. You’re kidding!

Usage: React to something hard to believe, often unwelcome news.
A: They moved the launch up by two weeks. B: You’re kidding! Do we even have time to test it?

5. Oh, nice!

Usage: Respond positively to good news.
A: I finally got an offer from that startup. B: Oh, nice! When do you start?

6. Oh no!

Usage: React sympathetically to bad news.
A: My connecting flight got canceled. B: Oh no! Were you able to rebook it?

column2: Congrats on + noun/V-ing · That’s great news! · Good for you!
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Respond warmly to someone’s good news or achievement.

1. Congrats on + noun/V-ing

Usage: Congratulate someone on an achievement; on takes a noun or V-ing. Congrats is the casual form of congratulations.
Congrats on the promotion!
Congratulations on passing your certification exam!

2. That’s great news!

Usage: React warmly to the good information itself.
A: We’re expecting our first baby in March. B: That’s great news!

3. Good for you!

Usage: Praise a person's effort or decision; a flat tone can make this sound sarcastic.
A: I finally signed up for a half marathon. B: Good for you!

column2: Well, + reply · So, + new topic/question/summary
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Start your turn in a way that signals its purpose.

1. Well, + reply

Usage: Begin a reply needing thought, qualification, or soft disagreement.
A: Did you like the redesigned app? B: Well, it looks better, but it feels slower.

2. So, + new topic/question/summary

Usage: Open a topic/question or introduce a summary.
So, how was your first week at the new job?
So, to recap: Maria will handle the slides, and I’ll draft the summary.

column2: I mean, + clarification/correction · ..., you know?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Use small spoken markers to adjust what you just said.

1. I mean, + clarification/correction

Usage: Clarify, qualify, or quickly correct what you just said.
The movie was good. I mean, it wasn’t amazing, but I enjoyed it.
Let’s meet on Tuesday. I mean Wednesday; I have a dentist appointment on Tuesday.

2. ..., you know?

Usage: Check that the listener shares your point; avoid using it in every sentence.
It’s hard to exercise regularly when you work such long hours, you know?

column2: kind of/sort of + adjective/verb · a bit/a little + adjective · a bit of a + noun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Soften a description or opinion so it sounds less direct.

1. kind of/sort of + adjective/verb

Usage: Soften a description/opinion conversationally; kind of and sort of overlap.
The new office is kind of far from the train station.
The new office is sort of far from the train station.
I sort of expected the meeting to run long, so I didn’t book anything afterward.

2. a bit/a little + adjective

Usage: Soften an adjective, often a negative or uncomfortable description.
The instructions were a bit confusing.
The instructions were a little confusing.

3. a bit of a + noun

Usage: Soften a noun phrase, such as a problem or a headache.
The new process has been a bit of a headache.

column2: ..., or something · ..., and stuff (like that) · ..., or whatever
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Keep a description general when the exact details do not matter.

1. ..., or something

Usage: Leave open the possibility of a similar alternative. All three expressions are casual; avoid vague wording in interviews or formal writing.
Let’s grab coffee or something after the workshop.

2. ..., and stuff (like that)

Usage: Leave similar items/activities unstated because their details do not matter.
I spent the weekend cleaning, doing laundry, and stuff like that.

3. ..., or whatever

Usage: Leave the choice open casually; tone can make this sound dismissive.
Bring chips, drinks, or whatever; we’ll have plenty of food anyway.

column2: I was like, "..." · subject + was like, "..." · I’m like / he’s like, "..."
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Report what someone said, thought, or how they reacted in a casual story.

1. I was like, "..."

Usage: Report your past words, thought, or reaction informally without promising an exact quotation. Said is a more suitable default in professional reporting or when exact wording matters.
My manager asked me to present in five minutes, and I was like, “Wait, today?”

2. subject + was like, "..."

Usage: Report someone else's past reaction in a casual story.
She looked at the bill and was like, “Did we really order all this?”

3. I’m like / he’s like, "..."

Usage: Switch to a present storytelling form to make the scene vivid.
So I’m explaining the bug, and he’s like, “Oh, I already fixed that.”

column2: There’s no way + clause · There’s no way to + verb
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Say that something is impossible or that you strongly reject it.

1. There’s no way + clause

Usage: Strongly reject a possibility or refuse to accept it.
There’s no way we can finish all of this by Friday.
There’s no way I’m paying forty dollars for parking.

2. There’s no way to + verb

Usage: Say no method exists; is there any way to asks whether a method is available.
A: Is there any way to recover the deleted file? B: Unfortunately, there’s no way to recover it now.

column2: It’s up to + person (to + verb) · I’ll leave it up to you
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Say who has the right or responsibility to decide.

1. It’s up to + person (to + verb)

Usage: Give someone the right to decide or identify who has responsibility to act.
A: Should we eat in or go out? B: It’s up to you. I’m fine either way.
It’s up to each team to decide how often they meet.

2. I’ll leave it up to you

Usage: Politely hand the choice to the other person.
I don’t have a strong preference, so I’ll leave it up to you.

column2: When it comes to + noun/V-ing, + clause · As for + noun, + clause · As far as + noun + is concerned, + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Introduce the topic your next statement is about.

1. When it comes to + noun/V-ing, + clause

Usage: Introduce a topic, often before a general observation about it.
When it comes to remote work, clear communication matters more than the tools you use.

2. As for + noun, + clause

Usage: Move to another person/item after discussing the previous one.
The design is finished. As for the backend, we’re still waiting on the security review.

3. As far as + noun + is concerned, + clause

Usage: Limit the statement to that topic; as far as I am concerned instead marks your personal view. In terms of narrows an evaluation/comparison to an aspect rather than simply naming the next topic.
As far as cost is concerned, both options are about the same.

column2: regarding/concerning + noun · with/in regard to + noun · with respect to + noun · in the case of + noun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Name the topic in professional or written English.

1. regarding/concerning + noun

Usage: Name a topic formally, without adding to after regarding/concerning; as regards is another formal option. About is usually a good casual default.
Do you have any questions regarding the new schedule?
Do you have any questions concerning the new schedule?
As regards the budget, we still need approval.

2. with/in regard to + noun

Usage: Mean about in professional/written English; to takes a noun.
With regard to your refund request, we have forwarded it to our billing team.
In regard to your refund request, we have forwarded it to our billing team.

3. with respect to + noun

Usage: Introduce a topic or dimension of discussion in relatively formal English.
With respect to latency, both models meet our requirements.

4. in the case of + noun

Usage: Focus on a particular case, often in contrast with other cases.
In the case of small teams, a lightweight review process usually works better.

column2: By the way, + clause · Oh, before I forget, + clause · That reminds me, + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Bring up something new or unrelated without a smooth transition.

1. By the way, + clause

Usage: Add a side point or new topic.
By the way, did you get a chance to look at my pull request?

2. Oh, before I forget, + clause

Usage: Flag something you might otherwise forget to mention.
Oh, before I forget, the client moved the call to Thursday.

3. That reminds me, + clause

Usage: Introduce a topic prompted by what the other speaker just said.
A: I’m flying to Denver next week. B: That reminds me, I still need to book my flight home for Thanksgiving.

column2: Not really · I’m not really into/not a big fan of + noun/V-ing · I’m more of a + noun + person · not … at all
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Answer with the right strength.

1. Not really

Usage: Give a soft negative answer.
A: Do you play video games? B: Not really, but my brother does.

2. I’m not really into/not a big fan of + noun/V-ing

Usage: Politely express limited interest or mild dislike.
I’m not a big fan of open-plan offices.
I’m not really into team sports; I’m more of a hiking person.

3. I’m more of a + noun + person

Usage: State your preferred type of activity or thing instead.
I’m not a big fan of open-plan offices.
I’m not really into team sports; I’m more of a hiking person.

4. not … at all

Usage: Strongly emphasize a negative claim.
I didn’t understand the second half of the lecture at all.

column2: You did? / Do you? / Have you? · You did what? · Like what? · How so? · What makes you say that?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Show interest and invite the speaker to say more.

1. You did? / Do you? / Have you?

Usage: Echo the matching helper with a rising tone to invite more information.
A: I grew up in Alaska. B: You did? What was that like?
A: I’ve never seen snow. B: You haven’t?

2. You did what?

Usage: Echo the surprising part with a question word.
A: I quit my job yesterday. B: You did what?

3. Like what?

Usage: Ask for examples.
A: The interview was kind of weird. B: Like what?

4. How so?

Usage: Ask in what way the claim is true.
A: The interview was kind of weird. B: How so?

5. What makes you say that?

Usage: Ask what evidence or experience prompted the claim.
A: The interview was kind of weird. B: What makes you say that?

column2: No problem · No worries · Don’t worry about it · Anytime · Never mind
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Brush off a small problem, thanks, or an apology.

1. No problem

Usage: Reply to thanks or a small apology.
A: Thanks for covering my shift. B: No problem.

2. No worries

Usage: Give a casual reassurance in response to a small apology/problem.
A: Sorry I’m late. B: No worries.

3. Don’t worry about it

Usage: Reassure someone that the issue does not need to worry them.
A: Sorry I’m late. B: Don’t worry about it; we just started.

4. Anytime

Usage: Reply to thanks and signal willingness to help again.
A: Thanks for covering my shift. B: Anytime.

5. Never mind

Usage: Cancel your question/request or say a small issue no longer matters.
Where did you put the… never mind, I found it.

column2: Don’t you think + clause? · Isn’t it + adjective? · Wouldn’t it be better to + verb?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Ask a negative question when you expect or want the listener to agree.

1. Don’t you think + clause?

Usage: Invite agreement with a view, often as a softened suggestion.
Don’t you think we should test it before the demo?

2. Isn’t it + adjective?

Usage: Ask a negative question about a quality; answer according to the actual fact.
A: Isn’t it cold in here? B: Yes, it is.
A: Isn’t it cold in here? B: No, it’s fine. — Yes means it is cold.

3. Wouldn’t it be better to + verb?

Usage: Suggest a better option through a negative question.
Wouldn’t it be better to ask the client first?

column2: That must be + adjective · That sounds + adjective · No wonder + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

React to someone’s situation by drawing a reasonable conclusion.

1. That must be + adjective

Usage: Infer how someone else's experience probably feels.
A: I’m working night shifts this month. B: That must be exhausting.

2. That sounds + adjective

Usage: React to an experience based on what you have just heard.
A: We’re moving to Lisbon in the spring. B: That sounds exciting!

3. No wonder + clause

Usage: Say that the new fact explains something you noticed.
A: I only slept four hours last night. B: No wonder you look tired.

column2: At least + clause
column3:
1. At least + clause

Usage: Point out the positive side of a disappointing situation. At least usually starts the clause or follows but. With a number, at least instead sets a minimum.
The flight was delayed, but at least we got free snacks.
We lost the bid. At least we learned what the client really wants.
A: It rained the whole weekend. B: Well, at least you got some rest.

column2: You know what? + comment/decision · Guess what? + news · Did you hear about + noun?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Get attention before saying something.

1. You know what? + comment/decision

Usage: Get attention before a comment or sudden decision.
You know what? Let’s just order pizza tonight.

2. Guess what? + news

Usage: Announce news, usually good or surprising.
Guess what? I passed my driving test.

3. Did you hear about + noun?

Usage: Open a conversation about news the listener may know.
Did you hear about the layoffs at Dana’s company?

column2: So far, + present perfect · So far, so good
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Report progress up to now.

1. So far, + present perfect

Usage: Report progress or experience through the current, unfinished period.
So far, we’ve migrated about half of the services.
I haven’t had any problems with the new laptop so far.

2. So far, so good

Usage: Say things have gone well up to now without claiming the process is finished.
A: How’s the new job? B: So far, so good.

column2: Keep in mind (that) + clause · keep + noun + in mind
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Remind someone of a fact that should affect a decision or plan.

1. Keep in mind (that) + clause

Usage: Introduce a complete fact someone should consider in making a decision. Keep in mind is more common than bear in mind in AmE.
Keep in mind that the API has a rate limit.
Keep in mind that hotel prices go up in the summer.

2. keep + noun + in mind

Usage: Put a short noun between keep and in mind to name the consideration.
When you choose a neighborhood, keep the commute in mind.

column2: go ahead and + verb · Go ahead.
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Say that you are about to do something, or tell someone they can start.

1. go ahead and + verb

Usage: Announce your next action or tell someone to proceed with a specified action.
I’ll go ahead and send the invite to everyone.
Go ahead and start without me; I’m running ten minutes late.

2. Go ahead.

Usage: Give permission to start or continue without restating the action.
A: Can I borrow your charger? B: Sure, go ahead.

column2: I doubt (that) + clause · I doubt it · I’m not so sure about that · I don’t think that’s right
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Respond with skepticism.

1. I doubt (that) + clause

Usage: Say a claim is probably untrue or an outcome unlikely; the following clause is usually positive.
I doubt they’ll finish the redesign by Friday.

2. I doubt it

Usage: Give the same skeptical answer without repeating the whole proposition.
A: Will it stop raining soon? B: I doubt it.

3. I’m not so sure about that

Usage: Question a claim relatively gently.
A: Remote workers are less productive. B: I’m not so sure about that.

4. I don’t think that’s right

Usage: More directly challenge a claim, often a factual mistake.
I don’t think that’s right. The logs show that the cache was already warm.

column2: after all
column3:
1. after all

Usage: After all has two common uses. At the end of a clause, it means despite what was expected or planned. At the start of a clause, it gives a reason that the listener should remember.
We didn’t need the reservation after all; the restaurant was half empty.
I decided to take the job after all.
Let him choose the restaurant. After all, it’s his birthday.

column2: I’m afraid + clause · I’m sorry, but + clause · I don’t want to worry you, but + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Soften unwelcome news, a refusal, or a disagreement.

1. I’m afraid + clause

Usage: Soften unwelcome news/refusal; afraid here need not mean fear.
I’m afraid I can’t make it on Friday.

2. I’m sorry, but + clause

Usage: Politely introduce a refusal, correction, or disagreement.
I’m sorry, but this ticket isn’t valid on the express train.

3. I don’t want to worry you, but + clause

Usage: Prepare the listener for a possible problem without claiming certainty.
I don’t want to worry you, but the client hasn’t replied since Friday.

column2: these days + present · lately/recently + present perfect · the other day + past · at the time + past
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Choose a time phrase and a tense that match the period you mean.

1. these days + present

Usage: Describe the current situation, often contrasted with an earlier one.
These days, most of our meetings are remote.

2. lately/recently + present perfect

Usage: Describe a recent period; recently also allows a simple-past event.
I’ve been sleeping badly lately.
I recently started a new job.

3. the other day + past

Usage: Refer to one event a few days ago, with a past form.
I ran into Jake the other day.

4. at the time + past

Usage: Refer to the circumstances at an earlier moment, often unlike your current view.
At the time, I didn’t realize how important that decision was.

column2: At this point, + clause · In the meantime, + clause · at some point
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Place an action within a process.

1. At this point, + clause

Usage: Identify what is possible or sensible at the current stage.
At this point, rolling back is probably the safest option.

2. In the meantime, + clause

Usage: Describe the interval before another event happens.
The parts won’t arrive until Monday. In the meantime, we can test the software.

3. at some point

Usage: Refer to an unspecified time.
We’ll need to replace the server at some point.

column2: In a way/In a sense, + clause · If you think about it, + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Present a claim as partly true or as one way of looking at things.

1. In a way/In a sense, + clause

Usage: Limit a claim to one interpretation or one respect; in a way/in a sense overlap.
In a way, the outage helped; it exposed gaps in our monitoring.
In a sense, the outage helped.
Working from home saves money in a way, but my electricity bill has gone up.

2. If you think about it, + clause

Usage: Invite the listener to notice a point they may have overlooked.
If you think about it, most of our delays come from waiting for approvals.

column2: Then again, + clause · On the contrary, + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Then again adds a second thought that balances or weakens what you just said.

1. Then again, + clause

Usage: Add a balancing second thought without denying the first statement.
The apartment is expensive. Then again, it’s right next to the station.

2. On the contrary, + clause

Usage: Reject an earlier statement and assert the opposite; compare on the other hand when both claims are true.
A: Was the class too easy? B: On the contrary, it was really demanding.
Living downtown is convenient. On the other hand, it’s noisy. — Both statements are true, so on the contrary does not fit.

column2: In theory, + clause; in practice, + clause
column3:
1. In theory, + clause; in practice, + clause

Usage: Contrast what should happen according to a plan, rule, or design with what really happens.
In theory, the cache should fix the problem; in practice, it only speeds up reads.
In theory, everyone has flexible hours. In practice, most people work nine to six.

column2: Other than that, + clause · other than + noun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Make an exception.

1. Other than that, + clause

Usage: Refer back to a named exception, then describe everything else.
The hotel was a little noisy. Other than that, it was perfect.

2. other than + noun

Usage: Mean except, followed by the exceptional item/person.
Other than a few typos, the report looks good.
I don’t know anyone there other than Maya.

column2: The best/worst part was (when) + clause · The good thing about + noun + is (that) + clause · One of the things I like about + noun + is (that) + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Highlight one part of an experience or one feature of something.

1. The best/worst part was (when) + clause

Usage: Highlight the strongest positive or negative moment in an experience.
The best part was when the whole crowd started singing.

2. The good thing about + noun + is (that) + clause

Usage: Identify an advantage of something.
The good thing about this neighborhood is that everything is within walking distance.

3. One of the things I like about + noun + is (that) + clause

Usage: Name one of several appreciated features; the main verb agrees with one, so use is.
One of the things I like about remote work is that I can focus without interruptions.

column2: What a/an (+ adjective) + noun! · How + adjective! · absolutely/totally + extreme adjective · couldn’t be + comparative
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Express a strong reaction.

1. What a/an (+ adjective) + noun!

Usage: Express a reaction with what a/an + singular count noun, optionally adding an adjective.
What a great idea!

2. How + adjective!

Usage: Express a reaction using how + adjective.
How nice of you to drive us!

3. absolutely/totally + extreme adjective

Usage: Intensify an extreme adjective naturally; compare very tired with absolutely exhausted.
I was absolutely exhausted after the flight.
I was very tired after the flight.

4. couldn’t be + comparative

Usage: Express the highest feasible degree through a negative comparative.
A: How’s the new job? B: Honestly, it couldn’t be better.

column2: I wouldn’t say + X, just + Y · not exactly + adjective/noun
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Tone down a judgment.

1. I wouldn’t say + X, just + Y

Usage: Reject a stronger label and offer a milder, more accurate one.
I wouldn’t say she’s unfriendly, just a little shy.
I wouldn’t say the trip was a disaster, just a bit disorganized.

2. not exactly + adjective/noun

Usage: Understate a negative judgment, often humorously or ironically.
Three meetings back to back isn’t exactly my idea of a productive day.

column2: Some people (might) argue that + clause, but + clause · It could be argued that + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Introduce a view you do not fully share before you respond to it.

1. Some people (might) argue that + clause, but + clause

Usage: Introduce a view before responding to it with your own point.
Some people might argue that remote work hurts collaboration, but our data shows the opposite.
Some people argue that tourism damages small towns, but it also creates jobs.

2. It could be argued that + clause

Usage: Present a possible argument impersonally and more formally.
It could be argued that the policy came too late to make a difference.

column2: …, let alone + parallel item
column3:
1. …, let alone + parallel item

Usage: Say that if the first, easier thing is not true, the second, harder thing is even less true. Use it after a negative or limiting statement, and keep the two items parallel.
I barely have time for lunch, let alone the gym.
He can’t boil an egg, let alone cook a full dinner.
Most people haven’t heard of the company, let alone used its products.

column2: Let’s move on to + topic · That’s a separate issue · Let’s not get into + topic · Let’s not go there
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Steer a conversation or meeting.

1. Let’s move on to + topic

Usage: Move the discussion to the next topic.
We’re running short on time, so let’s move on to the budget.

2. That’s a separate issue

Usage: Set aside a point as a different issue.
That’s a separate issue; let’s discuss it after the meeting.

3. Let’s not get into + topic

Usage: Avoid opening a sensitive or time-consuming topic.
Let’s not get into politics at dinner.

4. Let’s not go there

Usage: Casually decline to pursue a subject already understood.
A: What about your ex? B: Let’s not go there.

column2: Sorry to bother you, but + clause · Do you have a minute? · Can I have a word (with you)?
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Approach someone who may be busy.

1. Sorry to bother you, but + clause

Usage: Acknowledge an interruption before making a request.
Sorry to bother you, but do you know where the printer paper is?

2. Do you have a minute?

Usage: Check whether someone is available for a short conversation; Got a sec? is casual.
Do you have a minute? I have a question about the schedule.

3. Can I have a word (with you)?

Usage: Ask for a brief, often private conversation; this can sound serious.
Can I have a word with you after the meeting?

column2: Can I speak to + person? · Can I leave a message? · Could you tell + person + I called? · This is + name + returning your call
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Handle a phone call.

1. Can I speak to + person?

Usage: Ask to speak with the person you want on a call.
Hi, can I speak to Ms. Rivera, please?

2. Can I leave a message?

Usage: Ask to leave information when the person is unavailable.
A: She’s in a meeting right now. B: Can I leave a message?

3. Could you tell + person + I called?

Usage: Ask the intermediary to tell the person you called.
Could you tell him I called? My number is 555-0142.

4. This is + name + returning your call

Usage: Identify yourself and explain that you are calling back.
This is Daniel Chen returning your call from this morning.

column2: feel the same way (about + noun / as + person)
column3:
1. feel the same way (about + noun / as + person)

Usage: Say that you share another person’s opinion or emotional reaction. About introduces the topic; as introduces the person or comparison clause. A comparison clause can also follow directly: the same way he did. This expresses a shared feeling, not merely understanding why someone feels it.
I feel the same way about having fewer meetings; uninterrupted time helps me concentrate.
She felt the same way as I did after the interview.
I’d probably feel the same way he did in that situation.

column2: That way, + clause
column3:
1. That way, + clause

Usage: Refer back to an action or suggestion and explain how it makes a result possible. That way often introduces a consequence with can, will, could, or would; it does not require a hypothetical condition.
Let’s record the decisions. That way, everyone can check what we agreed on.
I’ll take an earlier train. That way, I’ll have time to find the meeting room.
I’d practice with a partner. That way, I could get immediate feedback.

column2: I wouldn't be surprised if + clause
column3:
1. I wouldn't be surprised if + clause

Usage: Say that an outcome seems plausible or expected. A past-form verb after if can describe a future possibility, not just past time. Wouldn’t here softens the expectation; it does not mean the outcome is impossible.
I wouldn’t be surprised if the deadline slipped; we still have several unresolved issues.
I wouldn’t be surprised if she accepted the offer; the role suits her experience.

column2: far from + adjective
column3:
1. far from + adjective

Usage: Say that something is not at all, or not nearly, in a particular state. Far from perfect means there is still a substantial gap from perfection. This is an evaluation, rather than physical distance from a place.
The proposed solution is far from ideal, but it keeps the service running.
It is far from clear whether the new policy will reduce commuting time.

column2: at once · in one go · at a time
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe timing or the size of a batch.

1. at once

Usage: Mean immediately or simultaneously; context distinguishes the two senses.
If the alarm sounds, leave the building at once. — Immediately.
I cannot review three proposals at once. — Simultaneously.

2. in one go

Usage: Complete something in a single continuous effort.
We completed the migration in one go instead of splitting it over several evenings.

3. at a time

Usage: State the quantity processed per occasion or batch.
The tool processes ten files at a time; I review one result at a time.

column2: at work · off work · have a day off
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe work status or a break from work.

1. at work

Usage: Say you are working or at your workplace.
I’m at work right now; I’ll call you after the meeting.

2. off work

Usage: Say you are not working during the stated period, including illness or scheduled leave.
She is off work this week while she recovers from the flu.

3. have a day off

Usage: Describe a day when you do not have to work, rather than leaving your job.
I have a day off on Friday, so I’m planning a short trip.

column2: set an example · lead by example
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Demonstrate behavior that others can follow.

1. set an example

Usage: Demonstrate behavior others might follow, whether good or bad.
My dad sets a good example for our family by taking responsibility for his mistakes.
The manager sets a bad example when he ignores the rules.

2. lead by example

Usage: Lead through your own actions rather than instructions alone.
Good leaders lead by example instead of just telling others what to do.

column2: For what it's worth, + clause
column3:
1. For what it's worth, + clause

Usage: Offer an opinion, observation, or advice without insisting it must influence someone's decision. Common in casual and professional conversation; it does not necessarily imply uncertainty.
For what it's worth, I think you made the right decision.
For what it's worth, I've used both frameworks, and the second was easier to maintain.

column2: Looking back, + clause · In retrospect/hindsight, + clause
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Reflect on past experiences from your current perspective.

1. Looking back, + clause

Usage: Reflect on an earlier experience from your present perspective.
Looking back, I wish I'd spent more time with my family.

2. In retrospect/hindsight, + clause

Usage: Reassess an earlier situation with what you know now; both expressions often overlap. These expressions often overlap rather than making mutually exclusive claims.
In retrospect, we should have tested the architecture more thoroughly.
In hindsight, turning down that offer was the right decision.

column2: can't help + V-ing · find myself + V-ing
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe an action/reaction you find hard to avoid, or one you notice yourself doing.

1. can't help + V-ing

Usage: Describe a reaction/action you find hard to avoid; can't help but + base verb is an alternative.
I can't help worrying about my future.
I can't help but worry about my future.
Whenever I read about AI breakthroughs, I can't help but wonder what jobs will look like in ten years.

2. find myself + V-ing

Usage: Notice yourself doing something, often without deciding to; inability to control it is not required.
I find myself comparing my progress with other people's.

column2: have/has been meaning to + base verb
column3:
1. have/has been meaning to + base verb

Usage: Describe something you have intended to do for some time but have not done yet. Often used for delayed plans, unfinished goals, or something you meant to ask someone.
I've been meaning to improve my spoken English, but other responsibilities keep getting in the way.
I've been meaning to ask you about the new project.
She's been meaning to update her résumé for months.

column2: X applies to Y · The same goes for Y · X holds true for Y
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Use these frames to extend a rule, instruction, or statement to another person or situation.

1. X applies to Y

Usage: Say which cases a rule/instruction covers; compare someone applies X to Y for using X.
This confidentiality rule applies to contractors. The same applies to temporary staff.

2. The same goes for Y

Usage: Conversationally extend the previous point to another case; the same means the point just made.
Keep vocabulary examples short and practical. The same goes for pattern examples.

3. X holds true for Y

Usage: Say a statement remains true for another case.
Regular feedback helps new employees improve. The same holds true for experienced staff.

column2: X is eating me up (inside) · X is weighing on me · X is getting to me
column3:
Shared idea / comparison

Describe how a feeling, thought, responsibility, or situation affects you emotionally.

1. X is eating me up (inside)

Usage: Describe consuming inner distress; eat away at someone is a close alternative for persistent worry. X is the feeling/situation causing the reaction; me is the affected person. Substitute you/him/her/us/them as needed.
The guilt is eating me up inside.
What I said yesterday is eating away at me.

2. X is weighing on me

Usage: Describe an emotional burden, such as worry or responsibility.
The uncertainty about my job is weighing on me.

3. X is getting to me

Usage: Describe something beginning to upset/annoy you; drive someone crazy expresses strong frustration.
The constant interruptions are getting to me.
These repeated delays are driving me crazy.
